concepts.name: Physics and its realm
concepts.statement: Physics is the science concerned with describing the interactions of energy, matter, space, and time, and it is especially interested in what fundamental mechanisms underlie every phenomenon. A surprisingly small and unified set of physical laws explains what we observe.

concepts.name: Model
concepts.statement: A model is a representation of something that is often too difficult or impossible to display directly, such as the planetary model of the atom. It is justified by experiment but accurate only under limited situations, and it lets us picture what we cannot see.

concepts.name: Theory
concepts.statement: To a scientist a theory is a testable explanation for patterns in nature, supported by scientific evidence and verified many times by different groups of researchers. It should describe every aspect of any system within its domain, and an experiment that contradicts it means the theory is thrown out or modified.

concepts.name: Law
concepts.statement: A law uses concise language, often a single equation such as F = ma, to describe a generalized pattern in nature that is supported by scientific evidence and repeated experiments. A law describes a single action, whereas a theory explains a whole group of related phenomena.

concepts.name: Scientific method
concepts.statement: The scientific method is the process scientists follow as they inquire about the world: an observation and a question, some research, a hypothesis, an experiment to test it, and a conclusion drawn from the results. The cornerstone is observation, since science must describe the universe as it is.

concepts.name: Classical physics
concepts.statement: Classical physics is the physics that developed from the Renaissance to the end of the 19th century. It is an excellent approximation when matter moves at less than about 1% of the speed of light, when objects are large enough to see with a microscope, and when only weak gravitational fields such as the Earth’s are involved. That is why most of this text deals with it.

concepts.name: Modern physics
concepts.statement: Modern physics consists of two revolutionary theories, relativity and quantum mechanics, which deal with the very fast and the very small. You need relativity above about 1% of the speed of light or in a strong gravitational field, and quantum mechanics for objects smaller than a microscope can show. Their combination, relativistic quantum mechanics, is the best universally applicable theory we have.

concepts.name: Quantum mechanics
concepts.statement: Quantum mechanics is the study of objects smaller than can be seen with a microscope. Together with relativity it makes up modern physics, and it is needed wherever the objects studied are that small.

concepts.name: Physical quantity
concepts.statement: You define a physical quantity either by saying how to measure it or by saying how to calculate it from other measurements. Methods for measuring them define distance and time, whereas average speed is distance traveled divided by time of travel.

concepts.name: Units
concepts.statement: Measurements of physical quantities are expressed in terms of units, which are standardized values. Without them it would be extremely difficult to express and compare measured values in a meaningful way; the two major systems in use are SI units and English units.

concepts.name: Fundamental units
concepts.statement: The most fundamental physical quantities can be defined only in terms of the procedure used to measure them, and their units are called fundamental units. In this text they are length, mass, time, and electric current, measured in the meter, the kilogram, the second, and the ampere.

concepts.name: Derived units
concepts.statement: All other physical quantities, such as force and electric charge, can be expressed as algebraic combinations of length, mass, time, and current; speed, for example, is length divided by time. The units of such quantities are called derived units.

concepts.name: Metric prefixes
concepts.statement: The metric system is convenient for calculation because its units are categorized by factors of 10, and a standard set of prefixes lets the same unit be used over extremely large ranges of values. Distances in meters suit construction, kilometers suit air travel, and nanometers suit optical design, with no need to invent new units.

concepts.name: Order of magnitude
concepts.statement: The order of magnitude of a value is the power of 10 that sets its scale. The numbers 800 and 450 can both be written as a number times 10², so they are of the same order of magnitude; the diameter of an atom is of order 10⁻¹⁰ m and the diameter of the Sun of order 10⁹ m.

concepts.name: Conversion factor
concepts.statement: A conversion factor is a ratio expressing how many of one unit are equal to another unit, such as 1000 meters in 1 kilometer or 60 seconds in 1 minute. Multiplying by the factor that cancels the unwanted unit leaves the desired unit in its place.

concepts.name: Converting units
concepts.statement: To convert, list the units you have and the units you want, find the conversion factor between them, and multiply so that the units cancel. If the factor is written upside down the units do not cancel, so checking the units of the answer is part of the method.

concepts.name: SI units
concepts.statement: SI units, also known as the metric system, are the international system of units that scientists in most countries have agreed to use, named for the French Système International. This text uses them almost exclusively.

concepts.name: English units
concepts.statement: English units, also known as the customary or imperial system, are the units historically used in nations once ruled by the British Empire and still widely used in the United States, such as feet, gallons, and pounds.

concepts.name: Second
concepts.statement: The second is the SI unit of time. It is defined as the time required for 9,192,631,770 vibrations of the cesium atom.

concepts.name: Meter
concepts.statement: The meter is the SI unit of length. It is defined as the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second.

concepts.name: Kilogram
concepts.statement: The kilogram is the SI unit of mass. It was once defined as the mass of a platinum-iridium cylinder kept near Paris, and since 2019 it is defined in terms of the second, the meter, and Planck's constant.

concepts.name: Length
concepts.statement: Length is one of the fundamental physical quantities, the distance between two points. Its SI unit is the meter.

concepts.name: Accuracy
concepts.statement: Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the correct value for that measurement. Three measurements of 11.1, 11.2 and 10.9 inches of paper that is 11.0 inches long are accurate; a measurement of 12 inches is not.

concepts.name: Precision
concepts.statement: The precision of a measurement system refers to how close the agreement is between repeated measurements made under the same conditions, that is, to the spread of the measured values. A measuring system can be accurate but not precise, or precise but not accurate.

concepts.name: Uncertainty
concepts.statement: Uncertainty is a quantitative measure of how much your measured values deviate from a standard or expected value, a disclaimer on the number: 45,000 miles plus or minus 500. All measurements contain some uncertainty, from the measuring device, the skill of the person, irregularities in the object, and anything else that affects the outcome.

concepts.name: Percent uncertainty
concepts.statement: One way to express uncertainty is as a percent of the measured value: the uncertainty divided by the value, times 100%. A bag of apples weighed at 5.1 lb with an uncertainty of 0.4 lb has a percent uncertainty of 8%.

concepts.name: Method of adding percents
concepts.statement: There is an uncertainty in anything calculated from measured quantities. When the measurements going in have small uncertainties, the percent uncertainty in a quantity calculated by multiplication or division is the sum of the percent uncertainties in the items used to make the calculation: a floor 4.00 m by 3.00 m, known to 2% and 1%, has an area of 12.0 m² known to 3%.

concepts.name: Significant figures
concepts.statement: When we express measured values we can list only as many digits as the measuring tool gave us, and the last digit written down is the first digit with some uncertainty. Counting the digits from the first measured digit on the left through the last on the right gives the number of significant figures, and zeros are significant except when they serve only as placekeepers.

concepts.name: Significant figures in multiplication and division
concepts.statement: For multiplication and division, the result should have the same number of significant figures as the quantity having the least significant figures entering into the calculation. A circle whose radius is known to two figures has an area known to two figures, even though π is good to at least eight.

concepts.name: Significant figures in addition and subtraction
concepts.statement: For addition and subtraction, the answer can contain no more decimal places than the least precise measurement. Potatoes weighed on scales good to 0.01 kg, 0.001 kg and 0.1 kg add up to a mass that can be given only to the tenth of a kilogram.

concepts.name: Area
concepts.statement: Area is the size of a surface, found for a rectangle as its length times its width. Its SI unit is the square meter.

concepts.name: Making an approximation
concepts.statement: Physicists, other scientists and engineers often need approximations or “guesstimates” for a quantity, based on formulae whose inputs are known only to limited accuracy. Scaling up from a known quantity, such as the height of a person, gives an estimate good to an order of magnitude, which is enough to rule out unrealistic numbers and to guide an approach.

concepts.name: Volume
concepts.statement: Volume is the space an object occupies, found for a box as its length times its width times its height. Its SI unit is the cubic meter.

concepts.name: Approximation
concepts.statement: An approximation is an estimated value based on prior experience and reasoning.

concepts.name: Reference frame
concepts.statement: A reference frame is what a position is given relative to, such as the Earth, a whiteboard, or the cabin of an airplane. Choosing the reference frame is the first step in describing any motion.

concepts.name: Position
concepts.statement: The position of an object is where it is at a particular time, given as a coordinate with a sign on the chosen axis. Every other quantity in one-dimensional kinematics is built from positions and times.

concepts.name: Displacement
concepts.statement: Displacement is the change in position, that is, the final position minus the initial position. It has a sign, and the sign gives the direction. In kinematics we nearly always deal with displacement rather than with the path taken.

concepts.name: Distance
concepts.statement: Distance is the magnitude of displacement between two positions, so it has no sign and no direction. It is not the same as distance traveled, the total length of the path.

concepts.name: Distance traveled
concepts.statement: Distance traveled is the total length of the path, and it can be much greater than the magnitude of the displacement. For example, a professor who paces 150 m during a lecture may end up only 2.0 m from where she started.

concepts.name: Kinematics
concepts.statement: Kinematics is the study of motion without considering its causes. In one- and two-dimensional kinematics we study only the motion of an object, without worrying about what forces cause or change it.

concepts.name: Average velocity
concepts.statement: Average velocity is displacement divided by the time of travel. It is a vector because displacement is a vector, so it has a direction, and its sign tells which way the object moved: an airplane passenger who takes 5 s to move −4 m toward the rear of the plane has an average velocity of −0.8 m/s. The average velocity says nothing about what happened between the starting point and the ending point.

forms.condition: the starting time t_0 taken to be zero

concepts.name: Acceleration
concepts.statement: Acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes, and the greater the acceleration, the greater the change in velocity over a given time. Because velocity is a vector, a change in velocity can be a change in magnitude or a change in direction, so a car turning a corner at constant speed is accelerating. Acceleration is a vector in the same direction as the change in velocity, and its SI unit is meters per second squared, which means by how many meters per second the velocity changes every second.

concepts.name: Constant-acceleration model
concepts.statement: When acceleration is constant, the average acceleration equals the acceleration at every instant, and the average velocity is simply the midpoint of the initial and final velocities. The kinematic equations all follow from this assumption, and you can describe many real motions in pieces within which it holds.

concepts.name: Displacement from average velocity
concepts.statement: Displacement equals the average velocity multiplied by the elapsed time. This is the definition of average velocity rearranged, so it holds whether or not the acceleration is constant.

concepts.name: Average velocity under constant acceleration
concepts.statement: When acceleration is constant, velocity changes at a steady rate, so the average velocity is the midpoint of the initial and final velocities. This step turns the definition of average velocity into the equations for displacement.

forms.condition: constant acceleration

concepts.name: Velocity from acceleration and time
concepts.statement: The final velocity depends on both the size of the acceleration and the time over which it acts. A modest acceleration that lasts a long time can produce a very large velocity.

forms.condition: constant acceleration

concepts.name: Displacement under constant acceleration
concepts.statement: Under constant acceleration, the displacement grows with the square of the elapsed time. For example, a dragster starting from rest covers only one quarter of the track in the first half of its run.

forms.latex: x = x_0 + v_0 t + \tfrac12 a t^2
forms.condition: constant acceleration

concepts.name: Velocity from displacement
concepts.statement: This equation relates velocity to displacement without involving time. Because the stopping distance of a car grows with the square of its speed, halving the speed reduces the stopping distance to one quarter.

forms.condition: constant acceleration

concepts.name: Choosing a kinematic equation
concepts.statement: To solve a problem, first list the quantities you know and the quantity you want to find, and then choose the equation in which the quantity you want is the only unknown.

concepts.name: Interpreting the solution physically
concepts.statement: The algebra can give two roots, a negative time, or a square root with two signs, but only one of these describes the motion. Deciding which solution is physically reasonable is part of solving the problem.

concepts.name: Instantaneous velocity
concepts.statement: The smaller the time intervals you consider in a motion, the more detailed the information. Carried to its logical conclusion, this leaves an infinitesimally small interval over which the average velocity becomes the instantaneous velocity, the velocity at a specific instant. A car’s speedometer shows the magnitude of the car’s instantaneous velocity. Finding it precisely can involve taking a limit, though in many cases you can find precise values without calculus.

concepts.name: Acceleration due to gravity
concepts.statement: The acceleration of a free-falling object is the acceleration due to gravity, so important that its magnitude has its own symbol, $\kg$, with the average value 9.80 m/s² on Earth. It points downward, toward the center of Earth, and in fact its direction defines what we call vertical. Whether the acceleration $\ka$ in the kinematic equations is $+\kg$ or $-\kg$ depends on your coordinate system: if up is positive, then $\ka = -\kg$.

forms.condition: the average value on Earth; g varies from 9.78 to 9.83 m/s² with latitude, altitude and local geology

concepts.name: Vector
concepts.statement: A vector is any quantity with both magnitude and direction, such as a displacement, a velocity of 90 km/h east, or a force of 500 newtons straight down. In one-dimensional motion its direction is given simply by a plus or minus sign, and on paper it is drawn as an arrow whose length is proportional to its magnitude and which points in the same direction as the vector.

concepts.name: Scalar
concepts.statement: A scalar is any quantity that has a magnitude but no direction. A temperature of 20 ºC, the 250 kilocalories in a candy bar, a 90 km/h speed limit and a distance of 2.0 m are all scalars, and a scalar can be negative, in which case the minus sign indicates a point on a scale rather than a direction. Scalars are never represented by arrows.

concepts.name: Assigning a coordinate system
concepts.statement: To describe the direction of a vector you must designate a coordinate system within the reference frame, which for one-dimensional motion is a single coordinate line. Motion to the right or upward is usually taken as positive, but it can be more convenient to make downward positive for a falling object or left positive for runners heading left. It does not matter as long as the system is clear and consistent, and once you assign a positive direction and start solving a problem, you cannot change it.

concepts.name: Time
concepts.statement: In physics the definition of time is simple: time is change, or the interval over which change occurs. Every measurement of time involves measuring a change in some physical quantity, whether a number on a digital clock, a heartbeat or the position of the Sun in the sky, and the amount of change is calibrated by comparison with a standard such as the second.

concepts.name: Elapsed time
concepts.statement: We usually want the elapsed time for a particular motion: note the time at the beginning and the end of the motion and subtract the two. Life is simpler if the beginning time is zero, as with a stopwatch, so in this text motion starts at $\kto = 0$ and the symbol $\kt$ stands for elapsed time unless stated otherwise.

forms.latex: \Delta t = t,\quad \Delta x = x - x_0,\quad \Delta v = v - v_0

concepts.name: Instantaneous speed
concepts.statement: Instantaneous speed is the magnitude of the instantaneous velocity, so it is a scalar with no direction. A passenger with an instantaneous velocity of −3.0 m/s toward the rear of the plane has an instantaneous speed of 3.0 m/s, and a shopper moving at 40 km/h due north has an instantaneous speed of 40 km/h.

concepts.name: Average speed
concepts.statement: Average speed is the distance traveled divided by the elapsed time. Because the distance traveled can be greater than the magnitude of the displacement, the average speed can be greater than the magnitude of the average velocity: a half-hour drive to a store and back that puts 6 km on the odometer has an average speed of 12 km/h and an average velocity of zero. Average speed is therefore not simply the magnitude of average velocity.

concepts.name: Average acceleration
concepts.statement: Average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time over which it changes, that is, the final velocity minus the initial velocity over the elapsed time. Its sign follows the sign of the change in velocity rather than the direction of motion: a train slowing from a negative velocity to rest has a positive average acceleration.

concepts.name: Instantaneous acceleration
concepts.statement: Instantaneous acceleration is the acceleration at a specific instant in time, found over an infinitesimally small interval, as for instantaneous velocity. With only algebra, you choose an average acceleration that represents the motion. When the acceleration varies only slightly, the average over the whole interval will do; when it varies greatly, split the motion into smaller time intervals and choose an average acceleration for each.

concepts.name: Deceleration
concepts.statement: Although acceleration is in the direction of the change in velocity, it is not always in the direction of motion. When an object slows down, its acceleration is opposite to the direction of its motion, and this is called deceleration. Deceleration always reduces speed.

concepts.name: Sign of the acceleration
concepts.statement: Negative acceleration is acceleration in the negative direction of the chosen coordinate system, and it may or may not be a deceleration: a negative acceleration will increase a negative velocity, and a positive acceleration slows a train that is moving to the left. If the acceleration has the same sign as the velocity, the object is speeding up, and if it has the opposite sign, the object is slowing down.

concepts.name: Calculating an average acceleration
concepts.statement: To find an average acceleration, draw a sketch and assign a coordinate system, identify the initial and final velocities with their signs and the elapsed time, find the change in velocity as the final velocity minus the initial velocity, and divide by the time. When the units are mixed, as with a velocity in kilometers per hour and a time in seconds, convert everything into meters and seconds before dividing.

concepts.name: Problem-solving steps
concepts.statement: No simple step-by-step method works for every problem, but six general procedures make problem solving easier and more meaningful. Examine the situation to find the physical principles involved, and draw a sketch with a positive direction marked on it. List what is given or can be inferred, the knowns. Identify exactly what you must determine, the unknowns. Find an equation or set of equations that contains only one unknown. Substitute the knowns with their units and obtain a numerical solution complete with units. Check whether the answer is reasonable. You will often take the steps in a different order or several at once, and with practice they become almost automatic.

concepts.name: Recognizing an unreasonable result
concepts.statement: Physics must describe nature accurately, and some problems have results that are unreasonable because one premise is unreasonable or because the premises are inconsistent with one another. A runner who accelerates at 0.40 m/s² for 100 s would reach 40 m/s, about 89 mph, which is four times faster than a person can run. To check a result, solve the problem in the usual way, ask whether the answer is too large or too small or has the wrong sign or the wrong units, and if it is unreasonable look for the premise that caused it, here the time of 100 s. Checking builds intuition about nature as well as uncovering errors.

forms.condition: the runner who accelerates at 0.40 m/s² for 100 s

concepts.name: Free fall
concepts.statement: The most remarkable fact about falling objects is that, if air resistance and friction are negligible, all objects at a given location fall toward the center of Earth with the same constant acceleration, independent of their mass, as a hammer and a feather did together on the Moon. An object falling without air resistance or friction is in free fall, and that assumption opens a broad class of situations to the kinematic equations.

concepts.name: Kinematic equations for free fall
concepts.statement: For straight up and down motion with no air resistance, the motion is one-dimensional with a constant acceleration of magnitude $\kg$, so the kinematic equations apply with $\ky$ for the vertical position and $\ka = -\kg$ when up is positive: $\kv = \kvo - \kg\kt$, $\ky = \kyo + \kvo\kt - \tfrac{1}{2}\kg\kt^2$ and $\kv^2 = \kvo^2 - 2\kg(\ky - \kyo)$. The same equations describe a rock thrown up, a rock thrown down and an object simply dropped; only the initial velocity differs.

forms.latex: y = y_0 + v_0 t - \tfrac12 g t^2
forms.condition: free fall with up taken as positive, so that a = −g
free fall with up taken as positive, so that a = −g
free fall with up taken as positive, so that a = −g

concepts.name: Free fall at the highest point
concepts.statement: A rock thrown upward slows, stops for an instant at its highest point and falls back. At that point its velocity is zero, but its acceleration is still −9.80 m/s², as it is for the whole trip, while the rock is moving up and while it is moving down. Knowing that $\kv = 0$ at the top is what lets us find the maximum height from the initial velocity, or the initial velocity from the height reached.

concepts.name: Speed of a falling object
concepts.statement: Because only the acceleration due to gravity is acting, the speed of a falling object depends only on its initial speed and its vertical position relative to the starting point, not on whether it was thrown up or down. A rock thrown up at 13.0 m/s passes its starting point again at −13.0 m/s, and 5.10 m below it is moving at −16.4 m/s, exactly the velocity it has when thrown straight down at 13.0 m/s. At any height on the way up and at the same height on the way down the speeds are equal and the velocities opposite.

concepts.name: Measuring the acceleration due to gravity
concepts.statement: You can find the precise acceleration due to gravity at a place in an introductory laboratory: drop an object for which air resistance is negligible and measure the time it takes to fall a known distance. With $\kvo = 0$, the position equation gives $\ka = 2(\ky - \kyo)/\kt^2$, so a fall of 1.0000 m in 0.45173 s gives $\kg = 9.8010$ m/s², more precise than the average value because the data are precise. Two velocities at two heights serve as well, through $\kv^2 = \kvo^2 - 2\kg(\ky - \kyo)$.

forms.condition: an object dropped from rest, v_0 = 0

concepts.name: Slope and intercept
concepts.statement: When two physical quantities are plotted against one another, the horizontal axis is usually the independent variable and the vertical axis the dependent variable, and a straight-line graph has the general form $y = mx + b$. Here $m$ is the slope, the rise divided by the run, and $b$ is the $y$-intercept, the point at which the line crosses the vertical axis. Reading a slope and an intercept off a graph of motion is how the motion equations appear in graphical form.

concepts.name: Slope of a position graph
concepts.statement: On a graph of position against time the rise is a change in position and the run is a change in time, so the slope is $\kdx / \kdt$, the velocity. A straight line means constant velocity, and its slope is the average velocity between any two points; a curve means the velocity is changing, and its steepness at each point is the velocity there. The intercept is the position at time zero, so the graph gives $\kx = \kxo + \kvb\kt$.

forms.condition: read from a straight-line graph of position against time, whose slope is v̄ and whose intercept is x_0

concepts.name: Slope of a velocity graph
concepts.statement: On a graph of velocity against time the rise is a change in velocity and the run is a change in time, so the slope is $\kdv / \kdt$, the acceleration. A straight line means the acceleration is constant, and with the intercept $\kvo$ the graph gives $\kv = \kvo + \ka\kt$, the same relationship that was derived algebraically. When the line curves, the acceleration is changing, and it can be read from the slope at each point.

forms.condition: read from a straight-line graph of velocity against time, whose slope is a and whose intercept is v_0

concepts.name: Finding a slope from a tangent
concepts.statement: The slope of a curve at a point is equal to the slope of a straight line tangent to the curve at that point. To find it, draw the tangent, read the coordinates of two widely separated points on it, and divide the change in the vertical quantity by the change in time; any error in reading data from the graph is proportionally smaller when the interval is larger. Done at every point of a position graph this gives the velocity graph, and done on the velocity graph it gives the acceleration.

concepts.name: Deriving one motion graph from another
concepts.statement: A graph of position against time can be used to generate a graph of velocity against time, and a graph of velocity against time a graph of acceleration against time, by finding the slope of the graph at every point. Where a graph is linear the slope is the same everywhere and the derived graph is flat; where it bends, the derived graph rises or falls. The reverse also holds: a flat velocity graph means a straight position graph, and a sloping one means a curve.

concepts.name: Reading a motion graph
concepts.statement: A graph, like a picture, is worth a thousand words, and a graph of motion can be read for the motion itself: where a position graph is steepest the velocity is greatest, where it is flat the velocity is zero, and where it falls the velocity is negative; where a velocity graph is flat the acceleration is zero, and where it falls the object is slowing. A ship whose velocity graph is level, then drops steeply, then drops more gently moves at constant velocity, decelerates hard, then decelerates gently until it stops.

concepts.name: Independent variable
concepts.statement: The independent variable is the quantity plotted on the horizontal axis of a graph, the one other quantities depend upon. Time is usually an independent variable.

concepts.name: Dependent variable
concepts.statement: The dependent variable is the quantity plotted on the vertical axis of a graph, which depends on the independent variable, as position depends on time.

concepts.name: Slope of a graph
concepts.statement: The slope of a graph is the difference in the vertical value, the rise, divided by the difference in the horizontal value, the run.

concepts.name: y-intercept
concepts.statement: The y-intercept is the value of the dependent variable where a graph crosses the vertical axis, that is, its value when the independent variable is zero.

concepts.name: Adding perpendicular displacements
concepts.statement: A walk of 9 blocks east followed by 5 blocks north covers 14 blocks, but the straight-line distance between the two points is only 10.3 blocks. The two legs of the trip and the straight-line path form a right triangle, and the Pythagorean theorem gives the hypotenuse. This is one example of a general characteristic of vectors: the total displacement is the sum of its perpendicular parts, and the theorem gives its magnitude. You cannot add vectors that are not perpendicular this way.

forms.condition: a right triangle with legs a and b and hypotenuse c

concepts.name: Components of a vector
concepts.statement: In two-dimensional motion, three vectors represent the path of an object: one for the straight-line path between the initial and final points, one for the horizontal component of the motion, and one for the vertical component. The horizontal and vertical components add together to give the straight-line path, and only the motion in its own direction affects each one.

forms.condition: as vectors; the magnitudes A_x + A_y ≠ A

concepts.name: Independence of perpendicular motions
concepts.statement: The horizontal and vertical components of two-dimensional motion are independent of each other: motion in the horizontal direction does not affect motion in the vertical direction, and vice versa. Drop one ball from rest and throw another horizontally at the same instant from the same height. At every flash of a stroboscope they share the same vertical position, while the thrown ball covers the same horizontal distance between flashes because nothing accelerates it horizontally. This is the key to projectile motion, which you resolve into motions along perpendicular directions.

concepts.name: Vector in two dimensions
concepts.statement: In two dimensions, an angle gives the direction of a vector relative to a reference frame. An arrow represents the vector, with a length proportional to its magnitude, its tail at the starting point and its head at the pointed end. This text writes a vector in boldface, its magnitude in italics and its direction as an angle, such as the total displacement $\mathbf{D}$ of 10.3 blocks at 29.1º north of east.

concepts.name: Resultant vector
concepts.statement: The resultant is the sum of two or more vectors, drawn from the tail of the first vector to the head of the last. Its magnitude is at most the sum of the magnitudes, when the vectors point the same way, and at least their difference, so two nonzero vectors add to zero only when they have equal magnitudes and opposite directions.

concepts.name: Adding vectors head to tail
concepts.statement: To add vectors graphically, draw the first as an arrow using a ruler and protractor. Place the tail of the second vector at the head of the first, and continue for every vector you add. Then draw the resultant from the tail of the first vector to the head of the last, and measure its length with a ruler and its angle with a protractor. The method works for any number of vectors, and only the precision of the drawing and of the measuring tools limits its accuracy.

concepts.name: Commutativity of vector addition
concepts.statement: The resultant is independent of the order in which the vectors are added: adding the same displacements in a different order ends at the same point. This is true in every case and is an important characteristic of vectors, just as you get the same result whether you add 2 + 3 or 3 + 2.

concepts.name: Vector subtraction
concepts.statement: The negative of a vector has the same magnitude but the opposite direction, and subtracting a vector is defined to be adding its negative. A sailor who follows the second leg of her directions in the opposite direction arrives at $\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{B}$ instead of at $\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B}$, a very different place from the dock, and the graphical method of subtraction is the head-to-tail method with $-\mathbf{B}$ in place of $\mathbf{B}$.

concepts.name: Multiplying a vector by a scalar
concepts.statement: When you multiply a vector by a scalar $c$, its magnitude becomes the absolute value of $c$ times the original magnitude. If $c$ is positive the direction does not change, and if $c$ is negative the direction reverses. Walking three times as far on a leg of 27.5 m at 66.0º north of east means walking 82.5 m in the same direction, and division is multiplication by a scalar between 0 and 1.

concepts.name: Resolving a vector into components
concepts.statement: Often we need the opposite of addition: to take a single vector and find what other vectors add together to produce it, usually its components along perpendicular axes such as north and east. Given a total displacement of 10.3 blocks in a direction 29.0º north of east, you can find how many blocks east and north the walk covered, graphically with a ruler and protractor or analytically with the right triangle the components form.

concepts.name: Angle
concepts.statement: An angle measures the turn between two directions. In two dimensions an angle, such as 29.1º north of east, gives the direction of a vector relative to a reference axis.

concepts.name: Head of a vector
concepts.statement: The head of a vector is its end point, the location of the tip of its arrowhead, also called the tip.

concepts.name: Tail of a vector
concepts.statement: The tail of a vector is its start point, at the opposite end of the arrow from the head.

concepts.name: Magnitude of a vector
concepts.statement: The magnitude of a vector is its length or size, and it is a scalar quantity.

concepts.name: Direction of a vector
concepts.statement: The direction of a vector is its orientation in space, given in two dimensions by an angle relative to a reference axis.

concepts.name: Head-to-tail method
concepts.statement: The head-to-tail method is a method of adding vectors in which the tail of each vector is placed at the head of the previous vector.

concepts.name: Vector addition
concepts.statement: Vector addition is the set of rules that apply to adding vectors together, giving their resultant.

concepts.name: Components from magnitude and direction
concepts.statement: If you know a vector by its magnitude $\kA$ and its angle $\theta$ from the $x$-axis, its components along the axes are the two legs of a right triangle, $\kAx = \kA\cos\theta$ and $\kAy = \kA\sin\theta$. The component vectors add to the vector, but their magnitudes do not add to its magnitude: 3 m east and 4 m north make 5 m, not 7 m, and no component can be greater than the magnitude of the vector itself.

concepts.name: Magnitude and direction from components
concepts.statement: If you know the perpendicular components of a vector, you can find the vector analytically. Its magnitude is $\sqrt{\kAx^2 + \kAy^2}$, the Pythagorean theorem for the right triangle the components form, and its direction relative to the $x$-axis is $\tan^{-1}(\kAy / \kAx)$. For components of 9 and 5 blocks this gives 10.3 blocks at 29.1º, as in the walk in the city.

concepts.name: Adding vectors by components
concepts.statement: To add vectors analytically, identify the $x$- and $y$-axes and find the components of each vector with $\kAx = \kA\cos\theta$ and $\kAy = \kA\sin\theta$. Add the components along each axis to get $\kRx = \kAx + \kBx$ and $\kRy = \kAy + \kBy$. Then find the magnitude $\kR = \sqrt{\kRx^2 + \kRy^2}$ and the direction $\theta = \tan^{-1}(\kRy / \kRx)$ of the resultant. The method works because components along the same axis add like ordinary numbers. Subtraction is identical, since the components of $-\mathbf{B}$ are the negatives of the components of $\mathbf{B}$. Analytical methods are more concise, accurate and precise than graphical ones, which are only as accurate as the drawing.

forms.condition: the resultant of A − B

concepts.name: Analytical method
concepts.statement: The analytical method determines the magnitude and direction of a resultant vector using the Pythagorean theorem and trigonometric identities.

concepts.name: Projectile motion
concepts.statement: Projectile motion is the motion of an object thrown or projected into the air, subject only to the acceleration of gravity; the object is a projectile and its path is its trajectory. Because gravity is vertical, the horizontal and vertical motions are independent. The key is to break the curved path into a horizontal motion with no acceleration and a vertical motion with $\kay = -\kg$. With air resistance negligible, the trajectory is a parabola.

concepts.name: Horizontal motion of a projectile
concepts.statement: With air resistance negligible there is no acceleration along the horizontal axis, so the horizontal component of the velocity stays at its initial value $\kvx = \kvo\cos\theta_0$ and the horizontal displacement is simply $\kvx\kt$. The horizontal motion continues at this constant velocity for as long as the vertical motion keeps the projectile in the air.

forms.condition: horizontal motion of a projectile, a_x = 0
horizontal motion of a projectile, a_x = 0

concepts.name: Vertical motion of a projectile
concepts.statement: Along the vertical axis a projectile is in free fall with the initial vertical velocity $\kvoy = \kvo\sin\theta_0$, so the kinematic equations apply with $\kay = -\kg$ when up is positive: $\kvy = \kvoy - \kg\kt$, $\ky = \kyo + \kvoy\kt - \tfrac{1}{2}\kg\kt^2$ and $\kvy^2 = \kvoy^2 - 2\kg(\ky - \kyo)$. The vertical velocity decreases as the object rises, is zero at the highest point and grows again downward as it falls. The time a projectile is in the air is governed by its vertical motion alone, and time is the one variable the two motions share.

forms.condition: projectile motion with negligible air resistance and up taken as positive, so that a_y = −g
projectile motion with negligible air resistance and up taken as positive, so that a_y = −g
projectile motion with negligible air resistance and up taken as positive, so that a_y = −g
projectile motion with negligible air resistance and up taken as positive, so that a_y = −g

concepts.name: Solving a projectile problem
concepts.statement: To analyze projectile motion, resolve the initial velocity into components along the horizontal and vertical axes. Treat the motion as two independent one-dimensional motions linked only by the time, and solve for the unknowns in each. When you want the total displacement or velocity, recombine the components with $\ks = \sqrt{\kx^2 + \ky^2}$ and $\kv = \sqrt{\kvx^2 + \kvy^2}$ and the angles $\theta = \tan^{-1}(\ky / \kx)$ and $\theta_v = \tan^{-1}(\kvy / \kvx)$. The vertical equation is often a quadratic in the time; discard the root that describes an event before the launch.

concepts.name: Maximum height of a projectile
concepts.statement: The highest point in any trajectory, called the apex, is reached when the vertical velocity is zero, and solving $\kvy^2 = \kvoy^2 - 2\kg\ky$ at that point gives the maximum height $\kh = \kvoy^2 / 2\kg$. It depends only on the vertical component of the initial velocity, so any projectile with a 67.6 m/s initial vertical component of velocity rises 233 m, whatever its horizontal velocity.

forms.condition: negligible air resistance

concepts.name: Range of a projectile
concepts.statement: On level ground, the range is the horizontal distance a projectile travels, $\kR = \kvo^2\sin 2\theta_0 / \kg$ when air resistance is negligible. The greater the initial speed, the greater the range. For a given speed the maximum range comes at 45º, and every other angle has a complement that gives the same range with a different maximum height. The range also depends on $\kg$, which is why a golf ball travels so far on the Moon. When the range is large, the Earth curves away beneath the projectile, until at a great enough speed it goes into orbit.

forms.condition: level ground and negligible air resistance

concepts.name: Motion
concepts.statement: Motion is the displacement of an object as a function of time.

concepts.name: Air resistance
concepts.statement: Air resistance is a frictional force that slows the motion of objects as they travel through the air. When solving basic physics problems, air resistance is assumed to be zero.

concepts.name: Projectile
concepts.statement: A projectile is an object that travels through the air and experiences only acceleration due to gravity.

concepts.name: Trajectory
concepts.statement: The trajectory is the path of a projectile through the air.

concepts.name: Relative velocity
concepts.statement: A velocity is always relative to some reference frame. A boat on a river or a plane in a crosswind has a velocity relative to the medium, while the medium has a velocity relative to an observer on solid ground. The object’s velocity relative to the observer is the vector sum of the two, so the boat moves diagonally to the shore and the plane does not move in the direction it points. In one-dimensional motion, velocities add like ordinary numbers: a ball driven at 30 m/s by a player running at 5 m/s moves at 35 m/s relative to the goalkeeper.

concepts.name: Adding velocities
concepts.statement: Velocity is a vector, so the rules of vector addition apply to it. The components are $\kvx = \kv\cos\theta$ and $\kvy = \kv\sin\theta$, and $\kv = \sqrt{\kvx^2 + \kvy^2}$ and $\theta = \tan^{-1}(\kvy / \kvx)$ give back the magnitude and direction. A coordinate system with one axis parallel to one of the velocities makes the mathematics easier, as for a boat heading straight across a river. When you know the total velocity, the same components give the unknown velocity of a wind or a current.

forms.condition: the plane of Example 3.7 heading due north, with the x-axis due east and the y-axis due north

concepts.name: Classical relativity
concepts.statement: Relativity is the study of how observers moving relative to each other measure the same phenomenon. Classical relativity, which Galileo and Newton first discussed correctly, holds below about 1% of the speed of light. Binoculars dropped from the mast of a moving ship fall straight down to an observer on the ship and along a curved path to an observer on shore, yet both see them strike the deck at the base of the mast. A coin dropped in an airliner falls at 5.42 m/s to the passenger and at 260.06 m/s, almost horizontally, to an observer on the ground. For a correct description, always state the velocities relative to the observer.

concepts.name: Velocity
concepts.statement: Velocity is speed in a given direction.

concepts.name: Kinetic friction
concepts.statement: When two surfaces in contact are moving relative to one another, the friction between them is called kinetic friction. It is the force that slows a hockey puck sliding on ice, and it is the one that behaves simply enough to be written as a single product.

concepts.name: Static friction
concepts.statement: When the surfaces are not moving relative to one another, static friction can act between them. It is a responsive force, growing to be equal and opposite to whatever you push with, up to a limit, which is why a heavy crate can be pushed harder and harder and still not move.

concepts.name: Coefficient of friction
concepts.statement: The coefficient of friction is the number that carries what the two materials are. It has no units, its magnitude is usually between 0 and 1.0, and for the same pair of surfaces the kinetic coefficient is smaller than the static one, which is why a crate is easier to keep moving than it was to start.

concepts.name: Magnitude of static friction
concepts.statement: Static friction can take any magnitude from zero up to a maximum, and the maximum is the coefficient of static friction times the normal force. The friction is whatever it needs to be to keep the surfaces at rest, until the applied force passes that maximum and the object moves.

forms.condition: the two systems are in contact and are not moving relative to one another
static friction has reached its maximum and the object is about to move

concepts.name: Magnitude of kinetic friction
concepts.statement: Once an object is moving, the friction on it is the coefficient of kinetic friction times the normal force. Friction that obeys this rule is said to behave simply, and its magnitude does not depend on the area in contact or, to a good approximation, on the speed.

forms.condition: the two systems are moving relative to one another and friction behaves simply

concepts.name: Friction on a slope
concepts.statement: On a slope, the normal force is not the whole weight but only its component perpendicular to the surface, so the kinetic friction is the coefficient times mg cos θ. An object that slides down the slope at constant speed therefore has a coefficient of kinetic friction equal to tan θ.

forms.condition: an object slides down a slope that makes an angle θ with the horizontal
the object slides down the slope at a constant velocity, so that the acceleration is zero

concepts.name: Atomic origin of friction
concepts.statement: Friction is proportional to the normal force but not to the total area in contact, and only a close look at the surfaces explains why. They touch at their high spots, the actual area of contact grows as they press together, and they warm because the rubbing sets their atomic lattices vibrating.

concepts.name: Drag force equation
concepts.statement: For a large object that is not moving too slowly, the drag force is proportional to the square of the speed, and the constant in front gathers the drag coefficient, the area facing the fluid and the density of the fluid. Doubling the speed of a car therefore multiplies the drag on it by about four.

forms.condition: a large object such as a bicyclist, a car or a baseball, not moving too slowly
a large object moving fast enough through a fluid

concepts.name: Drag coefficient
concepts.statement: The drag coefficient is the dimensionless number that carries the shape of the object. It is determined empirically, usually in a wind tunnel, and it is why aerodynamic shaping matters: a Toyota Camry has a coefficient of 0.28 and a Hummer H2 one of 0.64, and a skydiver's own coefficient changes with the position they fall in.

concepts.name: Terminal velocity
concepts.statement: A falling body speeds up until the drag force has grown equal to its weight. The net force is then zero, so by Newton's second law the acceleration is zero and the speed stays where it is. Terminal velocity is what free fall becomes once the air is no longer neglected.

forms.condition: at the terminal velocity

concepts.name: Magnitude of terminal velocity
concepts.statement: Setting the drag force equal to the weight and solving for the speed gives the terminal velocity in terms of the mass, the drag coefficient, the area facing the fluid and the density of the fluid. It is why a 75 kg skydiver falls at about 350 km/h head first and at about 200 km/h spread eagle.

forms.condition: the drag force has grown equal to the weight

concepts.name: Stokes’ law
concepts.statement: When the object is very small, is going very slowly, or is in a medium denser than air, the drag is proportional to the speed itself rather than to its square, and the force is 6πrηv. This is the drag that a bacterium, a grain of pollen or a dust particle feels.

forms.condition: the object is very small, is going very slowly, or is in a medium denser than air
a small sphere moving slowly in a fluid

concepts.name: Size and terminal velocity
concepts.statement: Divide an animal's length, breadth and height each by ten and its weight falls to a thousandth while its surface falls only to a hundredth, so the smaller animal meets relatively ten times the resistance. That is why a squirrel can fall from a tree and walk away and a person cannot.

concepts.name: Deformation
concepts.statement: A deformation is a change in shape caused by a force. Even very small forces cause some deformation, and small ones show two things: the object returns to its original shape when the force goes, and the size of the deformation is proportional to the force.

concepts.name: Elastic region and tensile strength
concepts.statement: The proportionality between force and deformation holds only so far. Past the straight part of the graph the deformation is still elastic, past that the object is permanently deformed, and at the tensile strength it fractures. Bones are brittle, so their elastic region is small and the fracture abrupt.

concepts.name: Young’s modulus
concepts.statement: The change in length of a wire or rod is proportional to the force and to the original length and inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area, and the constant that carries the substance is Young's modulus. A long guitar string stretches more than a short one, and a thick one stretches less than a thin one.

forms.condition: a force applied parallel to the length of a wire or rod, stretching or compressing it
the object is a uniform rod or wire of cross-sectional area A and length L₀

concepts.name: Stress
concepts.statement: The ratio of force to area is defined as stress, measured in newtons per square meter. Writing the force in this way is what lets one number describe a material rather than one particular rod, since the same force on a thinner wire is a larger stress.

concepts.name: Strain
concepts.statement: The ratio of the change in length to the original length is defined as strain, and it is a unitless quantity. Most materials behave elastically while the strain is less than about 0.1%, and a support tendon such as the ones in your leg can change its length by as much as ten percent.

concepts.name: Stress and strain
concepts.statement: Rearranged, the equation for the change in length says that the stress is Young's modulus times the strain. In this form it is Hooke's law again, with stress in place of force and strain in place of deformation, which is why one shape of statement covers a stretched wire, a sheared bookcase and a compressed cube.

concepts.name: Shear deformation
concepts.statement: A force applied perpendicular to the length and parallel to the cross-sectional area shears the object sideways, and the constant is the shear modulus. The equation is logical: it is easier to bend a long thin pencil than a short thick one, and both bend more easily than a steel rod of the same size.

forms.condition: the force is applied perpendicular to L₀ and parallel to the cross-sectional area A

concepts.name: Change in volume
concepts.statement: An object squeezed evenly on all its surfaces changes its volume rather than its length, and the constant is the bulk modulus. Gases compress easily because their molecules are far apart, while liquids and solids are extraordinarily difficult to compress, which is why seawater five kilometers down has lost only 2.3% of its volume.

forms.condition: the force per unit area is applied uniformly inward on all surfaces

concepts.name: Tensile strength
concepts.statement: The tensile strength of a material is the breaking stress, the stress that will cause permanent deformation or fracture of the material.

concepts.name: Work
concepts.statement: In science, work is not effort but a transfer of energy. A force does work on a system only when the system is displaced and the force has a component along that displacement, and the work is the product of that component and the distance the force acts through, $W = Fd\cos\theta$.

forms.condition: a constant force and one-way motion in one dimension

concepts.name: Sign of the work
concepts.statement: The angle between the force and the displacement decides the sign. The work is positive when the force has a component in the direction of the motion, zero when the force is perpendicular to the motion or when there is no displacement at all, and negative when the force opposes the motion and so removes energy from the system.

concepts.name: Joule
concepts.statement: Work and energy have the units of force times distance, and in SI that is the newton-meter, which is given the name joule. One joule is not a large amount of energy; it would lift a small 100-gram apple a distance of about 1 meter.

concepts.name: Calculating work
concepts.statement: Putting a force, a distance and the angle between them into the definition of work gives the energy the force transfers. Setting the answer beside the energy a person eats in a day gives a feel for the size of a joule.

concepts.name: Energy
concepts.statement: Energy is the ability to do work. Work done on a system transfers energy to it, and work done by a system transfers energy out of it.

concepts.name: Work transfers energy
concepts.statement: Work done on a system puts energy into it, and work done by a system takes energy out of it. Where that energy goes depends on the situation: friction carries it off as heat, while the work done carrying a briefcase up stairs is stored in the briefcase-Earth system and can be recovered at any time.

concepts.name: Net work
concepts.statement: The work that changes a system's motion is the work done by the net external force, and it is also the sum of the work done by each force separately. A force perpendicular to the displacement, such as the weight or the normal force on a package sliding along a belt, does no work and drops out of the sum.

forms.condition: the net force parallel to the displacement

concepts.name: Work as area under a graph
concepts.statement: Plot the component of the force along the motion against the distance and the work is the area beneath the line. That is plain when the force is constant, and it stays true when the force varies, since the area can be cut into strips and each strip is the work done over its own small distance.

concepts.name: Kinetic energy
concepts.statement: The quantity the net work changes is one half the mass times the speed squared, and it is given the name translational kinetic energy: the energy a body has by reason of its motion. Because the speed is squared, a car travelling at 100 km/h carries four times the kinetic energy it carries at 50 km/h, which helps explain why high-speed collisions are so devastating.

concepts.name: Work-energy theorem
concepts.statement: Put Newton's second law and the constant-acceleration relation between speed and distance into the net work and the distance cancels, leaving the net work equal to the change in the kinetic energy. It was derived here for a constant force along the motion, but it holds in general, even for forces that vary in direction and magnitude.

forms.condition: a constant net force parallel to the displacement

concepts.name: Using the work-energy theorem
concepts.statement: Once the net work and the kinetic energies are known, the unknown of a problem can be any one of the three: the final speed, the force that caused the change, or the distance over which it acted. Solutions that go through energy are generally shorter and easier than those that use kinematics and dynamics alone.

concepts.name: Potential energy
concepts.statement: Work done against a force that can give the energy back is not lost; it is stored in the system as potential energy. Potential energy is a property of a system rather than of a single body, since it belongs to the arrangement of the parts: lifting a mass stores energy in the mass-Earth system, and the system gives it back when the mass comes down.

concepts.name: Gravitational potential energy
concepts.statement: Lifting a mass at constant speed takes a force equal to its weight, so the work done in raising it through a height is the weight times the height. That work is the change in the gravitational potential energy of the object-Earth system, and it is the same whether the mass is lifted or lowered, with the sign of the height carrying the difference.

forms.condition: a change in height h that is small compared with the radius of Earth
an object lifted straight up at constant speed

concepts.name: Reference level for potential energy
concepts.statement: Gravitational potential energy depends on relative position, so a level has to be chosen at which it is called zero. Earth's surface is the usual choice, but the choice is arbitrary: what relates to the work done, and so what has physical significance, is the difference between two positions. The rise between the first two rungs of a ladder is worth the same as the rise between the last two.

concepts.name: Path independence of work against gravity
concepts.statement: The change in gravitational potential energy is the weight times the change in height for any path between two points, not only for a straight lift, as long as the height change is small compared with the radius of Earth. Multiplying mass, gravity and height therefore replaces working out the work done along a complicated path.

concepts.name: Potential energy into kinetic energy
concepts.statement: Release a raised mass and gravity does work equal to the potential energy given up, so the kinetic energy grows by exactly that amount. When friction is negligible, the speed of a falling body then depends only on its initial speed and on the change in height, and not on its mass or on the path it takes.

forms.condition: work done by frictional forces is negligible
work done by frictional forces is negligible

concepts.name: Finding a stopping force
concepts.statement: A body that lands has kinetic energy that must be taken away by the work the ground does on it, and that work is the stopping force times the distance the body travels while stopping. Because the distance sits in the denominator, stopping in half a centimetre takes a force hundreds of times the body's weight, and bending the legs to stop over half a metre cuts that force a hundredfold.

concepts.name: Conservative force
concepts.statement: A conservative force is one whose work, done by it or against it, depends only on where the motion starts and ends, not on the path between. Gravity is one and the force of an ideal spring is another. This property gives the force a potential energy, so you never need to calculate the work along the path at all.

concepts.name: Potential energy of a spring
concepts.statement: The force needed to stretch a spring grows from zero to the force constant times the stretch, so its average is half of that, and the work done is one half the force constant times the stretch squared. The same quantity is the area of the triangle under the graph of force against stretch, and because the spring force is conservative that work is stored and can be fully recovered.

forms.condition: Hooke's law applies to the spring
Hooke's law applies to the spring

concepts.name: Mechanical energy
concepts.statement: The total kinetic plus potential energy of a system is its mechanical energy. Writing it as one quantity lets you answer a problem by comparing two configurations. With only conservative forces acting, the energy changes only in form, moving between kinetic energy and the kinds of potential energy while the total stays put.

concepts.name: Conservation of mechanical energy
concepts.statement: If only conservative forces act, the work-energy theorem says the change in kinetic energy is the work done by those forces, and that work is minus the change in potential energy. The two changes therefore cancel, so the kinetic and potential energies of the system add to a constant and the values at the start equal the values at the end.

forms.condition: conservative forces only
conservative forces only
conservative forces only, a gravitational force and a spring

concepts.name: Using conservation of mechanical energy
concepts.statement: The way to use conservation of mechanical energy is to write every kind of energy the system has at the start and at the end, strike out the terms that are zero by choosing the heights and the moments well, and solve for the one that is left. The details of the path in between never enter, which is what makes the method so much shorter than following the forces.

concepts.name: Nonconservative force
concepts.statement: A nonconservative force is one for which the work done depends on the path taken, and friction is the plain example: the longer the route between two points, the more work is done against it. Because the work depends on the path, no potential energy can be defined for such a force, and the work it does has to be counted directly.

concepts.name: Dissipation by friction
concepts.statement: The work done by a nonconservative force adds mechanical energy to a system or removes it. Friction removes it: the energy becomes thermal energy that spreads out and leaves the system, and even where the thermal energy is caught and kept it cannot be fully turned back into work, so it is lost in that sense as well.

concepts.name: Work by nonconservative forces
concepts.statement: Split the net work into the part done by conservative forces and the part done by nonconservative ones, and replace the conservative part by minus the change in potential energy. What is left says that the total mechanical energy changes by exactly the work the nonconservative forces do: positive work adds to it, negative work takes from it, and zero work leaves it conserved.

concepts.name: Solving an energy problem with friction
concepts.statement: With friction in the problem, the work it does is the friction force times the distance, taken as negative because it opposes the motion, and it goes into the energy equation beside the kinetic and potential energies. Solving for the distance or the final speed then takes one line, where following the forces would mean combining the weight, the normal force and friction as vectors first.

concepts.name: Law of conservation of energy
concepts.statement: Total energy is constant in any process. It may change in form or pass from one system to another, but the total remains the same, and writing the law down means adding to the mechanical energy and the nonconservative work one more term for every other kind of energy the system holds. In most problems all but a few of those terms are the same at the start and at the end and simply cancel.

concepts.name: Forms of energy
concepts.statement: Energy takes many forms besides the mechanical ones. Electrical energy travels with a flow of charge, chemical energy sits in the bonds of a fuel or a food, and radiant energy travels in electromagnetic waves. Nuclear energy comes from changes inside a nucleus, and thermal energy lies in the random motion of atoms and molecules. Each can turn into any other, and each can do work.

concepts.name: Transformation of energy
concepts.statement: The changing of energy from one form into others is happening all the time, and most chains run through several forms: the chemical energy in coal becomes thermal energy in steam, which becomes the mechanical energy of a spinning turbine, which becomes electrical energy. Sunlight on a solar cell becomes electricity and then the motion of a motor.

concepts.name: Efficiency
concepts.statement: Energy is conserved in a conversion, but the useful energy or work that comes out is always less than the energy put in, and the efficiency is the ratio of the two. A coal-fired power plant turns about 40 percent of the chemical energy in its fuel into electricity, and the rest leaves as thermal energy through the flue and the cooling towers.

concepts.name: Solving an energy problem
concepts.statement: The strategy has six steps. Settle the system and what the problem asks. Look at every force and ask whether you know its potential energy. Use conservation of mechanical energy where every force is conservative and the general law where one is not. Strike out the zero terms before doing any algebra. Then check that the signs and the size of the answer are reasonable.

concepts.name: Electrical energy
concepts.statement: Electrical energy is the energy carried by a flow of charge.

concepts.name: Chemical energy
concepts.statement: Chemical energy is the energy in a substance stored in the bonds between atoms and molecules, which can be released in a chemical reaction.

concepts.name: Radiant energy
concepts.statement: Radiant energy is the energy carried by electromagnetic waves.

concepts.name: Nuclear energy
concepts.statement: Nuclear energy is energy released by changes within atomic nuclei, such as the fusion of two light nuclei or the fission of a heavy one.

concepts.name: Thermal energy
concepts.statement: Thermal energy is the energy within an object due to the random motion of its atoms and molecules, and it accounts for the object's temperature.

concepts.name: Power
concepts.statement: Power is the rate at which work is done, and since work is a transfer of energy it is also the rate at which energy is spent. A 60-W light bulb spends 60 J every second. Great power means a large amount of work done or energy spent in a short time, which is what a dragster, a volcano and a rocket have in common.

concepts.name: Watt
concepts.statement: The SI unit of power is the watt, one joule per second. The older horsepower is still used for motors and engines, and one horsepower is 746 watts, so the woman running up the stairs puts out a little less than a horsepower; a person can beat that for a few seconds, and a horse can hold it for hours.

concepts.name: Calculating power
concepts.statement: Finding a power output means first finding all the work or the energy that went into the job, kinetic and gravitational alike, and then dividing by the time it took. Doing it once shows where the effort really goes: of the woman's 538 W, climbing takes almost all of it and speeding up takes barely a fifteenth.

concepts.name: Energy from power
concepts.statement: Turn the definition of power around and the energy a device uses is its power times the time it runs. Electricity bills are written in kilowatt-hours, the product of a power in kilowatts and a time in hours, because household appliances draw about a kilowatt for hours at a stretch and that makes the number a convenient size.

concepts.name: Estimating the cost of energy
concepts.statement: The cost of running something is its power times the time it runs times the price of a kilowatt-hour, so it is high only when both the power and the hours are high. That is why it pays to go after water heaters and air conditioners rather than toasters, which draw a great deal for a few minutes, or electric clocks, which draw almost nothing all day.

concepts.name: Kilowatt-hour
concepts.statement: The kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy, the energy used in one hour at a power of one kilowatt, and it is the unit in which electric utility companies bill electrical energy.

concepts.name: Horsepower
concepts.statement: The horsepower is an older non-SI unit of power, with one horsepower equal to 746 watts.

concepts.name: Body as an energy converter
concepts.statement: Our own bodies are energy conversion machines, and conservation of energy applies to them as it does to anything else: the chemical energy stored in food becomes work, thermal energy, or chemical energy stored in fatty tissue. How much goes to each depends on how much is eaten and on how active the person is, and anything eaten beyond what is needed goes to fat.

concepts.name: Metabolic rate
concepts.statement: The rate at which the body uses food energy to stay alive and to do things is its metabolic rate, a power like any other. The rate at rest is the basal metabolic rate, about 85 W, and it is divided among the organs, with the liver and spleen taking the largest share and the brain the next. About 75 percent of the calories burned in a day go to these basic functions.

concepts.name: Oxygen consumption and energy use
concepts.statement: Digestion is the oxidation of food, so the energy a person spends is directly proportional to the oxygen they take in: about 20 kJ of energy for each litre of oxygen consumed, whatever the food. You can therefore measure a person's power output simply by measuring their breathing.

concepts.name: Useful work
concepts.statement: Work done by a person means work done on the outside world, such as lifting weights, climbing stairs or accelerating to a run. Internal work, such as the heart pumping blood or the muscles of a shiver pulling against one another, is not counted, even though it costs energy; the forces the body exerts are nonconservative, so they can change the mechanical energy of whatever is worked on.

concepts.name: Finding the efficiency of an activity
concepts.statement: A person's efficiency is the useful work they do divided by the food energy they metabolise doing it, and for most activities it is small: a fifth at best for cycling and climbing, a fiftieth for swimming at the surface. Knowing the rate from the table and the useful work from the physics gives the ratio, and it explains why exercise burns so much food for so little lifted.

concepts.name: Basal metabolic rate
concepts.statement: The basal metabolic rate is the total energy conversion rate of a person at rest.

concepts.name: Renewable energy sources
concepts.statement: Renewable forms of energy are those that cannot be used up: water, wind, solar and biomass. They are still a small share of the world's supply, but they are the fastest growing part of it, and some countries already draw a large fraction of their electricity from them, as New Zealand does from hydroelectric power.

concepts.name: Fossil fuels
concepts.statement: About 85 percent of the world's energy comes from the nonrenewable fossil fuels, oil, natural gas and coal, and roughly a third of it from oil alone, much of that for transport. Demand has tripled in the past fifty years and may triple again in the next thirty, and the likelihood of a link between fossil fuel use and global warming has made the shift away from them urgent.

concepts.name: Energy use and economic well-being
concepts.statement: In most countries a higher standard of living, measured as gross domestic product per capita, comes with a higher energy use per capita, so access to reliable energy is a condition of economic growth. Diversifying the sources changes that dependency and makes a grid quicker to bring back after a storm or a conflict, which the last twenty years of disruptions have shown.

concepts.name: Degradation of energy
concepts.statement: The law of conservation of energy says the total in an isolated system never changes; the philosophy of energy conservation is about using less of it. The two do not conflict. Most energy transformations end in degraded waste heat: the total is still there, but its potential to do useful work has gone. That is why resources run out even though energy does not.

concepts.name: First condition for equilibrium
concepts.statement: Newton's second law says that a system accelerates only when a net external force acts on it, so a system that does not accelerate has no net external force on it. That is the first condition for equilibrium, and because a force has components, it holds along every axis at once: the net external force is zero along the horizontal as well as along the vertical.

concepts.name: Static equilibrium
concepts.statement: A system in static equilibrium is motionless, so its acceleration is zero and the first condition holds. This is the case of the desks, bridges and mountains the chapter opens with, and it is the case almost every problem of the chapter sets.

concepts.name: Dynamic equilibrium
concepts.statement: A system moving at constant velocity also has zero acceleration, so it satisfies the first condition just as a motionless system does. Equilibrium is therefore not the same as being at rest, which is why a car driving steadily down a road belongs in a chapter about statics.

concepts.name: Point of application of a force
concepts.statement: Where a force is applied decides whether it rotates a body, so a zero net external force is necessary for equilibrium but not sufficient. Two equal and opposite forces along the same line leave an ice hockey stick motionless, while the same two forces applied at different places set it rotating.

concepts.name: Torque
concepts.statement: Torque is the rotational equivalent of a force: it measures how effective a force is at changing a rotation. Opening a door shows what it depends on. The harder you push the faster the door opens, so torque grows with the force; pushing near the hinges barely works, so it grows with the distance from the pivot; and pushing along the door does nothing at all, so only the component of the force perpendicular to that distance counts, which is what the factor $\sin\theta$ supplies.

concepts.name: Perpendicular lever arm
concepts.statement: The perpendicular lever arm is the shortest distance from the pivot point to the line along which the force acts. It gathers the distance and the angle into one length, and it is often easier to see in a drawing than $r$ and $\theta$ are to measure separately.

concepts.name: Torque from the lever arm
concepts.statement: Because the perpendicular lever arm already carries the angle, the torque is simply the lever arm times the force. The two expressions for torque are equally valid, and which one to use is a matter of what the drawing makes easy to find.

concepts.name: Pivot point for torque
concepts.statement: A torque has no meaning until you name a pivot point, because you measure both the distance and the angle in its definition from that point. The same force gives different torques about different points, and the point may lie anywhere in or out of the body, whether or not the body can turn about it. What matters is that you take every torque in a problem about the same point.

concepts.name: Clockwise and counterclockwise torques
concepts.statement: For rotation in a plane a torque has two possible directions, clockwise or counterclockwise about the chosen pivot, and torques in opposite directions are given opposite signs. The common convention is that counterclockwise torques are positive and clockwise torques negative, which is what lets the torques on a body be added as ordinary signed numbers.

concepts.name: Second condition for equilibrium
concepts.statement: The second condition necessary to achieve equilibrium is that the net external torque on the system is zero, so that the system has no accelerated rotation. It repairs what the first condition missed: the hockey stick pushed off centre has no net force but does have a net torque. If the condition holds for one choice of pivot, it holds for every other, so you can choose the pivot freely.

concepts.name: Center of gravity
concepts.statement: The weight of a body is spread over the whole of it, but for the purpose of torques the whole weight may be taken to act at a single point, the center of gravity. This is not an approximation, and it is what allows the distance to a child on a seesaw to be measured to one point rather than over the area the child covers.

concepts.name: Balancing a seesaw
concepts.statement: To balance a seesaw, take the torques about its pivot, which makes the torque of the supporting force zero, and set the two children's torques equal and opposite. The heavier child must then sit closer to the pivot, at $r_2 = r_1 m_1 / m_2$, and the first condition gives the supporting force as the sum of the two weights.

forms.condition: the torques taken about the pivot of the seesaw
the seesaw balanced
the seesaw balanced and of negligible mass
the seesaw of negligible mass

concepts.name: Newton-meter
concepts.statement: The SI unit of torque is newtons times meters, usually written as N·m. A force of 40 N pushing perpendicular to a door at 0.800 m from its hinges exerts a torque of 32 N·m.

concepts.name: Restoring torque
concepts.statement: The torque a body's own weight produces once it is displaced decides its kind of equilibrium. If that torque turns the body back toward where it was, the equilibrium is stable; if it turns the body further away, the equilibrium is unstable; and if there is none, the equilibrium is neutral.

concepts.name: Stable equilibrium
concepts.statement: A system is in stable equilibrium if, when displaced, it experiences a net force or torque in the direction opposite to the displacement, so that it is driven back where it came from. A marble at the bottom of a bowl and a pencil standing on its eraser are both stable, and most systems are stable at least for small displacements.

concepts.name: Unstable equilibrium
concepts.statement: A system is in unstable equilibrium if, when displaced, it experiences a net force or torque in the same direction as the displacement, so that it accelerates away from where it started. A ball resting on the crest of a hill and a pencil balanced on its point are both unstable, although both conditions for equilibrium are satisfied while they stand.

concepts.name: Neutral equilibrium
concepts.statement: A system is in neutral equilibrium if its equilibrium does not depend on where you displace it to. A marble on a flat table and a round pencil lying on its side simply stay where you put them, because the center of gravity stays directly above the point of support wherever the body moves. A body may be of one kind in one direction and another kind in another, as a marble on a saddle is.

concepts.name: Base of support
