concepts.statement: A body standing on a surface stays in stable equilibrium only while its center of gravity lies above its base of support. Once the center of gravity passes beyond the base, the torque from the weight changes direction and the body topples. So spreading your feet, which widens the base, and bending your knees, which lowers the center of gravity, make you more stable. A chicken, with its center of gravity below its hips and between two broad feet, is far more stable than a person.

concepts.name: Solving a static equilibrium problem
concepts.statement: Statics is a special case of Newton's laws, so the strategies of Chapter 4 still apply, with four steps of its own. Decide that the system really is in static equilibrium. Draw a free body diagram and label every force with its magnitude, direction and point of application. Apply either or both conditions for equilibrium. Check that the answer is reasonable in magnitude, direction and units.

concepts.name: Choosing the pivot
concepts.statement: Because the second condition holds for any choice of pivot, the pivot may be chosen to make the work easy. The useful choices are the ones that make the torques of unknown forces zero: a force applied at the pivot has no lever arm, and a force acting along a line through the pivot makes an angle of zero. Choosing the elbow, the hip or the hand a problem is asking about is what turns two unknowns into one.

concepts.name: Symmetric supports
concepts.statement: When supporting forces act symmetrically about the center of gravity, each carries an equal share of the weight. Both conditions then hold at once. The forces add to the weight, and about the center of gravity the weight has no lever arm while the two equal forces sit at equal distances, so their torques cancel. The four legs of a uniform table each carry a quarter of its weight for the same reason.

forms.condition: the center of gravity of the pole halfway between the hands

concepts.name: Unequal supports
concepts.statement: Move the center of gravity away from the middle and the two supports no longer share the weight equally: the support nearer the center of gravity carries more, exactly as the nearer of two people carrying a load does. The forces still add to the weight, so the first condition gives the second force once the second condition has given the first. If the center of gravity lies beyond both supports, one force reverses direction and both grow large, which is why holding a pole at one end is so much harder than holding it in the middle.

concepts.name: Simple machines
concepts.statement: A simple machine is a device that multiplies or augments the force we apply, usually at the expense of the distance through which we apply it. Levers, gears, pulleys, wedges and screws are the familiar examples. A machine does not create energy, since it cannot do more work than the work put into it; what it changes is how much force the job takes.

concepts.name: Mechanical advantage
concepts.statement: The mechanical advantage of a machine is the ratio of the output force to the input force. It is a pure number: a mechanical advantage greater than one means the machine gives out more force than is put in, and one less than one, as for a shovel or a car axle, means it gives out less and buys something else instead.

concepts.name: Lever
concepts.statement: A lever is a rigid bar pivoted at a fixed place called the fulcrum. Because the bar turns about that point, the second condition for equilibrium applies to it: while the load is not moving the torque of the input force equals the torque of the output force, so the input force times its lever arm equals the output force times its own. The nail puller, the wheelbarrow, the shovel and a seesaw are all levers, and they differ only in where the pivot sits relative to the two forces.

forms.condition: the nail not moving, so that the two torques about the pivot are equal

concepts.name: Mechanical advantage of a lever
concepts.statement: Rearranging the lever's torque balance turns it into a statement about forces: the mechanical advantage of a lever is the ratio of the input lever arm to the output lever arm. The longer the handle on a nail puller, the greater the force it can exert, and the shorter the handle, the less.

concepts.name: Cranks, wheels and gears
concepts.statement: A crank is a lever that turns through a full circle about its pivot, and a wheel driven by an axle is the same thing again. Such a machine may not look like a lever, but the physics is the same: its mechanical advantage is the ratio of the two radii. A crank usually has a large mechanical advantage, while a car axle driving a much larger wheel has one well below one.

concepts.name: Pulleys
concepts.statement: An ordinary pulley changes the direction of the force in a cord without changing its magnitude, so its mechanical advantage is one. Combinations of pulleys do multiply force: each cable that pulls directly upward on the load adds a force of about the tension, since the tension is nearly the same throughout a friction-free system, so the number of such cables is about the mechanical advantage of the system.

forms.condition: frictionless pulleys, with n cables pulling directly on the load

concepts.name: Muscles and joints as levers
concepts.statement: A limb is a lever whose fulcrum is a joint, and the muscle that moves it is attached by a tendon very close to that joint. The muscle's lever arm is therefore much shorter than the load's, so the system is a simple machine with a mechanical advantage well below one and the muscle must pull far harder than the limb pushes on the world. Muscles can only contract, which is why they come in pairs, a flexor to close the limb and an extensor to open it.

concepts.name: Force in a muscle
concepts.statement: Taking the pivot at the joint makes the torque of the joint force zero and leaves the muscle force as the only unknown, so the second condition alone gives it: the muscle's torque must balance the torques of the weights it holds. Because the muscle's lever arm is the small one, the answer is large. The biceps holding a forearm and a 4.00 kg book exerts 470 N, which is 7.38 times the weight it is supporting.

forms.latex: r_2 w_{\text{a}} + r_3 w_{\text{b}} = r_1 F_{\text{B}}
forms.condition: the pivot taken at the elbow joint

concepts.name: Force in a joint
concepts.statement: Once the muscle force is known, the first condition for equilibrium gives the force in the joint, and it is large too. A muscle can contract but cannot push, so the muscle and the joint pull in opposite directions and their forces subtract to leave the weight actually supported.

concepts.name: Posture and back strain
concepts.statement: Stand straight and the upper body's center of gravity sits directly above the pivot in the hips, so its weight has no lever arm, produces no torque, and needs no muscle action to balance it. Lean forward and the center of gravity moves in front of the hips. The muscles of the lower back must counter the resulting torque, and with their very small lever arms they must pull very hard. Lifting a load with the back rather than the legs makes the same forces several times larger again.

concepts.name: Muscle attachment close to joints
concepts.statement: Muscles are attached close to the joints they move because a short lever arm lets a small contraction swing the limb through a large distance in a short time. The arrangement pays in force for speed, and it also leaves room for many joints and the wide ranges over which they work.

concepts.name: Linear momentum
concepts.statement: Linear momentum is the product of a system’s mass and its velocity, and it is the quantity that says how hard a moving object is to stop. A large, fast-moving object has greater momentum than a smaller, slower one.

forms.condition: only the magnitude of the momentum is considered

concepts.name: Calculating momentum
concepts.statement: Momentum is a vector with the same direction as the velocity, and its SI unit is the kilogram meter per second. Multiplying a mass by a velocity, keeping the direction and the unit, gives the momentum from which a collision problem starts.

concepts.name: Newton’s second law in terms of momentum
concepts.statement: Newton stated his second law as the net external force equals the change in momentum of a system divided by the time over which it changes. This is the more general statement, because it holds for a system whose mass changes, such as a rocket, as well as for one whose mass is constant.

concepts.name: Second law for a constant mass
concepts.statement: When the mass of the system does not change, the change in momentum is the mass times the change in velocity, and dividing by the time gives the acceleration. The familiar form of the second law, $F_{\text{net}} = ma$, is therefore the special case of the momentum form for a constant mass.

forms.condition: the mass of the system is constant

concepts.name: Change in momentum
concepts.statement: The change in momentum is the difference between the final and the initial momentum, and for a constant mass it is the mass times the change in velocity. It is the quantity that a force acting for a time produces.

forms.condition: the mass of the system is constant
the mass of the system is constant

concepts.name: Impulse
concepts.statement: Rearranging Newton’s second law shows that the change in momentum equals the average net external force multiplied by the time this force acts, and that product is called the impulse. Impulse is the same as the change in momentum, so the effect of a force depends on how long it acts as well as on how great it is.

forms.condition: the ball strikes the wall along the perpendicular and rebounds with the same speed
the ball strikes the wall at 30° from the perpendicular and rebounds at the same angle with the same speed

concepts.name: Extending the collision time
concepts.statement: The change in momentum a stop requires is fixed by the mass and the speed, so if the stop is spread over a longer time the force is smaller. This is why a car has a padded dashboard, an airbag and parts that crumple, and why you roll on landing rather than land stiff-legged.

concepts.name: Average effective force
concepts.statement: A real force is not constant over the brief time of a collision, but you can always find an average effective force that produces the same result. On a graph of force against time, the area under the actual curve is the impulse, and the rectangle of the effective force over the same interval has the same area.

concepts.name: Finding an average force from impulse
concepts.statement: The average force of a collision is found from the mass and the velocities before and after it: form the change in momentum, keeping its direction, and divide by the time of contact.

concepts.name: Equal and opposite changes in momentum
concepts.statement: The two cars push on each other for the same length of time, and Newton’s third law makes the two forces equal and opposite. The impulses are therefore equal and opposite, so the momentum one car loses is the momentum the other gains, and this is the whole argument for conservation of momentum.

concepts.name: Conservation of momentum
concepts.statement: The total momentum of an isolated system is constant, whatever happens inside it and however many objects it holds. Momentum is one of the few quantities nature conserves, and every collision in the rest of the chapter is solved by writing the total momentum before the collision equal to the total momentum after it.

forms.condition: the system is isolated
the net external force on the two-object system is zero

concepts.name: Isolated system
concepts.statement: An isolated system is one for which the net external force is zero, and that is exactly the condition momentum needs in order to be conserved. Before you can use conservation of momentum you have to choose a system large enough that the forces that matter are internal to it.

concepts.name: Recoil
concepts.statement: The backward momentum felt by a body that exerts a force on another is called a recoil. When a football player runs into the goalpost the Earth recoils too, and because the Earth is so much more massive its recoil is immeasurably small, though it is real nevertheless.

concepts.name: Momentum conservation along one direction
concepts.statement: The three directions in space are independent, so momentum can be conserved along one of them while it is not conserved along another. For a projectile with negligible air resistance the horizontal forces are zero and the horizontal momentum is unchanged, while the vertical force of gravity is not zero and the vertical momentum is not conserved.

concepts.name: Momentum of subatomic particles
concepts.statement: Conservation of momentum is not a rule about billiard balls alone. Momentum is a property of every subatomic particle, massless ones such as photons included, and the analysis of what scatters from what is how the nucleus and the quarks inside a proton were found.

concepts.name: Quark
concepts.statement: A quark is a fundamental constituent of matter and an elementary particle.

concepts.name: Elastic collision
concepts.statement: An elastic collision is one that conserves internal kinetic energy as well as momentum. That second conservation law is the extra equation you need when both final velocities are unknown, so knowing whether a collision is elastic decides how you can solve it.

forms.condition: the collision is elastic, so internal kinetic energy is conserved

concepts.name: Internal kinetic energy
concepts.statement: The internal kinetic energy of a system is the sum of the kinetic energies of the objects in it. It is the quantity that is conserved in an elastic collision and changed in an inelastic one, so it is the bookkeeping that tells the two kinds of collision apart.

concepts.name: Solving a one-dimensional elastic collision
concepts.statement: Two unknown final velocities need two independent equations, and an elastic collision supplies them: conservation of momentum and conservation of internal kinetic energy. Solving the pair gives a quadratic with two roots, and the root that repeats the initial condition describes the situation before the collision and is discarded.

forms.condition: the second object is initially at rest

concepts.name: Nearly elastic collisions
concepts.statement: Only subatomic particles collide truly elastically. Macroscopic collisions always turn some kinetic energy into heat transfer due to friction and into sound. Two steel blocks on ice or two carts with spring bumpers on an air track count as elastic because they are nearly so, not exactly so.

concepts.name: Inelastic collision
concepts.statement: An inelastic collision is one in which the internal kinetic energy changes. The forces between the colliding objects do work that can turn internal kinetic energy into heat transfer, or turn stored energy into internal kinetic energy, so only momentum can be counted on here.

concepts.name: Perfectly inelastic collision
concepts.statement: A collision in which the objects stick together is called perfectly inelastic, because it reduces internal kinetic energy more than any other kind of collision can while still conserving momentum. Since the two objects share one final velocity afterwards, conservation of momentum alone is enough to find it.

forms.condition: the objects stick together and the second is initially at rest

concepts.name: Recoil velocity
concepts.statement: When a moving object is caught by one that is at rest, the two move off together at the incoming velocity reduced by the ratio of the incoming mass to the total mass. A goalie who catches a puck therefore recoils only a few centimetres a second, which is why the recoil of a heavy body is so easy to miss.

forms.condition: the objects stick together and the second is initially at rest

concepts.name: Finding the kinetic energy lost in a collision
concepts.statement: Once the final velocities are known you can add up the kinetic energies before the collision and after it and subtract. The difference is what was lost to thermal energy and sound, and in a perfectly inelastic collision it is nearly all of what there was to begin with.

concepts.name: Energy released in a collision
concepts.statement: An inelastic collision does not only remove internal kinetic energy; it can add it. When a compressed spring is released during the collision, or when exploding bolts push a satellite away from its launcher, stored energy is converted into internal kinetic energy and the system ends with more than it started with.

concepts.name: Two-dimensional collision
concepts.statement: When objects scatter to the side rather than along one line, you choose a convenient coordinate system and resolve the motion into components along perpendicular axes. Resolving the motion this way yields a pair of one-dimensional problems to be solved together, which is the same approach that carried kinematics and dynamics into the plane.

concepts.name: Point mass
concepts.statement: Two objects that collide off centre can begin to spin, and rotation is not treated until later. A point mass is a structureless particle that cannot rotate or spin, and restricting the analysis to point masses is what keeps the collision describable by the velocities alone.

concepts.name: Momentum along the x-axis
concepts.statement: With the x-axis chosen parallel to the velocity of the incoming object and the second object at rest, the whole of the initial momentum lies along x. Conservation of momentum along that axis then relates the one initial speed to the two final speeds and the two scattering angles.

forms.condition: the second object is initially at rest and the x-axis is parallel to the velocity of the incoming object

concepts.name: Momentum along the y-axis
concepts.statement: Neither object has any momentum along the y-axis before the collision, so the two y-components afterwards must add to zero. This is the second of the two independent equations, and it is the one that ties the two scattering angles to each other.

forms.condition: the second object is initially at rest and the x-axis is parallel to the velocity of the incoming object

concepts.name: Finding an unseen object’s velocity
concepts.statement: Two equations can be solved for two unknowns. Taking the ratio of the two conservation equations removes the unknown speed and leaves the unknown angle, and either equation then gives the speed, so a measurement of what comes out of a collision tells you about what you could not see going in.

forms.condition: the second object is initially at rest

concepts.name: Elastic collision of equal masses
concepts.statement: For two objects of equal mass, conservation of momentum along both axes gives an expression for the initial kinetic energy that carries one extra term beyond the elastic condition. The two statements can both be true only if that extra term is zero, and what follows from that is the whole of what pool players know about angles.

forms.condition: the two objects have equal masses and the second is initially at rest
the two objects have equal masses, the collision is elastic and the second object is initially at rest

concepts.name: Ninety-degree separation
concepts.statement: The extra term can be zero in three ways: the incoming object stops, the incoming object misses, or the angle of separation is ninety degrees. All three are familiar at a pool table, and the third is the one that lets you find the second object’s direction without any further calculation.

forms.condition: the two objects have equal masses, the collision is elastic and both of them move after it

concepts.name: Rocket propulsion
concepts.statement: A rocket, a jet engine, a deflating balloon and a squid all move for the same reason: matter is forcefully ejected from the system, producing an equal and opposite reaction on what remains. The exhaust does not push on the ground, which is why a rocket’s thrust is greater in outer space than on the launch pad.

concepts.name: Thrust of a rocket
concepts.statement: The exhaust velocity multiplied by the rate at which mass leaves the rocket is a quantity with the units of newtons, and it is the force the exhaust gases exert on the rocket. The faster the rocket burns its fuel, and the faster the gas leaves, the greater the thrust.

concepts.name: Acceleration of a rocket
concepts.statement: Equating the change in momentum of the whole system over a short time to the impulse of gravity gives a good approximation for the acceleration of what is left of the rocket, $a = (v_{\text{e}}/m)(\Delta m/\Delta t) - g$. It describes a system whose mass changes as it moves.

concepts.name: Factors in a rocket’s acceleration
concepts.statement: The equation says that a rocket accelerates harder the greater the exhaust velocity, the faster it burns its fuel and the smaller its mass. The last of the three changes as the rocket flies, because most of a rocket is fuel to begin with, so the acceleration increases continuously and reaches a maximum just before the fuel runs out.

concepts.name: Final velocity of a rocket
concepts.statement: Neglecting air resistance and gravity, the velocity a rocket gains depends only on the exhaust velocity and on the natural logarithm of the ratio of its initial mass to the mass that is left when the fuel is gone. Because the ratio enters through a logarithm, going faster costs a great deal more fuel than you might expect.

forms.condition: air resistance is absent, the gravitational force is neglected and the rocket starts from rest

concepts.name: Why rockets have stages
concepts.statement: Once you account for air resistance and gravity, the mass left at burnout can be only about one hundred and eightieth of the initial mass, and a rocket whose fuel outweighs everything else 180 times is hard to build. The answer is to give each stage only part of the final velocity and discard it when its fuel is spent, so that later stages can be smaller.

concepts.name: Uniform circular motion
concepts.statement: Uniform circular motion is motion in a circular path at constant speed, and it is the simplest form of curved motion. The centripetal acceleration, the centripetal force and the orbits of satellites are all worked out for this case first.

concepts.name: Arc length
concepts.statement: The arc length is the distance an object travels along a circular path, the distance of Chapter 2 measured along a curve rather than along a line. Every rotation angle and every linear speed of circular motion comes from it.

concepts.name: Rotation angle
concepts.statement: The rotation angle is the amount of rotation, defined as the ratio of the arc length to the radius of curvature, and it is the angular quantity that stands in for linear distance. Because it is a ratio of two lengths, every point of a rotating object turns through the same rotation angle in the same time, however far from the axis it sits.

concepts.name: Radian
concepts.statement: One complete revolution carries a point once round the circumference, so the rotation angle of a revolution is $2\pi r / r = 2\pi$. That fixes the unit: $2\pi$ rad is one revolution, and one radian is about 57.3º. A radian is a ratio of two lengths and carries no unit of its own, so you can insert it into an answer or drop it.

forms.condition: one complete revolution

concepts.name: Angular velocity
concepts.statement: The angular velocity is the rate of change of the rotation angle, and it answers the question of how fast an object is rotating. It is the angular quantity analogous to linear velocity, it is measured in radians per second, and with respect to the axis of rotation it has only two directions, clockwise and counterclockwise.

concepts.name: Linear and angular velocity
concepts.statement: A pit on a rotating CD moves an arc length $\Delta s = r\Delta\theta$ in a time $\Delta t$, so its linear speed is $v = r\omega$. Read one way, the relation says that a point on the rim moves faster than a point near the axis; read the other way, $\omega = v/r$ says that a car with small tires must spin them faster than a car with large ones to travel at the same speed.

concepts.name: Radius of curvature
concepts.statement: The radius of curvature is the radius of a circular path, the distance from the center of rotation out to the point that moves.

concepts.name: Pit
concepts.statement: A pit is a tiny indentation on the spiral track moulded into the top of the polycarbonate layer of a CD.

concepts.name: Centripetal acceleration
concepts.statement: In uniform circular motion the magnitude of the velocity never changes but its direction changes constantly, so there is an acceleration. Taking the difference of the velocities at two nearby points shows that the change points directly toward the center of curvature, and so does the acceleration. Centripetal means center seeking, and it is what you notice as a sideways acceleration when you turn a corner in your car.

concepts.name: Magnitude of centripetal acceleration
concepts.statement: The triangle formed by the two velocities and the triangle formed by the two radii are similar, and following that through gives $a_{\text{c}} = v^2/r$. Substituting $v = r\omega$ gives the second form, $a_{\text{c}} = r\omega^2$, and you may use whichever is more convenient. Because the speed enters squared, it is four times as hard to take a curve at 100 km/h as at 50 km/h, and a sharp corner, having a small radius, asks more again.

forms.condition: the triangle of the velocities and the triangle of the radii are similar

concepts.name: Centrifuge
concepts.statement: A centrifuge is a rotating device used to separate specimens of different densities, and it works because a high centripetal acceleration separates them far faster than gravity does and does so with small samples. An ultracentrifuge is one optimized for very high speeds, and a maximum centripetal acceleration of several hundred thousand $g$ is possible in a vacuum.

concepts.name: Quoting an acceleration in multiples of g
concepts.statement: Dividing a centripetal acceleration by the acceleration due to gravity states it in multiples of g, which tells you at once how it compares with what we feel standing still. Centrifuges carry ratings in multiples of g, astronauts' tolerance to launch and reentry is stated the same way, and the ratio shows whether a ride would be uncomfortable or dangerous.

concepts.name: Ultracentrifuge
concepts.statement: An ultracentrifuge is a centrifuge optimized for spinning a rotor at very high speeds.

concepts.name: Centripetal force
concepts.statement: Any net force causing uniform circular motion is a centripetal force. It is not a new kind of force: the tension in the rope on a tether ball, the force of Earth's gravity on the Moon, friction between skates and a rink floor, and a banked roadway's force on a car can each be the centripetal force. What makes a force centripetal is its direction, toward the center of curvature, and Newton's second law then gives its magnitude.

concepts.name: Magnitude of centripetal force
concepts.statement: Putting the two forms of the centripetal acceleration into $F_{\text{c}} = ma_{\text{c}}$ gives two forms of the centripetal force, and you use whichever is more convenient: the first when you know the speed, the second when you know the angular velocity. The force is always perpendicular to the path and always points toward the center of curvature, because the acceleration does.

concepts.name: Radius from centripetal force
concepts.statement: Solving the centripetal force for the radius shows that for a given mass and speed a large force makes a tight curve and a small force a wide one. It is the reading that tells you why a car with too little friction under it runs wide off the road rather than stopping, and why the stress in a high-speed tire depends on the tire's diameter.

concepts.name: Friction on a level curve
concepts.statement: On a level curve the only horizontal force on the car is friction, so friction is the whole centripetal force. Set $mv^2/r$ equal to the greatest static friction $\mu_{\text{s}}N = \mu_{\text{s}}mg$ and cancel the mass, and you get the smallest coefficient of friction that lets the car take the curve at that speed. The mass cancels because friction is proportional to the normal force, so the car's load does not matter.

forms.condition: an unbanked curve taken at the greatest speed static friction allows
an unbanked curve, where friction is the only horizontal force

concepts.name: Banked curve
concepts.statement: A banked curve slopes the road so that the slope helps you negotiate the curve, and the greater the angle, the faster you can take it. On an ideally banked curve you can take the curve at one speed with no friction at all, because the normal force alone supplies the centripetal force.

concepts.name: Ideal banking angle
concepts.statement: On a frictionless banked curve the horizontal component of the normal force $N\sin\theta$ must supply the centripetal force and the vertical component $N\cos\theta$ must balance the weight. Dividing one by the other removes the normal force and the mass together and leaves $\tan\theta = v^2/rg$. Roads must therefore be steeply banked for high speeds and for sharp curves, and the angle does not depend on the mass of the vehicle.

forms.condition: an ideally banked curve, no friction
an ideally banked curve, no friction
an ideally banked curve, no friction
an ideally banked curve, no friction

concepts.name: Ideal speed
concepts.statement: Reading the banking relation the other way gives the speed a curve of a given radius and bank is built for, which the book calls the ideal speed. It is the speed at which the road alone holds you on the curve, and friction then lets you take the curve at a greater or a lower speed without sliding.

forms.condition: an ideally banked curve, no friction

concepts.name: Solving a circular-motion problem
concepts.statement: A circular-motion problem is a Newton's second law problem in which you know the direction of the acceleration in advance: it points at the center of curvature. Draw the free-body diagram, put one axis along the radius, and set the net force along that axis equal to $mv^2/r$. The level curve, the banked curve, the vertical loop and the swinging cage all work this way.

concepts.name: Ideal banking
concepts.statement: Ideal banking is the sloping of a curve in a road at the angle that lets a vehicle negotiate the curve at a given speed without the aid of friction between the tires and the road.

concepts.name: Non-inertial frame of reference
concepts.statement: A non-inertial frame of reference is an accelerated frame. The car turning the corner and the rotating merry-go-round are both non-inertial, and inside such a frame Newton's laws do not hold as they stand unless forces with no physical origin are added to them.

concepts.name: Fictitious force
concepts.statement: A fictitious force is a force having no physical origin, invented so that Newton's laws can be applied inside an accelerating or rotating frame. Nothing pushes the passenger to the left as the car turns right; the passenger is going in a straight line and the car is moving to the right underneath. Either view allows us to describe nature, but the view from an inertial frame is the simplest and truest, because in it every force has a real origin.

concepts.name: Centrifugal force
concepts.statement: The centrifugal force is the fictitious force that appears to throw you off a rotating frame. Do not confuse it with the centripetal force, which is real and points the other way. In Earth's frame nothing throws the rider off the merry-go-round; the rider must hang on to go in a circle rather than travel straight off the edge. A centrifuge works for the same reason: the particles' inertia carries them along a tangent while the tube turns.

concepts.name: Coriolis force
concepts.statement: A ball slid straight out across a rotating merry-go-round follows a straight path over the ground but curves to the right across the boards. In the merry-go-round's frame, a fictitious force, the Coriolis force, accounts for that curve. Earth turns the same way seen from above the North Pole, so any motion in the northern hemisphere veers to the right and any in the southern hemisphere to the left. On the scale of a weather system the effect turns the winds flowing into a low pressure into a circulation, counterclockwise in the north and clockwise in the south.

concepts.name: Newton’s universal law of gravitation
concepts.statement: Every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force along a line joining them, directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. The force is always attractive, it depends on nothing but the masses and the separation, and the same formula holds for a father and a baby, for Earth and the Moon, and for one galaxy and another. The magnitude of the force on each of the two bodies is the same, consistent with Newton's third law, however different the two masses are.

concepts.name: Gravitational constant
concepts.statement: $G$ is the proportionality factor in the universal law of gravitation, measured to be $6.674 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2$ and thought to be the same everywhere in the universe. Its small size is why two 1.000 kg masses 1.000 m apart attract each other with only $6.674 \times 10^{-11}$ N, and why we are unaware that even large objects like mountains exert gravitational forces on us. Of all the fundamental constants in physics, $G$ is by far the least well determined.

concepts.name: Center of mass
concepts.statement: Bodies that attract by gravity tend to be large, so you apply the law by treating each body as if its entire mass sat at one point, its center of mass. The center of mass is the average location of the mass, and a system responds to external forces as if all its mass sat there. The distance $r$ in the law of gravitation runs between the two centers of mass.

concepts.name: Acceleration due to gravity from gravitation
concepts.statement: The weight of an object $mg$ is the gravitational force between it and Earth, so $mg = GmM/r^2$. The mass of the object cancels, leaving $g = GM/r^2$, and substituting Earth's mass and radius gives $9.80\ \text{m/s}^2$. This is why all masses fall with the same acceleration, and it takes Galileo's observation a step further by explaining it in terms of a force. The same expression gives $g$ on the Moon, on Mars, at the distance of the Moon, or wherever a mass and a distance are known.

forms.condition: the weight of an object is the gravitational force between it and Earth

concepts.name: Finding a body’s mass from its gravity
concepts.statement: Once you know $G$, you can turn $g = GM/r^2$ round to give the mass of the body rather than its surface gravity. That is how physicists finally obtained an accurate value for Earth's mass, more than a hundred years after Newton published the law, and it is one reason the measurement of $G$ mattered so much.

concepts.name: Gravity and the Moon’s orbit
concepts.statement: Newton's own test of his law was to ask whether the acceleration due to Earth's gravity at the distance of the Moon is the acceleration the Moon's orbit needs. Working out $GM/r^2$ at $3.84 \times 10^8$ m gives $2.70 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m/s}^2$, and working out $r\omega^2$ from the Moon's 27.3-day period gives $2.72 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m/s}^2$. The two differ by less than one per cent, and the clear implication is that Earth's gravitational force causes the Moon to orbit Earth.

concepts.name: Tides
concepts.statement: The Moon pulls the near side of Earth harder than it pulls Earth, and it pulls Earth harder than the water on the far side, so the water rises on both sides at once. The bulge stays lined up with the Moon while Earth rotates under it, which gives two high tides a day. The Sun has about half the Moon's effect. The largest tides, the spring tides, come when Earth, the Moon and the Sun line up, and the smallest, the neap tides, when the Sun is at 90º to that line.

concepts.name: Weightlessness and microgravity
concepts.statement: Weightlessness does not mean that gravity has stopped acting on an astronaut; there is no zero gravity in an orbit. The astronaut is in free fall, accelerating with the acceleration due to gravity, like the passengers in a lift whose cable has broken. Microgravity names an environment in which a body's apparent net acceleration is small compared with Earth's at its surface. Long stays in it waste muscle and bone.

concepts.name: Cavendish experiment
concepts.statement: Henry Cavendish measured the tiny gravitational attraction between two ordinary-sized masses hung on a torsion fiber, and so fixed the value of $G$ in 1798, more than a hundred years after Newton published the law; his value differs by less than one per cent from the best modern one. The measurement is important because it determines the strength of one of the four forces in nature and because it made Earth's mass calculable. Experiments of the same design are still run, to ask whether the gravitational force depends on substance as well as mass and whether the inverse square law holds over sub-millimetre distances.

concepts.name: Microgravity
concepts.statement: Microgravity is an environment in which the apparent net acceleration of a body is small compared with that produced by Earth at its surface.

concepts.name: Conditions for a simple orbit
concepts.statement: Kepler's laws and everything derived from them hold for a small mass $m$ orbiting a much larger mass $M$ in a system isolated from other masses. The first condition lets you view the motion as if $M$ were stationary, from an inertial frame placed on it; the second lets you neglect the small effects of everything else. Earth's satellites including the Moon, the objects orbiting the Sun, and the satellites of other planets all satisfy the two conditions to good approximation, which is why so much can be said about them without a computer.

concepts.name: Kepler’s first law
concepts.statement: The orbit of each planet about the Sun is an ellipse with the Sun at one focus. An ellipse is a closed curve such that the sum of the distances from a point on the curve to the two foci is a constant, and a circle is the special case in which the two foci coincide. The law holds for any closed gravitational orbit, not only for the planets it was stated for.

concepts.name: Kepler’s second law
concepts.statement: Each planet moves so that an imaginary line drawn from the Sun to the planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Because the areas are equal, the planet must move fastest when it is closest to the Sun and slowest when it is furthest away. The law was devised for planets orbiting the Sun but has broader validity.

concepts.name: Kepler’s third law
concepts.statement: The ratio of the squares of the periods of any two planets about the Sun equals the ratio of the cubes of their average distances from the Sun. It is a descriptive equation only: Kepler found it in Tycho Brahe's twenty years of observations and it gives no information as to the cause of the equality. It is enough, though, to find the period of one orbit from the period of another, which is how the period of a satellite 1500 km up is got from the period of the Moon.

forms.condition: two small masses orbiting the same large one

concepts.name: Orbital speed
concepts.statement: For a circular orbit gravity is the whole net external force, so $GmM/r^2 = mv^2/r$. The satellite's own mass cancels, leaving $GM/r = v^2$: at a given orbital radius all masses orbit at the same speed. This is the same fact as all masses falling with the same acceleration, seen from further out.

forms.condition: a circular orbit
a circular orbit
a circular orbit, in which gravity supplies the whole centripetal force

concepts.name: Kepler’s third law from gravitation
concepts.statement: Substituting the average speed $v = 2\pi r/T$ into $GM/r = v^2$ gives $T^2 = 4\pi^2 r^3/GM$, and taking the ratio of that expression for two satellites of the same parent body gives Kepler's third law, with $M$ cancelling. The derivation shows that the force of gravity is the cause of what Kepler only described, and why the third law compares satellites of one parent body only.

forms.condition: a circular orbit about a mass M
a circular orbit of period T

concepts.name: Finding a mass from an orbit
concepts.statement: Solving $T^2 = 4\pi^2 r^3/GM$ for the ratio $r^3/T^2$ gives a quantity that is the same for every satellite of one parent body and depends only on $G$ and the parent's mass. So if you know the radius and the period of one satellite, you can calculate the mass of the body it goes round. Astronomers use this principle to find the masses of heavenly bodies that have satellites.

concepts.name: Description versus cause
concepts.statement: Kepler's laws describe how the planets move; Newton's universal law of gravitation says why, and that single equation covers every situation in which gravity acts. The earlier Ptolemaic model was a list of facts, with a different rule for each heavenly body and no cause behind any of it, while the Copernican model needs a small set of rules and a single underlying force.

concepts.name: Non-uniform circular motion
concepts.statement: Non-uniform circular motion is circular motion in which the angular velocity changes, as it does for a merry-go-round a child starts from rest or a hard disk that slows to a halt.

concepts.name: Angular acceleration
concepts.statement: Angular acceleration is the rate of change of angular velocity, $\alpha = \Delta\omega / \Delta t$, exactly as linear acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. Its units are radians per second squared, and the faster the angular velocity changes, the greater the angular acceleration.

concepts.name: Tangential acceleration
concepts.statement: In circular motion the linear acceleration that changes a point's speed lies tangent to the circle, so we call it tangential acceleration. As in straight-line motion, it is the change in the magnitude of the velocity divided by the time taken, and it tells how fast a point on the rim speeds up or slows down along its path.

concepts.name: Independence of tangential and centripetal acceleration
concepts.statement: Centripetal acceleration changes the direction of the velocity but not its magnitude, and tangential acceleration changes the magnitude but not the direction. The two are perpendicular to each other, so a body in circular motion may have either, both or neither, and each may be considered on its own.

concepts.name: Tangential and angular acceleration
concepts.statement: Because the radius is constant in circular motion, the change in the linear velocity is the radius times the change in the angular velocity, and so the tangential acceleration is the radius times the angular acceleration. The greater the angular acceleration, the greater the tangential acceleration, and the smaller the wheel, the smaller the tangential acceleration it gives for the same angular acceleration.

concepts.name: Rotational and translational analogs
concepts.statement: The angle of rotation, the angular velocity and the angular acceleration are the rotational counterparts of position, velocity and acceleration, and the radius joins each pair. The angle is the distance divided by the radius, the angular velocity is the velocity divided by the radius, and the angular acceleration is the tangential acceleration divided by the radius. With the analogy, everything you learned about straight-line motion carries over to rotation.

concepts.name: Change in angular velocity
concepts.statement: The change in angular velocity is the difference between the final and the initial values of the angular velocity.

concepts.name: Rotational kinematic equations
concepts.statement: Substituting $v = r\omega$ and $a = r\alpha$ into each of the four kinematic equations for straight-line motion makes the radius cancel, leaving four equations in the angle, the angular velocity, the angular acceleration and the time. They describe the motion without any reference to the forces or masses that produce it, and they hold whenever the angular acceleration is constant.

forms.condition: constant angular acceleration
constant angular acceleration
constant angular acceleration

concepts.name: Average angular velocity
concepts.statement: When the angular acceleration is constant, the average angular velocity is halfway between the initial and the final value, just as the average velocity is halfway between the initial and the final velocity in straight-line motion. The angle turned through is then simply the average angular velocity multiplied by the time.

concepts.name: Linear quantities from angular ones
concepts.statement: Something spinning in place still carries its rim through a distance, and that distance is the radius times the angle turned through, in radians. In the same way the speed of a point on the rim is the radius times the angular velocity. Radians must always be used in these relationships, and because a radian is dimensionless the product of a length and an angle is a length.

concepts.name: Solving a rotational kinematics problem
concepts.statement: Solve a rotational kinematics problem the way you solve a straight-line one. Check that it involves rotation and needs no forces or masses, identify the unknown, and list what is given. Choose the equation that contains the unknown and nothing else unknown, substitute with units, and ask whether the answer is reasonable. Thinking of the translational analog helps, because that motion is already familiar.

concepts.name: Kinematics of rotational motion
concepts.statement: The kinematics of rotational motion describes the relationships among the rotation angle, angular velocity, angular acceleration and time, without regard to the forces and masses that cause the rotation.

concepts.name: Torque on a point mass
concepts.statement: A force applied perpendicular to the radius gives a point mass an acceleration $a = F/m$, and since $a = r\alpha$ this is $F = mr\alpha$. Multiplying both sides by the radius turns the left side into the torque, and the result is the rotational analog of Newton's second law for a single point mass, with $mr^2$ standing where the mass stands in $F = ma$.

concepts.name: Moment of inertia
concepts.statement: To rotate anything other than a point mass, extend the idea of $mr^2$ to a whole body: the moment of inertia is the sum of $mr^2$ over all the point masses that make up the body. It plays the part in rotation that mass plays in straight-line motion, and its unit is the kilogram meter squared. Because the distance to the axis enters it, a body has a different moment of inertia about every axis.

concepts.name: Mass distribution and moment of inertia
concepts.statement: The moment of inertia depends not only on how much mass a body has but on where that mass sits relative to the axis. A merry-go-round full of children is much easier to accelerate when the children stand close to the axis than when they all stand at the rim, though the mass is the same. The distance from the axis enters every term of the sum squared.

concepts.name: Newton’s second law for rotation
concepts.statement: The general relationship among torque, moment of inertia and angular acceleration is that the net torque equals the moment of inertia times the angular acceleration. The larger the torque the larger the angular acceleration, and the larger the moment of inertia the smaller it is. The relationship is valid for any torque, applied to any object, about any axis, which makes it the rotational form of Newton's second law.

concepts.name: Choosing a moment of inertia
concepts.statement: Calculating a moment of inertia by integration is beyond this text, so read it from the table of shapes for the body and axis at hand: a hoop about its axis, a disk, a rod about its end or its center, a sphere. When several bodies turn about one axis, their moments of inertia add, since each is a sum of $mr^2$ over the same axis.

concepts.name: Solving a rotational dynamics problem
concepts.statement: To set up a problem in rotational dynamics, check that it involves torque and mass and choose the system of interest. Draw a free body diagram of the external forces on it, and apply the rotational form of Newton's second law about the point of rotation. Take care over which moment of inertia belongs to the body and which axis you take the torques about. As always, check the answer for reasonableness.

concepts.name: Rotational work
concepts.statement: When a net force is kept perpendicular to the radius of a turning disk, the force is parallel to the displacement and the net work is the force times the arc length travelled. Multiplying and dividing by the radius turns the force into a torque and the arc length into an angle, so that the net work is the net torque times the angle turned through. Torque is analogous to force here, and angle to distance.

concepts.name: Rotational kinetic energy
concepts.statement: A body has kinetic energy by turning as well as by travelling, and the rotational kinetic energy is half the moment of inertia times the square of the angular velocity. The expression is exactly analogous to the translational one, with the moment of inertia standing where the mass stands and the angular velocity where the velocity stands.

concepts.name: Work-energy theorem for rotation
concepts.statement: Substituting the rotational form of Newton's second law into the expression for rotational work, and then using the kinematic relation between the angular velocity and the angle, gives the net work as the change in one half the moment of inertia times the square of the angular velocity. Net work changes the kinetic energy of a system, and for a turning body that kinetic energy is rotational.

concepts.name: Energy of a rolling body
concepts.statement: A body rolling down an incline without slipping converts its gravitational potential energy into two kinds of kinetic energy at once, translational and rotational. The greater its moment of inertia, the more energy goes into turning and the less remains to carry it down the slope. A can of thick soup, whose contents turn with the can, therefore loses the race to a can of thin soup, and a can that slides without rolling wins.

concepts.name: Solving a rotational energy problem
concepts.statement: Solve energy problems that involve rotation as you solve other energy problems. Check that work or energy is involved, choose the system, and decide which kinds of work and energy are present. For a closed system, set the initial kinetic and potential energy equal to the final, remembering that the kinetic energy may have both a translational and a rotational part. For an open system, account for the other forms of energy as well.

concepts.name: Angular momentum
concepts.statement: Angular momentum is the moment of inertia times the angular velocity, $L = I\omega$, just as linear momentum is the mass times the velocity. Its units are kilogram meters squared per second.

concepts.name: Torque and angular momentum
concepts.statement: The net torque on a body is the rate of change of its angular momentum, $\text{net}\;\tau = \Delta L / \Delta t$, which is the rotational form of Newton's second law written in terms of momentum.

concepts.name: Conservation of angular momentum
terms: law of conservation of angular momentum
concepts.statement: If the net torque on a system is zero, then its angular momentum does not change: this is the law of conservation of angular momentum, and it stands beside the conservation of energy and of linear momentum. It is why Earth keeps on spinning, since only the tides exert any significant retarding torque on it, and why a skater can spin for a long time on ice that opposes her very little.

forms.condition: zero net external torque

concepts.name: Spin rate and moment of inertia
concepts.statement: When no net torque acts, angular momentum stays constant, so a body that reduces its moment of inertia must increase its angular velocity to keep the product the same. A skater pulling in her arms and her extended leg spins several times faster, an air mass whose radius narrows becomes a tornado, and the cloud of gas and dust that became the Solar System sped up as gravity drew it together.

forms.condition: zero net external torque

concepts.name: Work done in pulling in
concepts.statement: The skater's angular momentum stays the same when she pulls in her arms, but her rotational kinetic energy rises sharply. The increase comes from the work she does pulling her arms inward against the force that holds them on their circles. Conserving angular momentum does not conserve rotational kinetic energy, because energy can enter from within the system while angular momentum cannot.

concepts.name: Angular momentum in a collision
concepts.statement: A body moving in a straight line has an angular momentum about any pivot point beside its path, $L = mvr$, where $r$ is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to its line of motion. This is what lets a collision that sets bodies spinning be treated by the conservation of angular momentum.

concepts.name: Solving a rotational collision
concepts.statement: When a body free to rotate takes part in a collision, set the angular momentum before equal to the angular momentum after, both about the same pivot point. Before, it is that of the incoming body as a point mass. After, it is the combined moment of inertia about the pivot times the angular velocity, where the combined moment of inertia is the sum of the separate ones about that axis.

concepts.name: Energy and momentum in a rotational collision
concepts.statement: A collision can conserve angular momentum while it loses kinetic energy, because the collision is inelastic. It need not conserve linear momentum either, because the force at the pivot may have a component along the incoming body's path. For the disk and stick, the kinetic energy falls from 22.5 J to 1.57 J while the linear momentum rises. The nail explains it: the stick pushes back on the nail, and the nail pushes forward on the stick.

concepts.name: Percussion point
concepts.statement: Striking the nailed stick at its far end pushes the nail backward and striking it near the nail pushes the nail forward, so there is a point in between at which no force is delivered to the pivot at all. That point is the percussion point. A tennis racquet and a baseball bat have one too, and a ball met there leaves little force and little vibration in the hand, which is what players call the sweet spot.

concepts.name: Using the right-hand rule
concepts.statement: Angular velocity and angular momentum are vectors, and their direction is found by curling the fingers of the right hand in the direction of the rotation: the thumb then points along the axis of rotation in the direction of both. Because the angular momentum is the moment of inertia times the angular velocity, and the moment of inertia is a positive number, the two point the same way.

concepts.name: Direction of a change in angular momentum
concepts.statement: The net torque is the rate of change of angular momentum, so the change in angular momentum points the way the torque points. When the torque is perpendicular to the angular momentum already there, the two add head to tail to give a new angular momentum of the same size pointing in a new direction, and the axis of rotation moves perpendicular to the forces applied rather than the way they push.

concepts.name: Gyroscopic precession
concepts.statement: The weight of a spinning gyroscope and the force from its stand create a horizontal torque, always perpendicular to the angular momentum, so the direction of the angular momentum changes while its magnitude does not and the gyroscope precesses about a vertical axis instead of falling over. A gyroscope that is not spinning simply acquires angular momentum in the direction of the torque and falls. Earth precesses in the same way, once in about 26,000 years, under the torque of the Sun and the Moon on its nonspherical shape.

concepts.name: Right-hand rule for rotation
concepts.statement: The right-hand rule defines the directions of angular velocity and angular momentum: when the fingers of the right hand curl in the direction of the rotation, the thumb points in the direction of $\omega$ and of $L$, along the axis of rotation.

concepts.name: Fluid
concepts.statement: A fluid is a state of matter that yields to a sideways, or shearing, force, while a solid resists one. Liquids, gases, and plasmas are all fluids, because in each of them the particles slide past one another and the substance flows. This one property is what the rest of the chapter rests on: because a fluid cannot withstand a shearing force, it cannot exert one either, and so the force it exerts on any surface is perpendicular to that surface.

concepts.name: Phases of matter
concepts.statement: Matter most commonly exists as a solid, a liquid, a gas, or a plasma. A solid has a definite shape and a specific volume, a liquid has a definite volume but takes the shape of whatever holds it, and a gas or a plasma has neither, since its particles move to fill the container. Knowing which phase a substance is in tells you at once whether it will flow and whether it can be compressed.

concepts.name: Atomic arrangement and phase
concepts.statement: The forces between atoms explain the phases. Atoms in a solid are in contact and held near their neighbors, so a solid keeps its shape and resists compression. Atoms in a liquid are also in close contact but can slide over one another, so a liquid flows and yet still resists compression. Atoms in a gas and charged particles in a plasma are far apart and pull on one another only weakly, so a gas both flows and compresses easily.

concepts.name: Density
concepts.statement: Density is the mass per unit volume of a substance or object, and it is what the old riddle about a ton of feathers and a ton of bricks turns on: the two have the same mass, but the feathers occupy a far greater volume, so their density is much lower. Density is crucial in determining whether an object sinks or floats in a fluid, which is why the chapter defines it before it defines anything else.

concepts.name: Density identifies a substance
concepts.statement: Every substance has its own density, so a measured density helps identify what an object is made of. Gold is about two and a half times as dense as iron, which is about two and a half times as dense as aluminum. Density also reveals the phase of matter and its substructure. Liquids and solids have roughly comparable densities because their atoms are in close contact, while gases are far less dense because large amounts of empty space separate their atoms.

concepts.name: Finding a mass from a density
concepts.statement: Solving $\krho = m/V$ for the mass gives $m = \krho V$, so once the volume of a body is known from its dimensions and its density is looked up, its mass follows. This is how the chapter weighs the water behind a dam, and it is the first step of almost every buoyancy calculation later in the chapter.

concepts.name: Pressure
concepts.statement: Pressure is the force divided by the area perpendicular to the force over which it acts. The same force can have a very different effect depending on the area it spreads over. A poke with a finger merely irritates, while the same force through the sharp end of a needle breaks the skin. Pressure applies to all states of matter, but it matters most in fluids.

concepts.name: Pascal
concepts.statement: The SI unit of pressure is the pascal, which is one newton per square meter. Everyday pressures run to large numbers of pascals, so several other units stay in common use: millibars in meteorology, pounds per square inch for tire pressure, and millimeters of mercury for blood pressure. Knowing what each is worth in pascals is what lets a measurement taken with one instrument be compared with another.

concepts.name: Direction of fluid pressure
concepts.statement: A static fluid cannot withstand a shearing force, and so it cannot exert one either. The force a fluid exerts on any surface is therefore perpendicular to that surface, and the fluid pushes on every surface at once: a swimmer feels pressure on all sides, and the air in a tire pushes outward on every part of it. The pressure itself is a scalar quantity and has no direction; only the forces it produces have one.

concepts.name: Finding a force from a pressure
concepts.statement: Rearranging the definition of pressure gives the force a pressure exerts on a surface, $\kF = \kPr A$. The force is directly proportional to the area acted upon as well as to the pressure itself, which is why the flat end of a gas cylinder must be strong and why a hammered nail can split wood.

concepts.name: Pressure due to the weight of a fluid
concepts.statement: The pressure due to the weight of a fluid at a depth $h$ below its surface is $P = h\rho g$, where $\rho$ is the density of the fluid. The bottom of a container supports the whole weight of the fluid above it, $\rho Ahg$, and dividing that weight by the area gives the pressure.

concepts.name: Pressure independent of container shape
concepts.statement: Because $\kPr = \kh\krho\kg$ contains no width and no length, the pressure at a point in a fluid does not depend on how much fluid there is or on the shape of its container. The average depth of the water at a dam sets the pressure on it, not how far the reservoir stretches behind it. A small column of water inside a ring of sandbags can balance a whole flooded river.

concepts.name: Pressure with depth in liquids and gases
concepts.statement: The result assumes the density is the same everywhere in the fluid. Liquids are nearly incompressible, so it holds in them to great depths. Gases compress easily, and their density falls with height, so the result applies to a gas only over a depth small enough that the density changes little, or with an average density standing in for the true one.

concepts.name: Atmospheric pressure
concepts.statement: Atmospheric pressure is pressure due to the weight of a fluid like any other, in this case the weight of the air above a given height. On average at sea level a column of air standing on one square meter weighs $1.01\times 10^{5}$ N, and that is one atmosphere. It falls as you climb, because there is less air above you, which is why your ears pop on a plane flight.

concepts.name: Finding the force on a wall
concepts.statement: Pressure increases linearly with depth, so the average pressure on a vertical wall is the pressure at its average depth, and the force on the wall is that average pressure times the area of contact. This is how the force on a dam is found, and it is why a dam is built thicker at the bottom, where the pressure is greatest.

concepts.name: Finding a density or a depth from a pressure
concepts.statement: Because $\kPr = \kh\krho\kg$ ties three quantities together, any one of them follows from the other two. Solving for the density gives the average density of a fluid from the pressure it exerts and the height of its column, and solving for the height gives the depth at which a fluid reaches a stated pressure.

concepts.name: Pascal’s principle
concepts.statement: A change in pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to all portions of the fluid and to the walls of its container. The atoms in a fluid are free to move about, so they carry the change everywhere, and an enclosed fluid cannot flow away from the push as a river would. This experimentally verified fact is what makes pressure so important in fluids, since a pressure applied at one place is then known at every other.

concepts.name: Addition of pressures
concepts.statement: A fluid transmits a change in pressure undiminished, so the total pressure in a fluid is the sum of the pressures from the different sources acting on it. The pressure 10.3 m down in a swimming pool is two atmospheres, half from the water above and half from the air above the water. The pressure anywhere in a fluid open to the air is the fluid's own pressure plus atmospheric pressure.

concepts.name: A hydraulic system
concepts.statement: A hydraulic system is an enclosed fluid system used to exert forces. Pushing on one piston raises the pressure everywhere in the fluid, and that pressure pushes on every other piston in the system. The advantage over a lever is that the pressure can be sent through tortuously curved lines to several places at once, which is what lets one brake pedal work four wheels.

concepts.name: Forces in a hydraulic system
concepts.statement: In a simple hydraulic system with its two pistons at the same height, the pressure at one piston equals the pressure at the other, so $F_1/A_1 = F_2/A_2$. The force on the larger piston is larger by the ratio of the areas.

concepts.name: Work in a hydraulic system
concepts.statement: A hydraulic system increases force the way a simple machine does, and like a simple machine it obeys conservation of energy. Work is force times the distance moved. The wheel cylinder moves through a smaller distance than the pedal cylinder by exactly the factor by which the force grows, so the work output equals the work input. The more wheel cylinders you add, the smaller the distance each one moves.

concepts.name: Gauge pressure
concepts.statement: Gauge pressure is the pressure relative to atmospheric pressure. Pressure gauges are built to read zero at atmospheric pressure, which is why a tire with a gaping hole in it reads zero even though there is air inside.

concepts.name: Absolute pressure
concepts.statement: Because pressures add, atmospheric pressure adds to the pressure in any fluid that is not enclosed in a rigid container. The total, or absolute, pressure is therefore the gauge pressure plus atmospheric pressure. Fluids push rather than pull, so in most cases the absolute pressure cannot be negative, and the smallest possible gauge pressure is $-\kPatm$; there is no theoretical limit on how large a gauge pressure can be.

concepts.name: Reading a manometer
concepts.statement: A manometer is a U-shaped tube with one side open to the atmosphere. With both sides open the fluid stands at the same depth on each side, because atmospheric pressure pushes down equally on both. Connect one side to a source of pressure and the levels shift until the height difference balances the difference in pressure, so the gauge pressure is $\kh\krho\kg$ and is found by measuring $\kh$. The height difference is positive when the source is above atmospheric pressure and negative when it is below.

concepts.name: Barometer
concepts.statement: A barometer is a tube with a nearly pure vacuum above the fluid rather than air, so it measures absolute pressure rather than gauge pressure, and what it measures is the pressure of the atmosphere. The mercury stands at whatever height makes the pressure due to its weight equal to atmospheric pressure, which is why atmospheric pressure is so often quoted in millimeters of mercury and why a barometer also works as an altimeter.

concepts.name: Measuring blood pressure
concepts.statement: An inflatable cuff on the upper arm squeezes until the pressure it applies cuts off blood flow below it, and a mercury manometer reads that pressure. As the cuff's pressure slowly drops, the value at which flow first begins is the systolic pressure, the maximum the heart produces. The value at which blood flows without interruption is the diastolic pressure, the minimum between beats. A young adult's typical reading is 120 mm Hg over 80 mm Hg. The manometer uses mercury because it is 13.6 times as dense as water and so gives a column short enough to read.

concepts.name: Systolic pressure
concepts.statement: Systolic pressure is the maximum blood pressure in the artery, reached during each beat because of the pumping action of the heart. In a young adult it is typically about 120 mm Hg.

concepts.name: Diastolic pressure
concepts.statement: Diastolic pressure is the minimum blood pressure in the artery, reached between beats of the heart. In a young adult it is typically about 80 mm Hg.

concepts.name: Millimeter of mercury
concepts.statement: A millimeter of mercury is the pressure that supports a column of mercury one millimeter high, which is 133 Pa. Mercury barometers and manometers are so common that atmospheric pressure and blood pressure are often quoted in this unit.

concepts.name: Buoyant force
concepts.statement: The buoyant force is the net upward force a fluid exerts on any object in it. It arises because pressure increases with depth, so the fluid pushes up on the bottom of the object harder than it pushes down on the top.

concepts.name: Floating and sinking
concepts.statement: The buoyant force competes with the object's weight. If the buoyant force is greater than the weight, the object rises to the surface and floats; if it is less, the object sinks; and if the two are equal, the object remains suspended at that depth. A submarine is built to move between the three by changing what it holds in its ballast tanks.

concepts.name: Archimedes’ principle
concepts.statement: The buoyant force on an object equals the weight of the fluid it displaces. If the object were taken out, the space it occupied would be filled by fluid that the surrounding fluid holds up, so the buoyant force must equal the weight of that fluid.

concepts.name: Average density and floating
concepts.statement: An object floats when its average density is less than the density of the fluid around it. The fluid, having the higher density, contains more mass and hence more weight in the same volume, so the buoyant force, which is that weight, exceeds the object's own. This is why a lump of clay sinks and the same clay molded into the shape of a boat floats: the shape changes the average density, not the mass.

concepts.name: Fraction submerged
concepts.statement: The fraction of a floating object that lies below the surface is the ratio of its average density to the density of the fluid, $\bar{\rho}_{\text{obj}}/\rho_{\text{fl}}$, because the volume submerged equals the volume of fluid displaced and the two have the same mass.

concepts.name: Specific gravity
concepts.statement: Specific gravity is the ratio of the density of an object to the density of a fluid, usually water, and it is dimensionless, so it comes out the same whatever units the densities are written in. A substance whose specific gravity is less than one floats, one greater than one sinks, and one exactly equal to one remains suspended, which is the state a scuba diver tries to reach. For a floating object the specific gravity is also the fraction submerged, which is what a hydrometer reads off directly.

concepts.name: Finding a density by weighing twice
concepts.statement: A submerged object appears to weigh less, and the apparent weight loss is exactly the weight of the fluid it displaces; on a balance that measures mass, the apparent mass loss is the mass of the fluid displaced. Weigh an object in air and again submerged in a fluid of known density, and its volume, and so its density, follow. The same two measurements give the density of the fluid instead when the density of the object is already known.

concepts.name: Cohesive forces
concepts.statement: Cohesive forces are the attractive forces between molecules of the same type. They are what hold a liquid together in an open container, what draw its surface into the smallest area it can take, and what let a column of sap in a tree be pulled upward like a chain held together at every link.

concepts.name: Adhesive forces
concepts.statement: Adhesive forces are the attractive forces between molecules of different types. They are what make a drop cling to a window pane, what let water spread across bare paint but bead up on wax, and what draw blood into a small-diameter tube that merely touches a drop. The competition between adhesion and cohesion decides how a liquid meets a solid.

concepts.name: Surface tension
concepts.statement: Molecules at the surface of a liquid are pulled inward by their neighbors below, while molecules inside the liquid feel no net force at all, so the surface contracts to the smallest area it can. The surface then behaves like a stretched elastic sheet: it dents under an insect's foot and holds up a steel needle although the needle is far denser than water. Surface tension $\kgamma$ is the force per unit length exerted by that stretched membrane, and it is greater for a liquid whose cohesive forces are stronger.

concepts.name: Pressure inside a bubble
concepts.statement: Surface tension pulls a bubble into a sphere and squeezes the gas inside, so the gauge pressure within a bubble is $4\kgamma/r$. The smaller the bubble, the greater that excess pressure, which is why opening a valve between a small balloon and a large one empties the small one into the large one rather than the other way about.

concepts.name: Surface tension in the lungs
concepts.statement: The lungs end in hundreds of millions of mucus-lined sacs called alveoli, about 0.1 mm in diameter, and surface tension in their lining is enough to push air out without any muscle action at all. Because the pressure rises as a sac shrinks, small alveoli would empty into large ones and collapse; a lipoprotein surfactant in the lining prevents this by raising the wall tension as a sac stretches and lowering it as the sac contracts. An infant born without the surfactant has lungs that are very difficult to inflate.

concepts.name: Contact angle
concepts.statement: Where a liquid meets a solid, the angle between the tangent to the liquid surface and the solid surface is the contact angle, and it says which of the two kinds of force is winning. A large angle means the cohesive forces are strong relative to the adhesive ones and the liquid draws itself into a droplet; a small angle means adhesion is flattening the drop against the solid. Water on waxed car paint stands at a large angle, water on bare paint at a small one.

concepts.name: Capillary action
concepts.statement: Capillary action is the tendency of a fluid to be raised or lowered in a narrow tube. Surface tension raises the liquid when the contact angle is less than $90^\circ$ and lowers it when the angle is greater, to a height $h = 2\gamma\cos\theta/\rho gr$.

concepts.name: Pressures in the body
concepts.statement: The pressures measured in the body are gauge pressures, quoted in millimeters of mercury, and they are among the most useful indicators medicine has. Table 11.5 lists them: over a hundred millimeters of mercury in the large arteries at each beat, a few in the large veins, twelve to twenty-four in the eye, and pressures that are negative between the lungs and the ribs and in the esophagus.

concepts.name: Blood pressure and height
concepts.statement: Blood is a fluid with weight, so the pressure in it varies with height in the body exactly as in any other fluid. Standing up puts the feet about 1.4 m below the heart, which raises the pressure there by 108 mm Hg. Standing still for a long time lets blood accumulate in the legs and the legs swell. That is why soldiers standing at attention sometimes faint and why doctors recommend tight stockings for long flights.

concepts.name: Pressure in the eye
concepts.statement: The pressure of the fluid inside the eye keeps its shape, normally in the range of 12.0 to 24.0 mm Hg. When something blocks the circulation of that fluid, the pressure builds, a condition called glaucoma, and it can reach 85.0 mm Hg. Over the $6.0\;\text{cm}^2$ at the back of the eye, that is a force of 6.8 N, the weight of about a 680 g mass resting on the eye, enough to damage the optic nerve permanently.

concepts.name: Pressures in the lungs
concepts.statement: The pressure inside the lungs drops below atmospheric pressure when muscle action in the diaphragm and the rib cage expands the chest, and that draws air in. It rises above atmospheric pressure when the muscles relax and surface tension in the alveoli contracts them, and that forces air out. The liquid attaching the lungs to the inside of the chest wall is at a negative gauge pressure of $-4$ to $-8$ mm Hg, and that attachment keeps the lungs from collapsing. Letting air into the chest cavity breaks it, and a lung may collapse.

concepts.name: Bladder pressure
concepts.statement: Bladder pressure climbs steadily from zero to about 25 mm Hg as the bladder fills to its normal capacity of $500\;\text{cm}^3$. That pressure triggers the micturition reflex, which produces the feeling of needing to urinate and also contracts the muscles around the bladder, raising the pressure to over 100 mm Hg and accentuating the sensation. Coughing, straining, tight clothes and the weight of a fetus all add to the pressure and can trigger the reflex.

concepts.name: Pressures in the skeletal system
concepts.statement: The largest pressures in the body are in the joints and between the vertebrae, because large forces are applied over small areas. Lifting an object improperly can create 5000 N between two vertebrae over an area as small as $10\;\text{cm}^2$, which is $5.0\times 10^{6}\;\text{N/m}^2$, about 50 atmospheres, and that is enough to damage the spinal discs and the bony vertebrae themselves.

concepts.name: Glaucoma
concepts.statement: Glaucoma is the condition caused by the buildup of fluid pressure in the eye when the circulation of that fluid is blocked. The raised pressure pushes on the retina and the optic nerve and can damage them.

concepts.name: Micturition reflex
concepts.statement: The micturition reflex is the feeling of needing to urinate, triggered by the pressure in the bladder as it fills toward its normal capacity.

concepts.name: Flow rate
concepts.statement: Flow rate is the volume of fluid that passes a location through an area during a period of time. Almost every question about a moving fluid asks for it: how much blood a heart pumps, how much water a hose delivers, how much air a duct carries. Because it counts volume rather than distance, it tells you nothing on its own about how fast the fluid is moving or how wide the conduit is, only about the product of the two.

concepts.name: Converting flow rate units
concepts.statement: The SI unit of flow rate is the cubic meter per second, but almost nothing uses it: a heart pumps liters per minute, a fire hose delivers liters per second, and a capillary carries cubic centimeters per second. A liter is a thousandth of a cubic meter. Use whatever metric units are most convenient for the situation, and expect to convert between them in almost every problem.

concepts.name: Flow rate and velocity
concepts.statement: The flow rate is the cross-sectional area of the conduit times the average velocity of the fluid across it, $Q = A\bar{v}$. Flow rate and velocity are therefore related but different quantities: a wide, slow river can carry more water than a narrow, fast one.

concepts.name: Incompressible fluid
concepts.statement: A fluid is incompressible when a given amount of it always occupies the same volume, however hard you press it.
