Liquids are nearly incompressible, so the equation of continuity is valid for all of them. Gases are compressible, and you must apply the equation to them with caution when they compress or expand. Every result of this chapter, Bernoulli’s equation and Poiseuille’s law included, assumes an incompressible fluid.

concepts.name: Equation of continuity
concepts.statement: Because the fluid is incompressible, the same amount of fluid must flow past any point of a tube in a given time, so the flow rate is the same at all points along it. Where the cross-sectional area decreases the velocity must necessarily increase, and where it increases the velocity drops. That is the purpose of a nozzle, and it is why water slows considerably when a river empties into a reservoir and picks up speed again when it leaves.

forms.condition: incompressible fluid

concepts.name: Continuity in branching flow
concepts.statement: In the cardiovascular system and in any other branching network, the flow does not stay in one tube. Continuity still holds, but for the sum of the flow rates in all the branches in any portion along the tube, so the number of branches enters the equation along with their areas and their speeds. The capillaries have an enormously greater total cross-section than the aorta, so the blood in them moves at about a millimeter per second. That is slow enough for the blood to exchange substances with the cells and still fast enough to avoid clotting.

forms.condition: incompressible fluid that branches

concepts.name: Fluid dynamics
concepts.statement: Fluid dynamics is the physics of fluids in motion.

concepts.name: Liter
concepts.statement: A liter is a unit of volume equal to $10^{-3}\;\text{m}^3$, or 1000 cubic centimeters.

concepts.name: Pressure drop in a fast fluid
concepts.statement: Where a fluid speeds up, its pressure drops. A fluid flowing into a narrower channel gains kinetic energy, and that energy comes from the net work done by the higher pressure behind it pushing it into the channel.

concepts.name: Bernoulli’s equation
concepts.statement: Bernoulli’s equation states the relationship between pressure and velocity in a fluid quantitatively: for an incompressible, frictionless fluid the sum of the pressure, the term in the square of the speed and the term in the height is constant along the path a bit of fluid follows. Various quantities in the sum may change as the fluid moves, but the total does not, so a gain in speed or in height has to be paid for out of pressure.

forms.condition: incompressible, frictionless fluid

forms.latex: P_1 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_1^2 + \rho gh_1 = P_2 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2 + \rho gh_2
forms.condition: incompressible, frictionless fluid

concepts.name: Bernoulli’s equation as energy per volume
concepts.statement: Bernoulli’s equation is a form of the conservation of energy principle. The second and third terms are the kinetic and the gravitational potential energy with the mass replaced by the density, so each is an energy divided by a volume, and the pressure is an energy per unit volume too, since a newton per square meter multiplied by meter over meter is a joule per cubic meter. Bernoulli’s equation is, in fact, just a convenient statement of conservation of energy for an incompressible fluid in the absence of friction.

concepts.name: Bernoulli’s equation for a static fluid
concepts.statement: When the fluid is not moving, both speed terms vanish and Bernoulli’s equation says that pressure increases with depth: going down by a height adds the weight of that column of fluid to the pressure. In the simplest case the pressure at the top is zero, and you recover the familiar relationship for the pressure due to the weight of a fluid. So although Bernoulli’s equation describes fluid flow, it includes much of what the preceding chapter found for static fluids.

forms.condition: static fluid, with the lower point taken as the reference height

concepts.name: Bernoulli’s principle
concepts.statement: When a fluid moves but its depth is constant, the terms in the height subtract out and Bernoulli’s equation becomes a statement about pressure and speed alone. Situations of that kind are so important that the equation has a name of its own. It says what the opening of the section argued: if the speed at one point is greater, the pressure there must be less for the equality to hold.

forms.condition: constant depth

concepts.name: Entrainment
concepts.statement: People have long put Bernoulli’s principle to work by using the reduced pressure in a high-velocity fluid to move things about: with a higher pressure on the outside, the fast stream forces other fluids into itself. Entrainment devices have been in use since ancient times as pumps to raise water small heights, and the same trick runs a Bunsen burner, an atomizer, a paint sprayer, an aspirator and the chimney of a water heater.

concepts.name: Lift on a wing
concepts.statement: The airplane wing is a beautiful example of Bernoulli’s principle in action. The wing tilts upward at a small angle and its upper surface is longer, so air flows faster over the top, the pressure there drops, and the difference is a net upward force. A sail has the characteristic shape of a wing too: the pressure on its front is lower than the pressure on its back, which gives a forward force and even lets a boat sail into the wind. Wings also gain lift by pushing air downward, and the deflected air pushes back on the wing by Newton’s third law.

concepts.name: Measuring fluid speed
concepts.statement: Two tubes small enough not to disturb the flow, joined by a manometer, measure the speed of a fluid. The tube facing the oncoming fluid creates a dead spot with zero velocity in front of it, while the fluid passing the other tube keeps its speed, so the pressure at the second opening is lower by the term in the square of the speed. The manometer fluid rises by a height proportional to that term, and the speed is therefore proportional to the square root of the height. The pitot tube built on this principle is the air speed indicator of an aircraft.

concepts.name: Torricelli’s theorem
concepts.statement: Fluid leaving a reservoir through an opening a height $h$ below its surface emerges at the speed it would have if it had fallen freely through that height, $v_2^2 = v_1^2 + 2gh$, whatever the size of the opening.

concepts.name: Applying Bernoulli’s equation
concepts.statement: Every earlier use of Bernoulli’s equation simplified it first, by holding the height constant or the pressure equal at both points. The general case keeps all three terms at both points. Find the speeds from the flow rate and the two cross-sections, measure the heights from whichever point you take as the reference, and solve for the remaining pressure. A fire hose that runs ten meters up a ladder to a narrow nozzle is exactly this case, and its pressure falls for both reasons at once.

concepts.name: Power in fluid flow
concepts.statement: Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is used or supplied. Every term of Bernoulli’s equation is an energy per unit volume, so multiplying the whole equation by the flow rate, which is a volume per unit time, gives a power. Each term then has a clear physical meaning: one is the power supplied to give the fluid its pressure, one the power supplied to give it its kinetic energy, and one the power that goes to gravitational potential energy.

concepts.name: Finding the power of a pump
concepts.statement: A pump that takes fluid in and sends it out through a hose of the same diameter at the same height changes neither the speed nor the height of the fluid. Its kinetic and gravitational potential energy stay the same, and only the pressure term remains. The power the pump supplies is then the pressure it adds multiplied by the flow rate. A pump that raises velocity and height as well, as the heart does, needs all three terms.

concepts.name: Laminar flow
concepts.statement: In laminar flow a fluid moves smoothly in layers that do not mix. The lines in this chapter's figures are streamlines, the paths that small volumes of fluid follow, and in laminar flow they are smooth and continuous. The precise definition of viscosity rests on laminar flow, and so does Poiseuille’s law.

concepts.name: Turbulent flow
concepts.statement: Turbulence is characterized by eddies and swirls that mix layers of fluid together, and its streamlines break up rather than running smoothly. It has two main causes: any obstruction or sharp corner imparts velocities perpendicular to the flow, and high speeds alone will do it, since the drag between adjacent layers and between the fluid and its surroundings forms swirls if the speed is great enough. Turbulent flow mixes the fluid, heats it more and resists more than laminar flow does.

concepts.name: Viscosity
concepts.statement: Viscosity is fluid friction, both within the fluid and between the fluid and its surroundings: juice pours freely and syrup sticks to the pitcher. To measure it, shear a fluid between two plates, one fixed and one moving at a steady speed, and find the force that keeps the top plate moving. That force grows with the speed, with the area of the plate and with the viscosity, and falls as the plates move apart. The viscosity is therefore the force times the separation divided by the speed times the area. Viscosities vary from one fluid to another by several orders of magnitude, gases being far less viscous than liquids, and most of them depend on temperature.

forms.condition: laminar flow

concepts.name: Velocity profile in a tube
concepts.statement: If the flow in a tube has negligible resistance the speed is the same all across it. When a viscous fluid flows, the layer in contact with the wall does not move at all, and the speed increases steadily to its maximum at the center of the tube. The shape of a Bunsen burner flame is that velocity profile made visible, even though the viscosity of natural gas is small.

concepts.name: Resistance to flow
concepts.statement: The resistance to flow is defined by the relationship between flow rate and pressure difference: the flow rate is the pressure difference divided by the resistance, $Q = (P_2 - P_1)/R$, and it is in the direction from high to low pressure. The resistance includes everything except pressure that affects the flow rate.

concepts.name: Poiseuille’s law for resistance
concepts.statement: For laminar flow of an incompressible fluid through a horizontal tube of uniform radius, the resistance is eight times the viscosity times the length, divided by pi times the fourth power of the radius. Resistance directly proportional to viscosity and to length makes good intuitive sense, since both directly affect the amount of friction encountered. The fourth power of the radius is the surprise. J. L. Poiseuille derived the law in an attempt to understand the flow of blood.

forms.condition: laminar flow in a horizontal tube of uniform radius

concepts.name: Poiseuille’s law
concepts.statement: Putting the resistance into the relationship between flow rate and pressure difference gives one equation for laminar flow through a tube: the flow rate is the pressure difference times pi times the fourth power of the radius, divided by eight times the viscosity times the length. It is the working equation of the section, and of every medical application in the chapter.

forms.condition: laminar flow in a horizontal tube of uniform radius

concepts.name: Sensitivity of flow to radius
concepts.statement: The radius enters to the fourth power, so any change in it has a very large effect on the resistance. Doubling the radius decreases the resistance by a factor of sixteen, and reducing a vessel’s radius by only five percent cuts the flow to about eighty-one percent of its original value. That is why the body regulates blood flow mostly by dilating and constricting vessels rather than by working the heart harder, and why plaque in an artery is dangerous out of all proportion to its thickness. The body may compensate by raising the blood pressure, but that puts the heart and any weakened vessel at risk.

concepts.name: Pressure drop from resistance
concepts.statement: Rearranged, the relationship between flow rate, pressure difference and resistance says that flow through a resistance makes the pressure drop along it. That is why the water pressure in a house is lower on a hot summer day when the neighborhood draws heavily: the flow rate in the main is large, so the drop along it is large, and less pressure arrives. The relationship holds for turbulent as well as laminar flow. It also applies to a system whose radius varies, where the drop is greatest at the narrowest place.

concepts.name: Reynolds number for flow in a tube
concepts.statement: The Reynolds number for flow in a tube, $N_{\text{R}} = 2\rho vr/\eta$, is a dimensionless quantity that reveals whether the flow is likely to be laminar or turbulent.

forms.condition: flow in a tube of uniform diameter

concepts.name: Onset of turbulence
concepts.statement: For a Reynolds number below about 2000 the flow is laminar, and above about 3000 it is turbulent. Between 2000 and 3000 the flow is unstable: it can be laminar, but small obstructions and surface roughness can make it turbulent, and it may oscillate randomly between the two. Most of the blood flow in the body is quiet and laminar; the exception is the aorta, where the speed rises above a critical value and the flow becomes turbulent.

concepts.name: Turbulence in the circulatory system
concepts.statement: An occlusion or narrowing of an artery is likely to cause turbulence, both because of the irregularity of the blockage and because of the complexity of blood as a fluid. Turbulence in the circulatory system is noisy and can often be heard: the Korotkoff sounds heard through a stethoscope when a blood pressure cuff is released, the sounds of an aneurysm, and the heart murmurs made by damaged valves that do not close. Ultrasound detects the same turbulence in a way analogous to Doppler-shift radar detecting a storm.

concepts.name: Chaotic behavior
concepts.statement: A system is chaotic when its behavior is so sensitive to some factor that it is extremely difficult to predict. Flow with a Reynolds number between 2000 and 3000 is a good example: whether it is turbulent is difficult but not impossible to predict, and the difficulty lies in the extremely sensitive dependence on roughness and obstructions, where a tiny variation in one factor has an exaggerated effect on the flow. Phenomena as disparate as turbulence, the orbit of Pluto and the onset of irregular heartbeats are chaotic and can be analyzed with similar techniques.

concepts.name: Reynolds number for an object
concepts.statement: The Reynolds number for an object moving in a fluid, ${N'}_{\text{R}} = \rho vL/\eta$, where $L$ is a characteristic length of the object, indicates whether the flow around it is laminar or turbulent. A moving object in a still fluid is equivalent to a stationary object in a flowing stream.

forms.condition: object moving in a fluid

concepts.name: Flow around an object
concepts.statement: Below about 1 the flow around an object can be laminar, particularly if the object has a smooth shape. Between 1 and about 10 the flow turns turbulent, the exact point depending on surface roughness, and a turbulent wake forms behind the object while some laminar flow remains over its surface. Between 10 and a million the flow may be either and may oscillate between the two, and above a million it is turbulent everywhere, even at the surface. Laminar flow occurs mostly when the objects are small, such as raindrops, pollen and blood cells in plasma, so most large objects, airplanes and sailboats among them, create significant turbulence as they move.

concepts.name: Viscous drag
concepts.statement: One consequence of viscosity is a resistance force called viscous drag, exerted on an object moving through a fluid. Unlike simple friction, it depends on the object’s speed, and how it depends on it changes with the Reynolds number. For laminar flow the drag is proportional to the speed, while between about 10 and a million it is proportional to the speed squared. That is why even a small headwind costs a bicycle racer so much and why cyclists take turns leading the pack. For laminar flow around a sphere the drag is proportional to the viscosity, the size of the object and its speed: a more viscous fluid and a larger object both mean more drag. Stokes’ law gives the constant.

concepts.name: Sedimentation and the centrifuge
concepts.statement: Because the viscous drag grows with speed, an object falling through a fluid does not accelerate indefinitely. The drag increases, the acceleration falls, and at the terminal speed the object continues to fall at a constant speed. This is the case for particles of sand falling in the ocean, cells falling in a centrifuge and sky divers falling through the air, and the terminal speed is greatest for low-viscosity fluids and for objects that are dense and small, which is why a skydiver falls more slowly with outspread limbs than in a pike position. Knowing it is useful for estimating how quickly small particles settle, and a centrifuge speeds that settling by replacing gravitational acceleration with a much greater centripetal acceleration.

concepts.name: Diffusion
concepts.statement: Atoms and molecules are in constant motion at any temperature, and in fluids they move about randomly even where there is no macroscopic flow. That motion is a random walk, and diffusion is the movement of substances that it produces. It explains how an ice cube picks up the odors of a freezer, and fluids can even diffuse through solids. It is a slow process over macroscopic distances, because the densities of common materials are great enough that a molecule cannot travel far before a collision scatters it in any direction, including straight backward.

concepts.name: Diffusion distance
concepts.statement: The root-mean-square distance a molecule travels by diffusion is proportional to the square root of the time, $x_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{2Dt}$, not to the time itself, which is what makes diffusion so slow over any large distance.

concepts.name: Diffusion constant
concepts.statement: The diffusion constant is determined experimentally and gathers into one number most of the things that set the rate: the molecule, the medium, the temperature and the cohesive and adhesive forces. It gets progressively smaller for more massive molecules, because the average molecular speed at a given temperature is inversely proportional to molecular mass, and it is far smaller in water than in air, because a molecule in water makes many more collisions in its random walk. It increases with temperature, since the average kinetic energy of the molecules is proportional to absolute temperature.

concepts.name: Rate and direction of diffusion
concepts.statement: A drop of food coloring placed carefully in still water spreads until its concentration is the same everywhere, which is free diffusion, since no barrier inhibits it. Molecular motion is random in direction, so simple chance dictates that more molecules leave a region of high concentration than enter it, and the net rate of diffusion is proportional to the difference in concentration; if the concentrations were the same there would be no net movement at all. The net rate is higher at the start than after the process is partly complete, and it is proportional to the diffusion constant as well.

concepts.name: Semipermeable membranes
concepts.statement: A semipermeable membrane allows only certain small molecules to pass through it. Membranes in living things are generally of this kind, and they affect the rates at which substances diffuse across them.

concepts.name: Osmosis
concepts.statement: Osmosis is the transport of water through a semipermeable membrane from a region of high concentration to a region of low concentration, and it is driven by the imbalance in water concentration. Water is more concentrated in the body than in Epsom salt, so soaking a swollen ankle in Epsom salt moves water out of the body into the lower-concentration region in the salt. Both osmosis and dialysis are used by the kidneys to cleanse the blood.

concepts.name: Dialysis
concepts.statement: Dialysis is the transport of any molecule other than water through a semipermeable membrane because of its concentration difference. It is the same process as osmosis with a different substance moving, and like osmosis it can create substantial pressures. The kidneys use both.

concepts.name: Osmotic pressure and back pressure
concepts.statement: Osmosis can create a substantial pressure. Water moving through a membrane raises the solution on the low-concentration side, and the movement continues until the pressure of the extra height of fluid stops further osmosis. That back pressure is the relative osmotic pressure if neither solution is pure water, and the osmotic pressure if one of them is. It can be very large. Pure water and sea water separated by a membrane that passes no salt come to equilibrium at 25.9 atmospheres, which would raise the salt water 268 meters above the pure water. Turgor, the pressure of a plant cell’s fluid against its wall, is the same effect holding a plant up. Where the back pressure is large enough to reverse the normal direction, the process becomes reverse osmosis or reverse dialysis, which desalinates water and lets a membrane act as a filter.

concepts.name: Active transport
concepts.statement: Substances sometimes pass through a membrane in the direction opposite to the one expected. Cypress tree roots extract pure water from salt water although osmosis would move it the other way. This is not reverse osmosis, because no back pressure causes it. It is active transport, in which a living membrane expends energy to move substances across it. Many living membranes do this, the kidneys among them, and at least a quarter of the body’s energy by some estimates goes to active transport at the cellular level.

concepts.name: Relative osmotic pressure
concepts.statement: Relative osmotic pressure is the back pressure that stops the osmotic process when neither solution is pure water.

concepts.name: Reverse osmosis
concepts.statement: Reverse osmosis is the process that occurs when back pressure is great enough to reverse the normal direction of osmosis, driving water out of the more concentrated solution. It is used to desalinate water by forcing it through a membrane that will not pass salt.

concepts.name: Reverse dialysis
concepts.statement: Reverse dialysis is the process that occurs when back pressure is great enough to reverse the normal direction of dialysis, and it can be used to filter out a substance that a membrane will not pass.

concepts.name: First law of thermodynamics
concepts.statement: The first law is the law of conservation of energy in the form most useful when heat transfer and work are the ways energy enters and leaves a system. The change in internal energy of a system equals the net heat transfer into the system minus the net work done by the system. Positive heat transfer adds energy to the system, positive work takes energy from it, and whatever comes in and is not spent as work stays as internal energy.

concepts.name: Sign conventions for heat and work
concepts.statement: In the first law, heat transfer is positive when it is into the system and work is positive when it is done by the system. The convention matters because the same physical event, heat leaving a body or work being done on it, enters the equation with a minus sign, and a reader who mixes the two conventions will find the internal energy going the wrong way. Some texts define work against the external pressure and so write the law with a plus sign; this book does not.

concepts.name: Heat and work as energy in transit
concepts.statement: Heat transfer and doing work are the two everyday ways of bringing energy into or out of a system, and they are different processes. Heat transfer is driven by a temperature difference and is disorganized; work is a macroscopic force exerted through a distance and is organized. Yet both can produce the same result: a tire grows warmer whether the Sun heated it or the pump compressed it, and once its temperature has risen, nothing tells which did it. A system stores neither as such; both change its internal energy, which is a different kind of thing.

concepts.name: Internal energy
concepts.statement: The internal energy of a system is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of its atoms and molecules, which is to say the sum of their mechanical energy. Because no one can keep track of every atom, the section deals with averages and distributions and, macroscopically, with a few quantities such as pressure, volume and temperature that the internal energy turns out to depend on. It is the account that heat transfer and work pay into and draw from.

concepts.name: Path independence of internal energy
concepts.statement: Experiment shows that the internal energy of a system depends only on the state of the system and not on how it reached that state. The change in internal energy between State 1 and State 2 is therefore the same for every path between them, while the heat transfer and the work done each depend on the path taken. This is what makes internal energy easier to work with than either heat or work: if the state is known, the change in internal energy follows from a few macroscopic variables.

concepts.name: Finding the change in internal energy
concepts.statement: Given the heat transfer into and out of a system and the work done on and by it, find the net heat transfer as heat in minus heat out and the net work as work by minus work on; the first law then gives the change in internal energy. The same procedure, run the other way, finds an unknown heat transfer from a known change in internal energy and a known work, as in problems about the human body.

concepts.name: Human metabolism and the first law
concepts.statement: Human metabolism is the conversion of food into heat transfer, work and stored fat. With the body as the system, heat transfer to the surroundings makes Q negative and the work the body does on the world makes W positive, so the body loses internal energy. Food, which enters as chemical potential energy and counts as work done on the body, replaces it. Eating too much makes the change in internal energy positive, and the body stores the surplus as fat; eating too little makes it negative, and the body metabolizes its own fat. The body also shows that many thermodynamic processes are irreversible: fat can become work and heat, but work and heat cannot become fat again.

concepts.name: Heat engine
concepts.statement: A heat engine is a machine that uses heat transfer to do work. Car engines and steam turbines are examples. Heat transfer into a gas in a cylinder raises its pressure, and the gas pushes a piston through a distance, doing work on the outside world. To repeat the process, heat must leave the gas so that its pressure falls and the piston can return. The first law governs every step, and a few simple processes are the pieces every heat engine is built from.

concepts.name: Work at constant pressure
concepts.statement: A process in which a gas does work on a piston at constant pressure is an isobaric process. The force on the piston is the pressure times the piston's area, the work is that force times the distance the piston moves, and the area times the distance is the change in volume, so the work done is the pressure times the change in volume. A positive change in volume means work done by the gas on the outside world. Pressure is an energy per unit volume, as the fluids chapters noted, and here some of that energy becomes work.

forms.condition: isobaric process
isobaric process, in the sign convention of texts that define work against the external pressure

concepts.name: Work as area on a PV diagram
concepts.statement: A graph of pressure against volume shows a process as a path, and the work done on or by a system in going from one state to another is the area under that path. For a constant pressure the area is a rectangle, the pressure times the change in volume. For a varying pressure, divide the area into strips, each its average pressure times its small change in volume, and add them up. A path toward smaller volume has a negative area, which is work done on the system.

concepts.name: Path dependence of work
concepts.statement: Two paths between the same two states on a PV diagram enclose different areas, so the work done along them differs, and more work is done along the path that runs at higher pressure. This is the path dependence that the first law's Q and W both have and that the internal energy does not, made visible: the endpoints fix the change in internal energy, and the path fixes how much of it arrives as work.

concepts.name: Isochoric process
concepts.statement: A process at constant volume is isochoric. The volume does not change, so the gas moves no piston and no work is done, and any heat transfer goes entirely into the internal energy. On a PV diagram an isochoric process is a vertical path, and it encloses no area.

forms.condition: isochoric process, constant volume

concepts.name: Net work of a cycle
concepts.statement: A cyclical process returns the system to its starting point, and its net work is the area inside the closed loop it forms on a PV diagram. The positive area under the outward legs and the negative area under the return legs leave only the interior. A loop run clockwise gives positive net work, so the engine puts work out; run counterclockwise, the same loop takes work in. The area is often easier to compute than the work along each leg, and comparing the areas of different loops shows which process produces the most work.

concepts.name: Isothermal process
concepts.statement: An isothermal process is one at constant temperature. For an ideal gas, PV is then constant, and because the internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas depends on temperature alone it does not change, so the net heat transfer into the gas must equal the net work done by the gas: just enough heat comes in to replace the work done. An isothermal process is inherently slow, since heat must flow continuously and spread through the gas so that no region is hotter than another.

forms.condition: isothermal process of an ideal gas, constant temperature

concepts.name: Adiabatic process
concepts.statement: An adiabatic process is one in which no heat transfer takes place, achieved by very effective insulation or by running the process so fast that heat has no time to flow. Because Q is zero, the work the gas does comes entirely from its internal energy, so the temperature falls during an adiabatic expansion and the pressure with it. The adiabatic path from a point therefore lies below the isothermal path from the same point, and less work is done along it.

forms.condition: adiabatic process, no heat transfer

concepts.name: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas
concepts.statement: The average kinetic energy of an atom in a monatomic ideal gas is three halves of Boltzmann's constant times the absolute temperature, and kinetic energy is the only internal energy such a gas has, so its total internal energy is N times that average. The internal energy of an ideal gas therefore depends on its temperature alone, which is what makes the isothermal and adiabatic arguments work. Diatomic gases such as air have different formulas.

forms.condition: monatomic ideal gas

concepts.name: Reversible process
concepts.statement: A reversible process is one in which both the system and its environment can return to exactly the states they were in by following the reverse path. Isothermal and adiabatic processes are reversible in principle, but real macroscopic processes never are. Any dissipative mechanism, such as friction or turbulence, produces heat transfer to the environment in both directions of the piston's travel, and reversibility would require that heat transfer to reverse. That real processes cannot reverse points to a second law of thermodynamics.

concepts.name: Isobaric process
concepts.statement: An isobaric process is one that takes place at constant pressure, as when a gas expands against a piston that keeps its pressure fixed.

concepts.name: Irreversible process
concepts.statement: An irreversible process is one that depends on path: it goes in one direction only under a given set of conditions, and the reverse path differs fundamentally. Heat transfer from hot to cold, the conversion of kinetic energy to heat by friction and the spread of a puff of gas through a vacuum chamber are all one-way, and none of them violates the first law, so some other law must forbid their reverse. That law is the second law of thermodynamics.

concepts.name: First expression of the second law
concepts.statement: The familiar direction of heat transfer is the first form of the second law. Heat transfer occurs spontaneously from higher- to lower-temperature bodies but never spontaneously in the reverse direction; put another way, no process can have as its sole result heat transfer from a cooler to a hotter object. A cold object in contact with a hot one never gets colder.

concepts.name: Second expression of the second law
concepts.statement: It is impossible in any system for heat transfer from a reservoir to convert completely to work in a cyclical process in which the system returns to its initial state. Every heat engine must therefore reject some heat to a cold reservoir; the wish that the work output equal the heat input, with nothing lost to the environment, cannot be granted. This is the form of the second law that limits the efficiency of every engine.

concepts.name: Cyclical process
concepts.statement: A cyclical process brings a system, such as the gas in a cylinder, back to its original state at the end of every cycle. Most heat engines, reciprocating pistons and turbines alike, use cyclical processes. Because the internal energy depends only on the state, it is the same at the start and end of every cycle, so its change over a cycle is zero and the first law reduces to the statement that the net work done equals the net heat transfer.

forms.condition: cyclical process, the internal energy the same at the start and end of every cycle

concepts.name: Work output of a heat engine
concepts.statement: Over a complete cycle the internal energy of the engine does not change, so the net work done by the engine equals the net heat transfer into it, which is the heat transfer from the hot reservoir minus the heat transfer into the cold reservoir. The trouble with every engine is that the heat transfer to the cold reservoir is never zero and is usually large.

forms.condition: cyclical process

concepts.name: Efficiency of a heat engine
concepts.statement: The conversion efficiency is the ratio of what we get to what we spend: for a heat engine, the net work output divided by the heat transfer into the engine. Since the work is the difference of the two heat transfers, the efficiency is also one minus the ratio of the heat transfer to the cold reservoir to the heat transfer from the hot one, which shows that an efficiency of one would need no heat transfer to the environment at all. All the Q's are positive, with direction shown by sign or on the schematic.

forms.condition: cyclical process

concepts.name: Finding an engine’s efficiency
concepts.statement: Given any two of the heat transfer into an engine, the heat transfer to the environment and the work output, the cycle's energy balance gives the third, and the efficiency follows as work over heat in. Run the other way, a stated efficiency and a heat input give the work and the waste heat. A large power station is a heat engine, so the same arithmetic gives its daily output, its efficiency and, with the fuel's energy content, the fuel it burns and the carbon dioxide it releases.

concepts.name: Otto cycle
concepts.statement: The Otto cycle is the thermodynamic cycle of the four-stroke gasoline engine, two adiabatic processes and two isochoric ones. An adiabatic compression corresponds to the compression stroke, heat transfer in at constant volume to the burning of the fuel, an adiabatic expansion to the power stroke, and heat transfer out at constant volume to the exhaust and intake. The work out along the expansion exceeds the work in along the compression because the pressure is higher, so there is a net work output, and the cooler the compression and the hotter the expansion the larger the loop and the more efficient the engine, which points to the reservoir temperatures as what sets the limit.

concepts.name: Second law of thermodynamics
concepts.statement: The second law of thermodynamics states that heat transfer occurs spontaneously only from a hotter body to a colder one, never the reverse, and that no cyclical process can convert heat transfer from a reservoir completely into work. The chapter gives it in several equivalent forms.

concepts.name: Carnot cycle
concepts.statement: Sadi Carnot devised in 1824 a theoretical cycle that is the most efficient cyclical process possible, made of two isothermal and two adiabatic processes, all of them reversible. Any heat engine that uses it is a Carnot engine. What defines the cycle is that only reversible processes are used, since irreversible processes involve dissipative factors such as friction and turbulence that increase the heat transfer to the environment and lower the efficiency. The ideal Carnot engine has zero power, like the drinking bird, which is why it is a limit and not a design.

concepts.name: Third expression of the second law
concepts.statement: Stated in terms of reversible processes, the second law has a third form: a Carnot engine operating between two given temperatures has the greatest possible efficiency of any heat engine operating between them, and all engines employing only reversible processes have this same maximum efficiency between the same temperatures. What Carnot discovered in his study of steam engines was this law.

concepts.name: Carnot efficiency
concepts.statement: For a perfect heat engine the ratio of the heat transfer to the cold reservoir to the heat transfer from the hot one equals the ratio of the absolute temperatures of the two reservoirs, so the maximum efficiency is one minus the cold temperature over the hot, both in kelvins. An efficiency of 100% would need a cold reservoir at absolute zero, which is impossible in practice and in theory, and the greatest efficiencies come from the hottest possible hot reservoir and the coldest possible cold one. No real engine reaches the Carnot efficiency.

forms.condition: temperatures in kelvins or any other absolute scale
Carnot engine, temperatures in kelvins
any reversible process

concepts.name: Finding a Carnot efficiency
concepts.statement: Convert the reservoir temperatures to kelvins and the Carnot efficiency follows; or use a stated efficiency and one reservoir temperature to find the other. A real engine that reaches some fraction of the maximum works the same way. Two engines in series, the second running on the exhaust of the first, have an overall Carnot efficiency equal to that of one engine between the outer temperatures.

concepts.name: Real engines and the Carnot efficiency
concepts.statement: All real processes are irreversible, so no real engine is as efficient as a Carnot engine between the same reservoirs; a nuclear station's 35% is a little better than 0.7 of its maximum, and coal, oil and gas stations reach about 42% because their boilers run hotter. Even the best engine has dissipative processes in its peripheral equipment, such as transformers and transmissions, which convert some of the work output back into heat transfer to the environment and lower the overall efficiency further.

concepts.name: Carnot engine
concepts.statement: A Carnot engine is a heat engine that runs on the Carnot cycle, using only reversible processes.

concepts.name: Heat pump
concepts.statement: Heat pumps, air conditioners and refrigerators move heat from cold to hot. They are heat engines run backward: heat flows out of a cold reservoir and into a hot one, and this requires a work input, which itself becomes heat transfer. The heat transfer to the hot reservoir is the heat from the cold reservoir plus the work. A heat pump's mission is the heat delivered to a warm space; a refrigerator's or an air conditioner's is the heat removed from a cold one. You pay only for the work and get the heat from the cold outdoors at no cost.

forms.condition: heat pump, refrigerator or air conditioner; all three quantities positive

concepts.name: Components of a heat pump
concepts.statement: A heat pump has a condenser, an expansion valve, an evaporator and a compressor, joined in a loop that a working fluid runs round. In the outdoor evaporator the fluid takes heat from the cold air and becomes a gas; the electrically driven compressor raises its temperature and pressure and forces it into the indoor condenser coils, where, being hotter than the room, it gives up heat and condenses; the liquid then passes back through the expansion valve and cools as it expands. In a cooling cycle the two coils exchange roles and the fluid runs the other way.

concepts.name: Coefficient of performance of a heat pump
concepts.statement: A heat pump earns its keep by the heat it delivers to the warm space compared with the work it takes, so its coefficient of performance is the heat transfer to the hot reservoir divided by the work input. A heat engine's efficiency is the work over that same heat transfer, so the coefficient of performance is the reciprocal of the efficiency. Because every efficiency is less than one, the coefficient is always greater than one: a heat pump always delivers more heat than the work put into it.

concepts.name: Heat pumps and temperature difference
concepts.statement: Because the coefficient of performance is the reciprocal of the efficiency and the Carnot efficiency shrinks as the two reservoir temperatures approach one another, a heat pump does best when the difference between outdoors and indoors is small and worst in very cold climates. Friction and other irreversible processes do not help a heat pump as they lower an engine's efficiency; they take part of the work input as heat before it reaches the pump and lower the coefficient of performance. Real heat pumps reach values from about 2 to 4, and they are most economical where winters are mild and summers warm.

concepts.name: Coefficient of performance of a refrigerator
concepts.statement: An air conditioner or refrigerator earns its keep by the heat it removes from the cold environment compared with the work input, so its coefficient of performance is the heat transfer from the cold reservoir divided by the work. What a heat pump counts as its benefit, a refrigerator counts as waste heat. The heat to the hot reservoir is the heat from the cold one plus the work, so for the same engine between the same temperatures the refrigerator's coefficient is the heat pump's minus one. Real refrigerators reach values from 2 to 6 because their temperature differences are small.

forms.condition: the same heat engine used as an air conditioner or a heat pump between the same two temperatures

concepts.name: Finding the best coefficient of performance
concepts.statement: A Carnot engine reversed gives the best possible heat pump or refrigerator, so the best coefficient of performance follows from the Carnot efficiency between the two reservoir temperatures in kelvins: the reciprocal for a heat pump, and one less than that for a refrigerator. With a work input given, the heat delivered or removed follows, and with a price per kilowatt-hour so does the cost, which is how the section compares a heat pump with burning natural gas.

concepts.name: Energy efficiency rating
concepts.statement: The energy efficiency rating is a coefficient of performance in mixed units: British thermal units of heat transfer from the cold environment per hour, divided by watts of power input. Several countries still use it for room air conditioners, which carry ratings from 6 to 12. The rating is not the same as the coefficient of performance, but it serves for comparison: the greater the rating, the cheaper the unit is to run and the more it is likely to cost to buy.

forms.condition: Q_c in British thermal units, t_1 in hours, W in joules, t_2 in seconds

concepts.name: Solving thermodynamics problems
concepts.statement: Work a thermodynamics problem in seven steps. Decide whether heat, work or internal energy is involved. Identify the system and draw a labeled diagram of the energy flow. List the unknowns, remembering that a maximum efficiency means a Carnot engine and that efficiency is not the same as coefficient of performance. List the knowns, distinguishing heat in from heat out and work in from work out, and name the kind of process. Solve the appropriate equation, substitute with units, and check that the answer is reasonable: an efficiency below one and a coefficient of performance above one.

concepts.name: Entropy
concepts.statement: Entropy is a measure of a system's disorder and of the unavailability of its energy to do work. All forms of energy can do work, but it is not always possible, even in principle, to convert all of a system's energy into work, and entropy measures how much cannot be converted. Like internal energy it is a property of state: the entropy of a system depends only on its state and not on how it got there, so you can compute its change for any process, real or imagined.

concepts.name: Change in entropy
concepts.statement: The change in entropy of a system in a reversible process is the heat transfer, positive into the system and negative out of it, divided by the absolute temperature at which it takes place, in joules per kelvin. For a Carnot cycle the heat transfers at the two reservoirs are in the ratio of their absolute temperatures, so this ratio is the same at both. Where the temperature changes a little during the process, use the average temperature. The definition holds strictly for reversible processes, but because entropy is a property of state, you can find the change for any real process by imagining a reversible one between the same two states.

forms.condition: reversible process, or any process whose end states a reversible process could join

concepts.name: Entropy increase in irreversible processes
concepts.statement: Spontaneous heat transfer from hot to cold is irreversible, and its total entropy change is found by imagining a reversible loss from the hot reservoir and a reversible gain by the cold one. Because the change in entropy is the heat over the temperature, the same heat makes a larger change at the lower temperature: the hot reservoir's loss is smaller than the cold reservoir's gain, and the total increases. The result is general: every irreversible process increases the entropy of the system.

concepts.name: Second law in terms of entropy
terms: second law of thermodynamics stated in terms of entropy
concepts.statement: The total change in entropy over a Carnot cycle is the hot reservoir's loss plus the cold reservoir's gain, and because the two heat transfers are in the ratio of the temperatures the total is zero; this holds for any reversible process, which changes neither the entropy of the system nor that of its surroundings. Real processes are irreversible and increase the total entropy. So there are only two possibilities, and the fourth form of the second law says so: entropy is constant in a reversible process and increases in an irreversible one, and it never decreases. Heat cannot flow spontaneously from cold to hot because entropy would decrease. Entropy, unlike energy, is not conserved.

forms.condition: Carnot engine, and any reversible process

concepts.name: Unavailable energy
concepts.statement: When entropy increases, a certain amount of energy becomes permanently unavailable to do work. The energy is not lost, but its character changes, so some of it can never again become an organized force acting through a distance. The amount that becomes unavailable is the increase in entropy times the lowest temperature used. Two perfect engines fed the same heat give different work when one receives it only after the heat has fallen to a colder reservoir, and the difference is exactly this quantity.

concepts.name: Heat death of the universe
concepts.statement: As entropy increases, less and less of the energy in the universe is available to do work. Temperature differences, which heat engines run on, arose as the universe matured and are being used up. On Earth the stores of fuel and the temperature differences behind wind, geothermal and tidal energy will be spent. The Sun will replenish some of them for another five billion years, but in the very long run all stars will die and all temperatures will equalize. The universe is headed for thermodynamic equilibrium, maximum entropy, when no work can be done, though calculations suggest that is at least 10¹⁰⁰ years away.

concepts.name: Entropy and disorder
concepts.statement: Entropy is related not only to the unavailability of energy but also to disorder, as Boltzmann first proposed. Melting a block of ice turns a structured arrangement of molecules into a liquid with no fixed positions, and the entropy rises by a large amount. Mixing equal masses of warm and cool water has three results at once. The entropy increases; some energy becomes unavailable to do work, because no temperature difference remains to run an engine; and a single mass at one temperature is less orderly than two masses at two. These three results are essentially equivalent.

concepts.name: Local decreases in entropy
concepts.statement: Living organisms are highly structured and much lower in entropy than what they grow from, and some take this to mean that evolution violates the second law. It does not. The entropy of one part of the universe can always decrease, provided the environment's entropy increases by more, so that the total change is positive. Picking up scattered marbles or building a bridge lowers the entropy of those systems by energy transfer. The Earth, intercepting a small part of the Sun's heat transfer into deep space, is a heat engine of high complexity that produces small local decreases in entropy at the cost of a large total increase.

forms.condition: any real process

concepts.name: Finding an entropy change
concepts.statement: The heat transfer and the absolute temperature at which it takes place give the change in entropy. Where the temperature changes a little, use the average temperature in kelvins, and for a phase change the heat transfer is the mass times the latent heat. For a transfer between two bodies, the total change is the sum of a negative change at the hotter temperature and a positive one at the colder. Multiply the total by the lowest temperature to find the energy made unavailable.

concepts.name: Macrostate and microstate
concepts.statement: A macrostate is an overall property of a system, such as the total number of heads and tails in a toss or the pressure, volume and temperature of a gas; it does not specify the details. A microstate is a detailed description of every element of the system, such as the order in which the heads and tails came up or the positions and velocities of every atom. Each macrostate can be reached by some number of microstates, and the analysis assumes that every microstate is equally probable, which requires the coins to be fair.

concepts.name: Probability of disorder
concepts.statement: The most orderly macrostates, all heads or all tails, have the fewest microstates and are the least likely; the most disorderly, an even split, have the most and are the most likely. With five coins the odds are 30 to 2 that a toss leaves an orderly array less orderly; with a hundred, there is one way to get all heads and 10²⁹ ways to get fifty, and a toss a second would produce all heads once in 2 × 10²² years, a trillion times the age of the universe. The growth in the odds favoring disorder continues as the system grows, so for the atoms of a gas the orderly macrostate, all in one corner, is so unlikely that it never happens.

concepts.name: Boltzmann’s entropy
concepts.statement: Boltzmann proved that the entropy of a system in a given macrostate is Boltzmann's constant times the natural logarithm of the number of microstates corresponding to that macrostate, and that this expression agrees with the definition of the change in entropy as heat transfer over temperature. Because the number of microstates is proportional to the probability of the macrostate, entropy is directly related to probability: the more likely the state, the greater its entropy. This explains the second law at the most basic level. A decrease in entropy is a move to a less probable state, and for a macroscopic system the odds against it are so long that no one ever observes it.

forms.condition: k the Boltzmann constant, W the number of microstates of the macrostate

concepts.name: Finding entropy from microstates
concepts.statement: The change in entropy between two macrostates is Boltzmann's constant times the difference of the logarithms of their numbers of microstates, read from a table or counted. The ratio of the two numbers of microstates tells how much more likely one macrostate is than the other, and so whether a given decrease in entropy could ever occur. A change of 10⁻²¹ J/K is a one in 10³⁰ chance, so a macroscopic decrease of the order of 10³ J/K is an utter impossibility.

forms.latex: \Delta S = S_{\text{f}} - S_{\text{i}} = k\ln W_{\text{f}} - k\ln W_{\text{i}}

concepts.name: Statistical interpretation of the second law
concepts.statement: The several statements of the second law say what happens; the statistical view says why. Heat flows only from hot to cold, energy becomes ever less available and the universe grows more disorderly because disorder is vastly more probable than order, and a macroscopic system has so many atoms that the improbable never occurs. The gas that fills its container will never gather in one corner. Energy transfer from outside could force it there and lower its entropy, but only at the cost of a larger increase elsewhere, and left alone it disperses again. Entropy can decrease, but for any macroscopic system the outcome is so unlikely that no one will ever observe it.

concepts.name: Solving entropy problems
concepts.statement: Work an entropy problem in seven steps. Decide whether entropy is involved. Identify the system and draw a labeled diagram of the energy flow. List the unknowns. List the knowns, identifying the heat transfer, the temperature at which it takes place and the initial and final states. Solve the appropriate equation, remembering that a reversible process joining any two states gives the change in entropy between them. Substitute with units, and check that the answer is reasonable: the total entropy increases in any real process, and disordered states are the more probable.

concepts.name: Macrostate
concepts.statement: A macrostate is an overall property of a system, such as the total number of heads and tails in a set of coin tosses, without regard to the order in which they arise.

concepts.name: Microstate
concepts.statement: A microstate is one detailed arrangement of a system, such as one particular sequence of heads and tails, and many microstates may belong to the same macrostate.

concepts.name: Statistical analysis
concepts.statement: Statistical analysis examines a system by counting its possibilities, such as the microstates that belong to each macrostate, to find how likely each outcome is.

concepts.name: Heat
concepts.statement: Heat is the spontaneous transfer of energy due to a temperature difference. When two objects at different temperatures are brought into contact, energy passes from the hotter to the colder one until they reach the same temperature, and no force acts through a distance while it does, so the transfer is not work. Heat is therefore a form of energy in transit: it exists only while the temperature difference drives it, and it ceases once the temperatures are equal.

concepts.name: Heat versus temperature
concepts.statement: We may say the heat was unbearable when we mean the temperature was high. Heat is a form of energy, measured in joules; temperature is not an energy but a measure of the average kinetic energy of the atoms and molecules. The confusion arises because we sense the flow of heat rather than the temperature itself. Keeping the two apart lets the rest of the chapter show that adding heat need not raise a temperature at all.

concepts.name: Units of heat
concepts.statement: Because heat is a form of energy, its SI unit is the joule, but heat is also measured in the calorie, the energy needed to warm 1.00 g of water by 1.00 °C, and most often in the kilocalorie, which warms 1.00 kg of water by the same amount. A food calorie is a kilocalorie, a fact not easily determined from package labeling, and converting among these units is part of almost every problem in the chapter.

concepts.name: Mechanical equivalent of heat
concepts.statement: Doing work can also change the temperature of a substance, and James Prescott Joule's experiments established the mechanical equivalent of heat, the work that produces the same effects as heat transfer. The best modern value is 1.000 kcal = 4186 J, which we treat as the conversion between two units of energy. In Joule's apparatus falling weights turn paddles in water. Gravitational potential energy becomes kinetic energy, viscosity randomizes it into the motion of the molecules, and the thermometer rises exactly as it would have with heat added instead.

forms.condition: the 15 °C calorie

concepts.name: Changing internal energy by heat or work
concepts.statement: Heat added to a system changes its internal energy and usually its temperature, and so does work done on the system, by stirring or by rubbing. A system has a well-defined internal energy, but it does not have a heat content or a work content: once the energy is inside, nothing about the sample says which way it came. This is why the book says heat transfer rather than heat, and it is the idea Chapter 15 will build the first law of thermodynamics on.

concepts.name: Kilocalorie
concepts.statement: The kilocalorie is a unit of heat, 1000 calories, the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1.00 kg of water by 1.00 °C. A food calorie is a kilocalorie.

concepts.name: Factors in heat transfer
concepts.statement: Experiments show that the heat transferred to change a body's temperature depends on three factors: the change in temperature, the mass of the body, and the substance and its phase. Doubling the temperature change of a given mass takes twice the heat, doubling the mass takes twice the heat for the same change, and the same change in the same mass of water takes 10.8 times the heat it takes in copper. The first two follow from the internal energy being proportional to the absolute temperature and to the number of molecules; the third is a property of the material.

concepts.name: Heat and temperature change
concepts.statement: The heat transferred is the mass times the specific heat times the change in temperature, provided there is no phase change and no work is done. The temperature change is the same in kelvin and in degrees Celsius, so either will do, and with heat in kilocalories the specific heat is in kcal/(kg·°C). This is the working equation of the whole chapter, since every later method of heat transfer comes back to the temperature change it produces.

forms.condition: no phase change and no work done

concepts.name: Specific heat
concepts.statement: The specific heat is the amount of heat necessary to change the temperature of 1.00 kg of a substance by 1.00 °C. It depends on the material and its phase, must generally be looked up in a table because there is no simple way to calculate it, and varies little with temperature for most solids and liquids. Water's is among the largest of any material, five times that of glass and ten times that of iron, which is important for sustaining life on Earth.

concepts.name: Finding the temperature rise from work
concepts.statement: When work turns into internal energy, the same equation, solved for the temperature change, gives the rise: the energy delivered divided by the mass and the specific heat of what absorbs it. Truck brakes on a downhill run convert the gravitational potential energy the truck loses into internal energy of the brake material. Because the brakes are small compared with the truck, even a tenth of that energy warms them quickly.

concepts.name: Calorimetry
concepts.statement: When two bodies at different temperatures touch in an insulated container, heat passes from the hotter to the colder until they reach a common temperature. No heat leaves the pair, so the heat the hot body loses is the heat the cold one gains. With signs, the heat into the cold body is positive, the heat out of the hot body is negative, and the two sum to zero. This is a calorimetry problem, and calorimetry measures the heat content of foods and the specific heats of materials.

forms.condition: no heat exchanged with the surroundings

concepts.name: Finding the final temperature of two bodies
concepts.statement: Solving the calorimetry balance for the final temperature gives a weighted average of the two starting temperatures, each weighted by its body's mass times specific heat. The pan at 150 °C and the water at 20.0 °C meet at 59.1 °C, much closer to the water, because water's specific heat is more than four times aluminum's and its mass times specific heat is the larger weight. The skill is to write the heat lost and the heat gained in terms of the one unknown temperature and then collect the terms.

forms.latex: T_{\text{f}} = \frac{m_{\text{Al}} c_{\text{Al}} T_{\text{i},\text{Al}} + m_W c_W T_{\text{i},W}}{m_{\text{Al}} c_{\text{Al}} + m_W c_W}
forms.condition: two bodies exchanging heat with no phase change

concepts.name: Water moderating temperature
concepts.statement: Because water has a greater specific heat than most common substances, it undergoes a small temperature change for a given heat transfer. A large body of water such as a lake needs a great deal of heat to warm appreciably, so its temperature stays nearly constant through a day even when the air's changes a great deal, while it does change over the longer times from summer to winter. Land warms and cools faster than water, which is what drives land breezes and sea breezes.

concepts.name: Latent heat
concepts.statement: Heat transfer causes no temperature change while a substance changes phase. The energy goes into breaking the cohesive bonds between molecules rather than into their kinetic energy, so ice at 0 °C stays at 0 °C until all of it has melted. The same energy comes back out, usually as thermal energy, when the bonds form again in freezing or condensation. The heat that changes the phase of a mass is that mass times a latent heat coefficient, a material constant. It is latent, or hidden, because the energy enters or leaves without changing the temperature.

forms.condition: during a phase change

concepts.name: Heat of fusion
concepts.statement: The latent heat of fusion is the heat that melts a kilogram of a substance at its melting point, and the kilogram releases the same heat when it freezes. For water it is 334 kJ/kg, enough to warm a kilogram of liquid water from 0 °C to 79.8 °C. A bag of ice at 0 °C therefore absorbs far more energy than a bag of water at the same temperature, and water freezing on a sprayed orchard warms the trees.

forms.condition: melting or freezing
melting at the melting temperature

concepts.name: Heat of vaporization
concepts.statement: The latent heat of vaporization is the heat that turns a kilogram of liquid into vapor at the boiling point, and the vapor releases the same heat when it condenses. For water it is 2256 kJ/kg, nearly seven times its heat of fusion, so boiling away a kilogram of water costs more than raising it from ice-cold to boiling. Condensation on a glass of iced tea releases energy into the glass and speeds the melting of the ice.

forms.condition: vaporization or condensation

concepts.name: Heating curve of water
concepts.statement: Adding heat to ice at −20 °C traces a graph with slopes and plateaus. The temperature rises linearly while the ice warms, stops at 0 °C while the ice melts and every joule goes into the phase change, rises again more slowly through the liquid because water's specific heat is twice ice's, stops at 100 °C for a much longer plateau while the water boils, and rises once more as steam. The plateaus are the latent heats, and their lengths beside the slopes show that the energy of a phase change is enormous compared with that of a temperature change.

concepts.name: Evaporation below the boiling point
concepts.statement: Water evaporates at temperatures below its boiling point, and it costs more energy per kilogram to do so, because the molecules have less kinetic energy to draw on: at body temperature the heat of vaporization is 2430 kJ/kg, about ten percent higher than at 100 °C. Perspiration takes this heat from the skin, which is why sweating cools, and high humidity slows evaporation so that the sweat stays on your brow. The same evaporation is why air temperatures in humid climates rarely rise above 35 °C.

concepts.name: Condensation and freezing release heat
concepts.statement: To make vapor condense or liquid freeze, you must remove exactly the energy the phase change absorbed in the other direction, and the surroundings receive it. That is why condensation on a cold glass speeds the melting of the ice inside, why temperatures in humid weather rarely fall below the dew point, why spraying an orchard with water protects it from a hard frost, and why freezing water stays at 0 °C and no colder.

concepts.name: Heat of sublimation
concepts.statement: Sublimation is the transition from the solid phase directly to the vapor phase, as when snow disappears without a trace of liquid, dry ice makes its smoke, or frost forms on a cold window from vapor alone. It occurs because the equilibrium vapor pressure of a solid is not zero. The energy required is the mass times the heat of sublimation, a constant of the same order as the other latent heats, so dry ice is an effective coolant and frosting releases energy.

forms.condition: solid to vapor, or vapor to solid

concepts.name: Finding the final temperature with a phase change
concepts.statement: When a phase change takes part in a heat exchange, work the problem in stages. The heat that melts the ice, then the heat that warms the melted water, balance the heat the other body gives up, with every term in the one unknown final temperature. Try the problem without a phase change first. If the temperature change would carry a body past a melting or boiling point, go back and do it in steps, and check at the end that you have missed no phase change.

forms.condition: the soda and the ice exchange heat with nothing else

concepts.name: Three methods of heat transfer
concepts.statement: Whenever there is a temperature difference, heat transfer occurs, and every process by which it does takes place by only three methods: conduction, convection and radiation. All three have one thing in common, that they transfer heat solely because of a temperature difference, and we control their rates by choosing materials, controlling the movement of air and choosing colors. A fireplace shows all three at once.

concepts.name: Conduction
concepts.statement: Conduction is heat transfer through stationary matter by physical contact. The matter is stationary on the large scale, though its atoms and molecules are in thermal motion at any temperature above absolute zero, and the heat passes between the electric burner of a stove and the bottom of a pan, or from a hot floor into the sole of a foot, without anything moving from one place to the other.

concepts.name: Convection
concepts.statement: Convection is heat transfer by the macroscopic movement of a fluid. The fluid itself carries the energy from one place to another, as the air does in a forced-air furnace, in the draft up a chimney and in the weather, and as water does in the cooling system of a car.

concepts.name: Radiation
concepts.statement: Heat transfer by radiation occurs when microwaves, infrared radiation, visible light or another form of electromagnetic radiation is emitted or absorbed. The Sun warms the Earth this way across empty space, a fire warms the room mostly this way, and the human body radiates infrared whether or not anything touches it.

concepts.name: Conduction by molecular collisions
concepts.statement: The molecules of a hotter body have the greater average kinetic energy, and when a fast molecule and a slow one collide at the surface where two bodies touch, energy passes from the faster to the slower. The cumulative effect of all the collisions is a net flux of heat from the hot body to the cold one that grows with the temperature difference and with the area of contact, and that falls to zero when the temperatures are equal. Because it relies on random motion, conduction is slow over distances larger than a molecule's reach.

concepts.name: Rate of conductive heat transfer
concepts.statement: The rate at which heat flows through a slab of material by conduction is proportional to the temperature difference across it and to its area, inversely proportional to its thickness, and set by a constant of the material, its thermal conductivity. Experiment revealed and confirms these four factors, and the equation holds whether the slab is window glass or walrus blubber. It gives the rate in watts.

forms.condition: steady conduction through a slab

concepts.name: Thermal conductivity
concepts.statement: Thermal conductivity measures a material's ability to conduct heat, and it spans more than four orders of magnitude across common substances. The best thermal conductors, silver, copper, gold and aluminum, are also the best electrical conductors, because of the density of free electrons in them, and cooks use utensils made of them. Styrofoam, fiberglass, wool and down conduct poorly because they trap many small pockets of air, whose own conductivity is among the lowest of all.

concepts.name: R factor
concepts.statement: A good insulator combines a small conductivity with a large thickness, and the ratio of thickness to conductivity is the R factor. The rate of conductive heat transfer is inversely proportional to it, so the larger the R factor, the better the insulation. Household insulation quotes it, still in non-metric units: 3.5-inch fiberglass batts rate 11 and 6.5-inch batts 19.

concepts.name: Finding the mass melted by conduction
concepts.statement: The conduction equation gives a rate; multiplying it by a time gives the heat, and that heat may be spent on a phase change. A Styrofoam ice box in a hot car trunk lets heat in at a rate set by its walls, and over a day that heat melts a mass of ice equal to the total heat divided by the heat of fusion. The skill is to carry a rate into an amount and an amount into a mass, keeping each step's units.

concepts.name: Finding the temperature difference from a heat flow
concepts.statement: Solved the other way, the conduction equation gives the temperature difference that a known rate of heat transfer keeps across a slab. Through the aluminum bottom of a pan boiling away a gram of water a second, 2.26 kW crosses with a difference of only 5.33 °C, because aluminum conducts so well; across a ceramic stove top of the same area the same rate would need a thousand degrees. A small temperature difference with a large heat flow is the mark of a good conductor.

concepts.name: Scaling of the conduction rate
concepts.statement: Because area is the product of two lengths and thickness is one, doubling every dimension of a slab quadruples the area and only doubles the thickness, and the rate of conductive heat transfer doubles. Comparisons of this kind, a thin window against a thick wall, a callus against a bare sole, are answered by ratios of the four factors without evaluating either rate.

concepts.name: Natural convection
concepts.statement: Buoyant forces drive natural convection. A heated fluid expands, its density falls, and it rises through the cooler, denser fluid around it, which sinks to take its place; the loop that forms carries heat with the moving matter. A gravity furnace heats a house this way, a pot of water on a stove circulates this way, and ocean currents and the atmosphere carry energy across the globe this way. Forced convection, in a car's cooling system or the blood vessels of the skin, is the same transport driven by a pump.

concepts.name: Finding heat transfer by convection
concepts.statement: To find the heat convection carries, find the mass of fluid moved, from its density and volume, and multiply by its specific heat and its temperature change. Divide by the time in which that mass is replaced to get the rate. Warming the air of a house by 10.0 °C, when all of it is replaced every half hour, takes 4.64 kW, the power of forty-six 100 W bulbs, which is why houses are weather-stripped.

forms.condition: the mass m of fluid is moved or replaced in the time t

concepts.name: Wind chill
concepts.statement: A cold wind is much more chilling than still cold air, because convection combines with conduction in the body to increase the rate at which energy leaves it. Wind-chill factors are the temperatures of still air that would produce the same rate of cooling as air of a given temperature and speed, and they are a dramatic reminder of convection's ability to transfer heat faster than conduction: a 15.0 m/s wind at 0 °C chills like still air at about −18 °C.

concepts.name: Trapped air is an insulator
concepts.statement: Air transfers heat rapidly by convection but conducts poorly, so whether it insulates depends on whether it can flow. The 9 cm space inside a house wall is large enough for convection, so builders fill it with insulation to stop the air moving. The 1 cm gap of a double-paned window is too small for convection and takes advantage of air's low conductivity. Fur, feathers and fiberglass all trap air in pockets too small for convection, which is why they are light and warm.

concepts.name: Evaporation rate
concepts.statement: When convection is accompanied by a phase change, the moving fluid carries the latent heat with it, and the rate at which mass evaporates to remove a given power is that power divided by the heat of vaporization. Sweat evaporating from the skin can carry away a resting body's 120 W at about 3 g per minute, even when the air is as warm as the skin, provided air flow replaces the saturated air. The same process carries heat from the ocean into the atmosphere, drives thunderheads 20 km into the stratosphere by positive feedback, and lets a melting iceberg cool the sea it drifts through.

forms.condition: the heat is carried away by evaporation alone

concepts.name: Radiation spectrum and temperature
concepts.statement: A hot body emits electromagnetic waves that need no medium to travel, and shorter wavelengths carry more energy. Because a body radiates more heat at higher temperatures, its color changes with its temperature: from the infrared you feel from a stove element that has not yet begun to glow, to red, to the yellow and white of steel in a blast furnace. The spectrum of an ideal radiator rises dramatically with temperature, and its peak shifts toward the visible and the ultraviolet.

concepts.name: Absorbers and emitters
concepts.statement: The rate of heat transfer by radiation is largely determined by the color of the object. Black absorbs best and radiates best, so black asphalt is hotter than gray sidewalk by day and colder by night; white and silver absorb poorly and radiate poorly, reflecting radiation like a mirror. An ideal radiator is the same color as an ideal absorber, and the balance of radiation into and out of an object depends only on how well the object itself emits and absorbs.

concepts.name: Emissivity
concepts.statement: The emissivity is a measure of how well an object radiates. An ideal jet-black radiator, a black body, has an emissivity of 1, a perfect reflector has 0, and real objects fall between: tungsten filaments about 0.5, carbon black about 0.99, and skin 0.97 in the infrared, so that we are all nearly black in the infrared whatever our visible color. The Earth's average emissivity is about 0.65, complicated by its varying cloud cover.

concepts.name: Stefan-Boltzmann law
concepts.statement: The rate of heat transfer by emitted radiation is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant times the emissivity times the surface area times the fourth power of the absolute temperature in kelvin. The radiation rate goes as the surface area, which is why knocking apart the coals of a fire makes it noticeably hotter to stand near, and it goes as the fourth power of the temperature, a remarkably strong dependence that the next two results turn on. The temperature must be absolute; a Celsius value in this equation is wrong.

forms.condition: T in kelvin

concepts.name: Fourth-power dependence of radiation
concepts.statement: Because the radiated power goes as the fourth power of the absolute temperature, small temperature differences produce detectable differences in radiation: a body at 40 °C radiates about 30 percent more than the same body at 20 °C, and skin at 34.0 °C radiates 1.31 percent more than at 33.0 °C, enough for a thermograph to map. At larger ratios the effect is enormous, a radiator at four times the absolute temperature emitting 256 times the power.

concepts.name: Net rate of heat transfer by radiation
terms: net rate of heat transfer by radiation
concepts.statement: All objects emit and absorb radiation, so the net rate is the absorption minus the emission, which for an object at one temperature surrounded by an environment at another is the Stefan-Boltzmann expression in the difference of the two fourth powers, with the emissivity of the object alone. It does not matter whether the surroundings are white, gray or black; when the surroundings are hotter the net transfer is into the object, and when they are colder it is out. An unclothed person in a 22.0 °C room loses about 99 W this way.

forms.condition: an object at T_1 in surroundings of uniform temperature T_2, both in kelvin

concepts.name: Greenhouse effect
concepts.statement: The Earth receives almost all its energy as radiation from the Sun and radiates energy back into a dark sky at about 3 K, and its steady temperature is the balance of the two. The atmosphere is transparent to the Sun's visible light and most of its infrared, but the infrared the cooler Earth emits is at longer wavelengths that carbon dioxide and water vapor absorb and re-radiate, part of it back to the surface, which keeps the Earth about 40 °C warmer than it would be with no atmosphere. Eunice Newton Foote first measured this in flasks of carbon dioxide left in the sun, and the effect is central to global warming from the gases that industry and farming emit.
