concepts.statement: Both coils sit on the same core and so see the same $\Delta\Phi/\Delta t$; Faraday's law then gives each a voltage proportional to its own number of turns, and dividing one by the other leaves a ratio of turns. So the output voltage is the input voltage times the turns ratio, and a transformer's job is settled entirely by how its two coils are wound.

concepts.name: Transformer current ratio
concepts.statement: A transformer is not a source of energy, and a good one wastes very little: transformer efficiency often exceeds 99 per cent, so the power out equals the power in. Setting $I_\text{p}V_\text{p} = I_\text{s}V_\text{s}$ and using the voltage ratio gives a current ratio that is the turns ratio upside down. Raising a voltage lowers the current in the same proportion, which is why power is sent across country at hundreds of kilovolts and why a step-up transformer's spectacular arcs are relatively safe.

concepts.name: Choosing a step-up or step-down transformer
concepts.statement: A transformer with more turns on the secondary raises the voltage and is a step-up transformer; one with fewer lowers it and is a step-down transformer. Decide which you need, then find the turns, the current or the power from the two ratios. The arithmetic is only ever one ratio and one multiplication. The check that keeps it honest is that the power out must equal the power in.

concepts.name: Transformers and DC
concepts.statement: Since the secondary voltage depends on the rate at which the flux changes, a steady primary current induces nothing at all. Switching DC on and off does produce something, but it is a train of spikes rather than the sinusoid most appliances need. This is the plainest reason for using AC wherever voltages must rise or fall. Once you know the turns ratio, do not expect it to work on a battery.

concepts.name: Step-up transformer
concepts.statement: A step-up transformer has more turns on its secondary coil than on its primary, so it raises the voltage.

concepts.name: Step-down transformer
concepts.statement: A step-down transformer has fewer turns on its secondary coil than on its primary, so it lowers the voltage.

concepts.name: Three-wire system
concepts.statement: Modern wiring carries three conductors rather than two. The live wire supplies the voltage and the current. The neutral wire is the return path; it connects to the earth at both the source and the user, which forces it to zero volts. The earth/ground wire holds the appliance's case at zero volts as well. A circuit breaker or fuse sits in series on the live wire against thermal overload, and the case itself keeps a person from touching what is inside. Each of the three has its own job and prevents its own hazard.

concepts.name: Grounding the case
concepts.statement: Worn insulation can bring the live wire into contact with a metal case, and a person touching that case and a tap completes a circuit to earth. With the earth/ground wire intact, the breaker trips instead, and the fault must be repaired. Grounding also deals with a subtler problem that belongs to this chapter. The alternating current in an appliance induces an emf on its own case, and if the case is not held at zero volts that emf can drive a leakage current through anyone who touches it.

concepts.name: Ground fault interrupter
concepts.statement: A GFI carries both wires through one coil so that equal currents induce equal and opposite emfs in it and nothing happens. If some of the current is returning by another path, the two are unequal, an emf appears, and the circuit is interrupted, usually at a difference of about 5 mA, which is the largest shock taken to be harmless. It is the only device in the section that works by induction rather than by heating, and it is the only one that acts before the person is badly hurt rather than after.

concepts.name: Isolation transformer
concepts.statement: An isolation transformer usually has equal input and output voltages, so it changes nothing about what the appliance receives. What it changes is that neither output wire connects to the original source or to earth. A person touching one of them is therefore not part of any complete circuit: for current to flow it would have to cross the high resistance of the material between the coils. It is a safety device that works by removing a path rather than by interrupting one.

concepts.name: Inductance
concepts.statement: Some arrangements induce a large emf for a given change and some induce almost none, and inductance says which. Once the geometry of a device is fixed, only the current changes the flux, so inductance relates an induced emf to a rate of change of current. It is the property that makes a transformer worth building and the property an appliance's designer keeps small between its coils and its case.

concepts.name: Mutual inductance
concepts.statement: Mutual inductance is one device's effect on another: a change in the current in the first induces an emf in the second, and $M$ is the constant between them. Nature is symmetric here, and the same $M$ works the other way round, so a transformer run backward works as well as forward. A transformer's coils need a large $M$; an appliance's heating element and its case need a small one, a distinction that matters again for electrical safety.

concepts.name: Self-inductance
concepts.statement: A device also induces an emf in itself: its own changing current changes its own flux, and by Lenz's law the induced emf opposes the change. The constant is the self-inductance $L$, and a device with a large one is an inductor. The minus sign matters practically as well as formally. Switching off a large current quickly can raise thousands of volts and strike an arc across the switch, which is why you cannot simply switch off a 1 H coil carrying 10 A in a millisecond.

concepts.name: Henry
concepts.statement: The unit of both mutual and self-inductance is the henry, named for Joseph Henry, and it is volt-seconds per ampere, which is the same as an ohm-second. Knowing that identity is not bookkeeping: it is what makes the time constant $L/R$ come out in seconds in the next section and what makes $2\pi fL$ come out in ohms in the section after that. A 1 H inductor is a large one, and a solenoid of ordinary size has an inductance of about a millihenry.

concepts.name: Inductance from flux and current
concepts.statement: Equating Faraday's law with the definition of self-inductance and cancelling the time gives a relation with no time in it at all: the inductance is the number of turns times the change in flux per unit change in current. This is always true, and it says what inductance really depends on, which is how effectively the device's own current makes flux through its own turns. It is also the route to the one inductance the book calculates from a shape.

concepts.name: Inductance of a solenoid
concepts.statement: For most shapes the inductance is too hard to calculate and the book simply gives it. A solenoid, though, has a nearly uniform field inside, almost none outside and a simple shape, so you can work out its inductance from $B = \mu_0 NI/\ell$ and the relation above. The answer depends only on the solenoid's own geometry, as the definition of inductance says it must. It is proportional to the square of the number of turns, since more turns make more flux and more turns feel it.

concepts.name: Energy stored in an inductor
concepts.statement: There is a second way to see why an inductor opposes a change in current: its magnetic field stores energy, and putting energy in and taking it out both take time. The stored energy is $\frac{1}{2}LI^2$, the same shape as the energy in a capacitor, and it can make a spark when the current stops suddenly. It is also the energy the exponential decay of an RL circuit spends.

concepts.name: Counterwinding a coil
concepts.statement: The flux a coil makes depends on which way it is wound, so winding half the turns one way and half the other makes the two fields cancel, and the inductance with them. This keeps an appliance's heating element from inducing a dangerous emf on its case, and keeps a laboratory resistor from behaving like an inductor under alternating current. Knowing what makes inductance large is knowing how to make it small.

concepts.name: Inductor
concepts.statement: An inductor is a device with a large self-inductance, usually a coil, whose induced emf strongly opposes any change in the current through it.

concepts.name: RL circuit
concepts.statement: Put an inductor in series with a resistor and a battery and the current does not jump to its final value. The inductor's own induced emf opposes the change, most strongly at the beginning when the change is fastest. Take the battery out and the current does not stop either, since the inductor keeps it going while the resistor dissipates the energy stored in its field. The RL circuit shows how long the opposition lasts.

concepts.name: RL time constant
concepts.statement: One number, $L/R$, sets the whole of the timing, and it comes out in seconds because a henry is an ohm-second. Both dependences make sense. A larger inductance opposes change more strongly, and a smaller resistance means a larger final current and so a greater change to make. Either way the inductor stores more energy and needs more time to move it in and out. This is Chapter 21's RC time constant with a different pair of components.

concepts.name: Current growth in an RL circuit
concepts.statement: The opposing emf is proportional to how much change remains, the hallmark of exponential behaviour, so the current climbs toward its final value $V/R$ along a curve that never arrives. In the first time constant it covers 0.632 of the way, and 0.632 of what remains in each time constant after that. After a few multiples of $\tau$ it is there for any practical purpose.

concepts.name: Current decay in an RL circuit
concepts.statement: With the battery cut out, the inductor drives the current on while the resistor dissipates the stored energy, and since the dissipation rate is $I^2R$ the decay slows as the current falls. The current drops to 0.368 of its value in each time constant. The same $\tau$ governs both the growth and the decay, just as it did in the RC circuit.

concepts.name: Counting in time constants
concepts.statement: Because the current covers the same fraction in every time constant, you can answer many questions by counting. After one $\tau$ the current is 0.368 of what it was, after two it is 0.368 of that, and so on; counting upward with 0.632 answers the growth. The book does its own worked example this way, in two steps rather than by substituting into the exponential. The approximation is good to a few per cent, and one of the problems measures exactly how good.

concepts.name: Phase lead in an inductor
concepts.statement: Drive an inductor with a sinusoidal voltage and the current does not follow it in step. The current starts at zero and reaches its peak a quarter of a cycle after the voltage that drives it, just as it lagged when a DC voltage switched on in the RL circuit. Inductors oppose a change in current, so the current is always behind. Understand this before you calculate any reactance, since the algebra of the RLC circuit rests on it.

concepts.name: Inductive reactance
concepts.statement: An inductor's opposition to an alternating current behaves like a resistance: the rms current is the rms voltage divided by a quantity measured in ohms, and that quantity is $2\pi fL$. Both factors make sense, since a larger inductance opposes change more strongly and a higher frequency means a faster change to oppose. The consequence is that an inductor impedes high frequencies most, which is what a filter in series with a computer's power supply is for.

concepts.name: Phase lag in a capacitor
concepts.statement: A capacitor does the opposite of an inductor. Its voltage is greatest when it is fully charged and the current has stopped, and the current is greatest when the capacitor is empty and its voltage is zero, so the voltage follows the current by a quarter of a cycle. Hold the two rules side by side, voltage ahead in an inductor and behind in a capacitor, and the cancellation in an RLC circuit becomes expected rather than surprising.

concepts.name: Capacitive reactance
concepts.statement: A capacitor also limits an alternating current, and the ohms it offers are $1/2\pi fC$. Both dependences are inverse, and both are reasonable: a larger capacitor stores more charge and passes more current, and a higher frequency leaves less time to charge up and stop the current. So a capacitor impedes low frequencies most, which is the exact opposite of an inductor and is why a capacitor in series is what removes a 60 Hz hum.

concepts.name: Phase in a resistor
concepts.statement: A plain resistance does not care about frequency and introduces no phase difference at all: the voltage across a resistor rises and falls with the current through it. It is the simplest of the three rules, but do not take it for granted. In an RLC circuit the resistor fixes where the total voltage sits between the inductor's lead and the capacitor's lag.

concepts.name: Filtering by frequency
concepts.statement: The two reactances run opposite ways with frequency, so choosing between them lets a circuit pass some frequencies and block others. An inductor in series blocks high frequencies, which keeps power-line noise out of a computer. A capacitor in series blocks low ones, which keeps a hum out of a loudspeaker. A capacitor to earth shorts the high frequencies away instead. Know which way each reactance runs and you can answer all of these without a calculation.

concepts.name: Impedance
concepts.statement: Put a resistor, an inductor and a capacitor in series on one AC source and their oppositions do not simply add. The inductor's voltage leads the current and the capacitor's lags it by the same quarter cycle, so the two are opposite and partly cancel. What remains is the impedance: the resistance and the difference of the reactances combined as the two legs of a right triangle. It is an ohm like any other ohm, and it plays the part resistance plays in a DC circuit.

concepts.name: Ohm’s law for an AC circuit
concepts.statement: With impedance in hand, the current follows from the law of Chapter 20: the current is the voltage divided by the impedance, in peak values or in rms values, whichever the problem gives. The greater the impedance, the smaller the current, and the reason for computing $Z$ at all is that this one line then answers the circuit.

concepts.name: Adding voltages in an RLC circuit
concepts.statement: The current is the same everywhere in a series circuit and is in phase with itself, but the three voltages peak at different moments: $V_R$ with the current, $V_L$ a quarter cycle ahead and $V_C$ a quarter cycle behind. So $V_L$ and $V_C$ are half a cycle apart and tend to cancel, and the source's peak voltage is not the sum of the three peaks but $\sqrt{V_{0R}^2 + (V_{0L} - V_{0C})^2}$. This is the fact the whole section rests on, and it is the fact a reader is most likely to get wrong by treating an AC circuit as a DC one.

concepts.name: Resonant frequency of an RLC circuit
concepts.statement: One reactance grows with frequency and the other falls, so somewhere between they are equal and cancel exactly. There the impedance is just the resistance, which is the least it can be, and the current is the greatest. Setting $X_L = X_C$ and solving gives the frequency, and it depends only on the inductance and the capacitance. This is the natural frequency at which the circuit would oscillate on its own, and it is Chapter 16's resonance in an electrical system rather than a mechanical one.

concepts.name: Resonance peak and resistance
concepts.statement: Plotting the current against frequency gives a peak at $f_0$, and its shape depends on the resistance: a small resistance gives a tall narrow peak and a large one gives a low broad peak. A radio receiver is an RLC circuit tuned by a variable capacitor, and the narrowness of its peak is what lets it pick one station and reject the next, so a circuit with too much resistance would not be selective. This is the same relation between damping and the sharpness of resonance that Chapter 16 drew for a driven oscillator.

concepts.name: Phase angle
concepts.statement: Because the source voltage and the current are out of step, there is an angle between them, and it is fixed by how much of the impedance is resistance: $\cos\phi = R/Z$. At resonance, or in a circuit with nothing but resistance, $Z = R$ and the angle is zero. Where a capacitor dominates, as it does at low frequency, the angle approaches 90°, which is what a pure capacitive circuit gives.

concepts.name: Power factor
concepts.statement: In a circuit where the voltage and the current are out of step, the average power is not simply their product. It is their product times $\cos\phi$, the power factor, which runs from 0 to 1. The resistance dissipates all of the power; the inductor and the capacitor take energy in and give it back without spending any. Engineers design efficient motors for a power factor near 1, and at resonance the factor is exactly 1.

concepts.name: LC oscillation
concepts.statement: With the resistance negligible, energy moves back and forth between the capacitor's electric field and the inductor's magnetic field, and the circuit oscillates at $f_0$ of its own accord. That is how a clock circuit in a digital watch keeps time. The mechanical counterpart is exact: the charge on the capacitor is the stretch of a spring, the current is the speed of the mass, and the resistance is the shock absorber that damps a car's wheel on a corrugated road. It is the closest analogy between two systems in the whole book, and it holds as physics, not as a figure of speech.

concepts.name: RLC circuit
concepts.statement: An RLC circuit contains a resistor, an inductor and a capacitor, and in a series RLC circuit the same alternating current passes through all three.

concepts.name: Magnetic poles
concepts.statement: All magnets attract iron, but a magnet brought near another magnet may attract it or repel it, because every magnet has two ends that behave differently. Suspend a magnet freely and one end points toward the north. The two ends are the north magnetic pole and the south magnetic pole, named for the directions they seek. Every later rule of the chapter, from the direction of a field line to the torque on a loop, uses these two poles.

concepts.name: Like poles repel
concepts.statement: Bring two magnets together and you find that two north poles push each other apart, two south poles do the same, and a north pole and a south pole pull together. Compare this with the electrostatic rule, unlike charges attract and like charges repel. The two look alike, and it is tempting to carry the whole of electrostatics across, but later sections show where the analogy holds and where it breaks.

concepts.name: No magnetic monopoles
concepts.statement: Cut a bar magnet in half and you do not get a north pole in one hand and a south pole in the other; you get two shorter magnets, each with both poles. Cut again and the same thing happens, down to the iron atom itself. This is where the analogy with charge fails, since a positive charge and a negative charge separate easily, and it is the fact that later forces the chapter to explain all magnetism as current: a current loop always produces a pair of poles and never a single one.

concepts.name: North magnetic pole
concepts.statement: The north magnetic pole of a magnet is the end or side that is attracted toward Earth's geographic north pole, the end that points north when the magnet is free to turn.

concepts.name: South magnetic pole
concepts.statement: The south magnetic pole of a magnet is the end or side that is attracted toward Earth's geographic south pole.

concepts.name: Ferromagnetic materials and magnetization
concepts.statement: Only a few materials, iron, cobalt, nickel, gadolinium and some rare earth alloys among them, show strong magnetic effects. These are called ferromagnetic, after ferrum, the Latin word for iron. They do more than respond to a magnet: they can be magnetized themselves, which means they can be induced to be magnetic or made into permanent magnets, and this is why a magnet held near an unmagnetized piece of iron attracts it.

concepts.name: Magnetic domains
concepts.statement: Inside a ferromagnetic material there are regions called domains, each of which acts like a small bar magnet because the poles of its individual atoms are aligned. In an unmagnetized object the domains are small and point in random directions, so their effects cancel. In an external magnetic field the domains that already point the right way grow at the expense of the others and the rest swing into line, and the material as a whole becomes a magnet. Heating it and cooling it, or tapping it while the field is applied, makes the alignment permanent.

concepts.name: Curie temperature
concepts.statement: Thermal motion works against the alignment of domains, so heating a permanent magnet in the absence of another magnet demagnetizes it, as do hard blows. For each ferromagnetic material there is a well-defined temperature, the Curie temperature, above which it cannot be magnetized at all; for iron it is 1043 K, which is 770 °C and well above room temperature. Some elements and alloys have Curie temperatures below room temperature and are ferromagnetic only when they are cold.

concepts.name: Electromagnet
concepts.statement: Oersted found in 1820 that a current-carrying wire deflects a compass needle, the first evidence that moving charge has anything to do with magnets. Using an electric current to make a magnet is called electromagnetism, and a magnet made this way is an electromagnet. Iron filings scattered around a current-carrying coil form the same pattern they form around a bar magnet. An electromagnet also has north and south poles that cannot be separated and that repel and attract by the same rule, so the two kinds of magnet are the same kind of thing.

concepts.name: Current as the source of magnetism
concepts.statement: An electromagnet makes a field with a current, and a ferromagnet does too, at a scale too small to see. An electron in orbit about a nucleus is a closed current loop, the electron's spin is a second current, and both produce a magnetic field with a north pole and a south pole. Ferromagnetism is the cooperative alignment of these spins. Isolated poles are never found, because a current loop always produces a pair of poles. The rest of the chapter rests on this idea.

concepts.name: Electromagnetism
concepts.statement: Electromagnetism is the use of electric currents to produce magnetism, and more broadly the single subject that electricity and magnetism become once a current is known to make a magnetic field.

concepts.name: Magnetized
concepts.statement: A material is magnetized when it has been turned into a magnet, either induced to be magnetic for a time or made into a permanent magnet.

concepts.name: Magnetic field
concepts.statement: The magnetic field, traditionally called the B-field, is the representation of magnetic forces. Like the gravitational and electric fields, it maps the forces that surround an object and can act on another object at a distance, and it represents the object that generates it, not the probe that tests it.

concepts.name: Direction of magnetic field lines
concepts.statement: We draw the field with magnetic field lines, a pictorial tool for showing its strength and its direction. The direction of the lines is the direction in which the north end of a small compass needle points, so you can check it with a compass on a table. Small compasses do not disturb the field they test, just as a small test charge does not disturb an electric field, so the map they trace is a map of the magnet alone.

concepts.name: Rules for magnetic field lines
concepts.statement: Mapping many fields has settled four rules. The field is tangent to the field line at every point, so a compass lies along the line. The strength of the field is proportional to how closely the lines are packed, exactly to the number of lines crossing a unit area held perpendicular to them. Lines never cross, because the field has one value at each point in space. And the lines are continuous closed loops with no beginning and no end, which is the deepest of the four, since electric field lines begin and end on charges and magnetic lines have no monopoles to begin or end on.

concepts.name: Magnetic field lines
concepts.statement: Magnetic field lines are a pictorial representation of a magnetic field: the field points along them, and they are closer together where the field is stronger.

concepts.name: Magnetic force on a moving charge
concepts.statement: A magnetic field exerts a force on a charge only while the charge moves. The size of that force is the charge times the speed times the field strength times the sine of the angle between the velocity and the field. The sine matters as much as the rest: a charge moving along a field line feels no force at all, and a charge moving across the lines feels the most. This force is often called the Lorentz force, and it is how one magnet pushes another, since every magnet is made of moving charge.

concepts.name: Magnetic field strength
concepts.statement: Field lines show what a magnetic field looks like; turning the force law around says what its strength is. Solving for $B$ defines the strength of a field as the force per unit charge per unit velocity, measured across the field, just as the electric field strength is the force per unit charge. So we know the field only through what it does to a moving charge.

concepts.name: Tesla
concepts.statement: Because the sine is a pure number, the unit of magnetic field strength follows from the definition: one tesla is one newton per coulomb per metre per second, which is one newton per ampere-metre. A smaller unit, the gauss, is $10^{-4}$ tesla. The strongest permanent magnets reach about 2 T, and superconducting electromagnets 10 T or more. The Earth's field at the surface is only about $5 \times 10^{-5}$ T, half a gauss, which is why you never feel the Earth pushing on the charge in your pocket.

concepts.name: Right hand rule 1
concepts.statement: The direction of the magnetic force is perpendicular to the plane formed by the velocity and the field, which is not a direction that can be read off a flat drawing without a convention, so the book gives one. Point the thumb of the right hand along the velocity, the fingers along the field, and the force on a positive charge comes out of the palm. One velocity, one thumb; many field lines, many fingers; the force is the way you would push. The force on a negative charge is exactly opposite.

concepts.name: Force and the sign of charge
concepts.statement: Right hand rule 1 applies to a positive charge, and the force on a negative charge moving the same way points in exactly the opposite direction. The charges that actually move in a wire are electrons, so throughout the chapter you will translate between the direction of a conventional current and the direction the carriers travel. The reversal also lets the Hall effect reveal which sign of carrier is moving.

concepts.name: Gauss
concepts.statement: The gauss is a smaller unit of magnetic field strength than the tesla, with $1\;\text{G} = 10^{-4}\;\text{T}$.

concepts.name: Magnetic force doing no work
concepts.statement: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, and a force perpendicular to the motion does no work. So the kinetic energy of the particle and its speed do not change: only the direction of the motion is affected. This is the single fact that decides everything else in the section, because a force of constant magnitude that is always perpendicular to the velocity is what uniform circular motion requires.

concepts.name: Circular motion in a magnetic field
concepts.statement: When a charge moves perpendicular to a uniform field, the magnetic force is the centripetal force, so $qvB$ equals $mv^2/r$. You have already solved circular motion in Chapter 6; here you need only recognise which force plays the centripetal part. In a vacuum the magnetic field alone decides the motion, and the particle circles forever at constant speed.

concepts.name: Radius of a charged particle’s path
concepts.statement: Solving the centripetal equation for the radius gives the mass times the speed divided by the charge times the field. Everything the chapter does with curved tracks follows from this fraction: a heavier or faster particle swings wider, and a stronger field or a larger charge pulls the circle tighter. Fixing the speed, the charge and the field makes the radius proportional to the mass, which is how a mass spectrometer weighs an ion. It is also why a magnet held against the glass turns an electron in a television tube through a circle less than a millimetre across.

concepts.name: Spiral along field lines
concepts.statement: Only the component of the velocity perpendicular to the field bends; the component along the field stays the same, since the magnetic force is zero for motion parallel to the lines. A particle that enters at an angle therefore circles about a field line while drifting along it, in a spiral rather than a circle. Charged particles approaching a magnetic field are far more likely to spiral about the lines than to cross them. That explains the aurora, the shape of the tracks in Figure 22.20 and the whole of the next idea.

concepts.name: Magnetic mirror
concepts.statement: Where the field lines crowd together, the field grows stronger along the direction of travel. The force then has a component that slows the particle's motion along the line and can turn it back. A region of strong field at each end therefore traps a particle bouncing between them, which is a magnetic mirror. The Earth is such a trap. Its two Van Allen belts hold particles from the Sun and from deep space, which migrate along the field lines and reflect away from the poles. Those that do enter the atmosphere near the poles light the aurora and give a higher radiation dose there than at the equator.

concepts.name: Confining and steering charged particles
concepts.statement: Engineers build the same trapping on purpose. Accelerators use magnetic fields not only to bend a beam around its ring but to focus it and hold it together against the repulsion of its own like charges. A tokamak bends a solenoid into a doughnut so that the charged particles of a plasma circle the field lines without ever reaching the wall, the leading hope for containing a fusion reaction. A microwave oven's magnetron holds oscillating electrons the same way. All of these apply one idea.

concepts.name: Hall effect
concepts.statement: A magnetic field acts on the charges moving inside a conductor just as it acts on a free charge, and since the charges cannot leave the metal, they pile up on one side and leave the other side with the opposite sign. The separated charge makes an electric field across the conductor, and that field pushes the carriers back. The pile-up therefore stops almost at once, at the point where the electric force $qE$ equals the magnetic force $qvB$, so that $E = vB$. The voltage this separation produces across the conductor is the Hall emf.

concepts.name: Hall emf
concepts.statement: For a uniform field across a uniform conductor the electric field is uniform too, so the voltage is the field times the width, $E = \varepsilon/l$. Putting that into the balance gives the Hall emf as the field times the width times the speed, when the three are mutually perpendicular. It is a small voltage, tens of microvolts for blood in an artery, and the section is careful to say so, since the difficulty of measuring it against the millivolts of a heartbeat is why a Hall flow probe applies an alternating field.

concepts.name: Finding the sign of charge carriers
concepts.statement: Reverse the sign of the carriers and, for the same conventional current, they move the other way. The magnetic force pushes them to the same side, but they carry the opposite charge there, so the Hall emf changes sign. Knowing the directions of the field and the current therefore tells you the sign of whatever carries the current. Historically, this showed that electrons carry the current in metals and that positive carriers do so in some semiconductors.

concepts.name: Hall probes and flow meters
concepts.statement: Two applications follow directly from the formula. Run a known current through a small conductor and the Hall emf measures the field: this is a Hall probe, which can be very small and, once calibrated, very accurate. Or fix the field and the width, and the Hall emf measures the speed of whatever moves, which is how instruments measure blood flow in an artery and water flow in a pipe without touching the fluid. Here the sign of the emf depends only on the directions of the field and the velocity, not on the sign of the charges, so a fluid carrying both signs still gives a reading.

concepts.name: Force on a current-carrying wire
concepts.statement: Charges cannot escape a wire, so the magnetic force on the charges moving inside it passes to the wire itself. Add the force on every carrier in a length of wire, and recognise that the number of carriers per unit volume times the charge times the drift velocity times the area is the current. The force on one charge then becomes a force on the wire: the current times the length in the field times the field times the sine of the angle between the current and the field. This derivation bridges a law about particles and a law about circuits.

concepts.name: Force per unit length on a wire
concepts.statement: Dividing by the length gives the force per metre of wire. Use this form whenever the wire is long or its length is not given, as for a lightning bolt, a power line or the two parallel conductors of 22.10. It is the same result written so that only the current, the field and the angle appear.

concepts.name: Right hand rule 1 for a current
concepts.statement: The same right hand rule gives the direction of the force on a wire as on a single charge, with the thumb now along the current rather than along one charge's velocity. The substitution is exact because a conventional current points the way positive carriers would move, so you need no second rule.

concepts.name: Magnetohydrodynamic pump
concepts.statement: If the current runs through a conducting fluid rather than a wire, the force falls on the fluid and pushes it along the tube, and the pump has no moving parts at all. That is attractive for a hot or chemically active liquid such as the sodium in some nuclear reactors, for an experimental artificial heart, and for a submarine drive that would run more quietly than a propeller. The direction of the force does not depend on the sign of the carriers, so a fluid carrying both signs still moves one way.

concepts.name: Torque on a current loop
concepts.statement: Put a rectangular loop of wire on a shaft in a uniform field. The forces on its two vertical sides are equal and opposite, so the loop does not move off, but each produces a torque about the shaft in the same sense, so the loop turns. Adding the two torques gives the width times the force. Putting $F = IlB$ into it and recognising the width times the height as the area gives the torque as the number of turns times the current times the area times the field times the sine of the angle. The derivation uses a rectangle, but the result holds for a loop of any shape.

concepts.name: Torque and angle
concepts.statement: The angle in the formula is between the field and the perpendicular to the loop, so the torque is greatest when the loop's plane lies along the field and falls to zero when the loop faces the field squarely. Past that point the sine changes sign and so does the torque, which means that a loop left to itself does not keep turning: it oscillates back and forth about the position of zero torque, exactly as a compass needle settles onto a field line.

concepts.name: Net force on a loop
concepts.statement: The forces on the top and bottom segments of the loop are vertical, parallel to the shaft, equal in size and opposite in direction, so they neither turn the loop nor push it anywhere. The forces on the two vertical sides are equal and opposite as well. The loop therefore feels no net force in a uniform field, only a torque, and a motor turns without wandering across the room.

concepts.name: Brushes keep a motor turning
concepts.statement: A coil that only oscillates is no use, so a motor reverses the current each time the coil passes the position of zero torque, using automatic switches called brushes. The torque then always acts the same way round and the coil keeps turning in one direction, which is how electrical energy is turned into mechanical work. This is the whole of the motor: a loop, a field, and a switch that changes the current twice a revolution.

concepts.name: Analog meter as a motor
concepts.statement: An analog meter is built the same way, but its magnet poles are shaped so that the field stays perpendicular to the loop over a wide range of angles. The sine is then always about one, the torque depends on the current and not on the angle, and a spring supplies a counter-torque that grows with the deflection, so the needle's position is proportional to the current. A sensitive galvanometer for a voltmeter or an ammeter wants a large loop area, a strong field and low-resistance coils.

concepts.name: Number of turns
concepts.statement: A coil is a wire wound into loops, and its number of turns $N$ is how many loops it has. Each turn feels the same torque in a field and encloses the same flux, so many quantities of a coil are $N$ times those of a single loop.

concepts.name: Electric motor
concepts.statement: An electric motor is a loop of wire, or a coil of many loops, mounted on a shaft in a magnetic field, so that the torque the field exerts on its current turns the shaft.

concepts.name: Field of a long straight wire
terms: magnetic field strength (magnitude) produced by a long straight current-carrying wire
concepts.statement: Experiment gives the field round a long straight wire as the permeability of free space times the current, divided by two pi times the shortest distance to the wire. The field falls off as one over the distance, not one over the distance squared, and, because the wire is long, it does not depend on where along the wire the point is. The section's own example is the most useful reading of it: 25 A in a wire makes twice the Earth's field 5.0 cm away, which is why an overhead power line disturbs a surveyor's compass.

concepts.name: Right hand rule 2
concepts.statement: Compasses set around a straight wire show that the field lines are circles centred on the wire, and the second right hand rule gives the sense of the circles: point the thumb along the current and the fingers curl the way the field goes. It holds for any segment of current, not only a straight wire, so the same rule gives the field of a loop and of a solenoid. The first right hand rule gives a force and this one gives a field, and keeping the two apart is most of the work.

concepts.name: Permeability of free space
concepts.statement: The constant in the field formulas, $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ T·m/A, is the permeability of free space, one of the basic constants of nature and the magnetic counterpart of the permittivity that appeared in the electric field. Its value is exact rather than measured, which is what makes the definition of the ampere in 22.10 possible, and the book notes that it is related to the speed of light, a connection the later chapters make good.

concepts.name: Ampere’s law
concepts.statement: Every segment of a current makes a field like a short piece of a long straight wire, and the field of a current of any shape is the vector sum of the fields of its segments. Stating that for one segment is the Biot-Savart law, and summing it with calculus gives Ampere's law, which relates field and current in general. Ampere's law is one of Maxwell's equations, the four that describe all electromagnetic phenomena; the book keeps the general features, the right hand rule and the rules for field lines, and leaves the integrals to a later course.

concepts.name: Field at the center of a loop
terms: magnetic field strength at the center of a circular loop
concepts.statement: The field of a current loop is complicated everywhere except at its centre, and there it is simple: the permeability times the current divided by twice the radius, and $N$ times that for a flat coil of $N$ loops. The larger the loop, the weaker its centre field, because the current is farther away. Outside the loop the field has the shape of a bar magnet's, which puts numbers to the iron-filing pattern of 22.2.

concepts.name: Field inside a solenoid
terms: magnetic field strength inside a solenoid
concepts.statement: Wind the wire into a long coil and the fields of the turns add inside and very nearly cancel outside. The field inside is uniform in magnitude and direction over most of the coil's length, and the field just outside is nearly zero. Its strength is the permeability times the number of turns per unit length times the current, with no radius in it at all. That is why a solenoid, as in an MRI magnet, is the way to make a strong and uniform field over a large volume.

concepts.name: Solenoid
concepts.statement: A solenoid is a thin wire wound into a long coil, and the number of loops per unit length, $n = N/l$, describes how tightly it is wound.

concepts.name: Biot-Savart law
concepts.statement: The Biot-Savart law gives the magnetic field made by each small segment of a current, so that the field of any current is the sum of the fields of its segments.

concepts.name: Force between parallel currents
concepts.statement: Nothing new is needed for this result, only the two things the chapter already has: the first wire makes a field at the second, and the second wire feels a force in that field. Putting the straight-wire field into the force on a current and dividing by the length gives the force per unit length as the permeability times the two currents divided by two pi times the separation. By Newton's third law each wire feels the same size of force, which is why one number serves for both.

concepts.name: Attraction and repulsion of currents
concepts.statement: Following the two right hand rules around gives the sense of the force: wires carrying current the same way pull together, and wires carrying current opposite ways push apart. This is the reverse of what you might guess from like charges repelling, so check it once with your hand. The hot and neutral wires of an appliance cord and the two conductors of a light-rail line are everyday cases of it.

concepts.name: Pinch effect
concepts.statement: Because parallel currents attract, a current spread over a region squeezes itself into a narrower one. In an electric arc or a plasma this is the pinch effect, and it is not a curiosity: in a large circuit breaker it concentrates the arc between the plates that are trying to interrupt the current, burning holes and sometimes igniting the equipment. The jets of ionized material in a solar flare are shaped the same way.

concepts.name: Definition of the ampere
concepts.statement: Putting one ampere in each of two wires one metre apart makes a force of exactly $2 \times 10^{-7}$ N/m, exactly because the permeability of free space is itself defined as exactly $4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ T·m/A. That statement, run backwards, is the operational definition of the ampere, and with it the coulomb, since one coulomb is the charge that flows in one second at one ampere. In practice a current balance uses coils a few centimetres apart rather than infinite wires, and measuring force is the most accurate way known of fixing both units.

concepts.name: Mass spectrometer
concepts.statement: The radius of a charged particle's circle is its mass times its speed divided by its charge times the field, so if the speed, the charge and the field are all fixed, the radius is simply proportional to the mass. That is a mass spectrometer: an ion source, a stage that fixes the speed, and a uniform field in which each ion swings round an arc whose width reports its mass. The charge comes in multiples of the electron's, so it is easy to allow for. The instrument identifies chemicals and biological molecules by their mass-to-charge ratios and measures the isotope tracers used in medicine.

concepts.name: Velocity selector
concepts.statement: Cross an electric field with a magnetic field so that they push a moving charge opposite ways, and only the particles for which the two forces balance go straight through. Setting $qE$ equal to $qvB$ cancels the charge and leaves the speed as the electric field divided by the magnetic field, which means the selected speed does not depend on the charge or the mass of the particle at all and can be dialled by changing either field. It is the stage that makes a mass spectrometer's arcs mean something.

concepts.name: Steering an electron beam
concepts.statement: A cathode ray tube, an old computer monitor, an x-ray machine and a two-mile linear accelerator are all versions of the same electron gun, and many of them use magnetic fields to point the beam. Two pairs of coils, one for the vertical and one for the horizontal, bend the electrons to wherever they are wanted on the screen. The rays are called cathode rays because they start at the cathode in the gun.

concepts.name: Magnetic resonance imaging
concepts.statement: Certain nuclei, hydrogen's single proton above all, have small magnetic fields of their own, like the current loops of this chapter. In a strong external field they settle into one of two energy states, and a radio signal of exactly the right frequency flips them between the two. The frequency they absorb and re-emit depends on the nucleus, on its chemical surroundings and on the field strength. Sweeping the field across the body therefore turns position into frequency, and the strength of the returned signal shows how much of that nucleus is there. That is nuclear magnetic resonance, and imaging with it is MRI.

concepts.name: Biomagnetic measurement
concepts.statement: Currents in nerve cells and in the heart make magnetic fields like any other currents, and those fields can be recorded without touching the body: the heart's is a magnetocardiogram and the brain's a magnetoencephalogram. They are between a million and a hundred million times weaker than the Earth's field, so they are read with a SQUID, a superconducting detector that works at liquid helium temperatures. They report activity rather than structure, which is what makes them useful for epilepsy and for fetal studies and different from an electrocardiogram.

concepts.name: Nuclear magnetic resonance
concepts.statement: Nuclear magnetic resonance is the interaction of an applied magnetic field with the nuclei of certain atoms, whose own small magnetic fields line up with it and absorb radio waves at a frequency set by the field strength.

concepts.name: Magnetocardiogram
concepts.statement: A magnetocardiogram is a recording of the heart's magnetic field as it beats.

concepts.name: Magnetoencephalogram
concepts.statement: A magnetoencephalogram is a measurement of the brain's magnetic field.

concepts.name: Maxwell’s equations
concepts.statement: Maxwell gathered the work of Oersted, Coulomb, Gauss and Faraday into four statements that together make a complete theory of electricity and magnetism. Electric field lines begin on positive charges and end on negative ones. Magnetic field lines have no beginning and no end. A changing magnetic field induces an electric field. Moving charges and changing electric fields make magnetic fields. Everything else in this chapter follows from these four.

concepts.name: Changing electric field as a source of magnetism
concepts.statement: Faraday had shown that a changing magnetic field makes an electric field. Maxwell added the symmetric statement, that a changing electric field makes a magnetic field, and this addition is what turns four separate laws into a theory that predicts a wave. Each field, in changing, creates the other, so a disturbance can keep itself going and travel away from whatever started it. Without this one hypothesis there is no electromagnetic wave to predict.

concepts.name: Speed of an electromagnetic wave
concepts.statement: Maxwell's theory does not merely say that a wave exists; it says how fast the wave goes. It gives that speed from two constants measured in the laboratory with charges and with currents, which have nothing to do with light. The permittivity of free space sets the strength of the electric force and the permeability of free space sets the strength of the magnetic force. The square root of their product sets the one speed at which the two fields can carry each other along.

concepts.name: Light as an electromagnetic wave
concepts.statement: The speed Maxwell calculated from two electrical constants is the speed of light, and a coincidence of that size is not a coincidence. Maxwell concluded that light is an electromagnetic wave of the particular wavelengths the eye happens to detect. The conclusion carries a prediction with it: if light is one band of a wave, other wavelengths should exist and should be findable, and the whole of the next two sections is spent on them.

concepts.name: Hertz’s observations
concepts.statement: A prediction is worth what its test is worth. Starting in 1887, Hertz drove a loop of wire from a circuit resonating at a known frequency, so that sparks jumped a gap in it, and set a second tuned loop across the laboratory, where sparks also appeared. He then measured the wavelength from the interference patterns, and since he knew the frequency, he could find the speed from $v = f\lambda$ and show that it was the speed of light. The SI unit of frequency carries his name.

concepts.name: Electromagnetic wave
concepts.statement: An electromagnetic wave is a pair of changing electric and magnetic fields that generate each other and travel together through space, carrying energy, at the speed of light in a vacuum.

concepts.name: Hertz
concepts.statement: The hertz is the SI unit of frequency, one cycle per second, named for Heinrich Hertz, who first generated and detected electromagnetic waves.

concepts.name: Radiation from accelerated charges
concepts.statement: Whenever a current varies, the electric and magnetic fields around it vary, and the variation moves out from the source as a wave. The general statement is simpler still: accelerating charges radiate. That is why an alternating source drives a broadcast antenna, why an unshielded circuit leaks energy, and why a microwave oven has an antenna carrying an oscillating current.

concepts.name: Antenna electric field over one cycle
concepts.statement: An alternating source at the centre of a straight wire drives charge to one end and then to the other. At the instant of greatest separation, the electric field beside the antenna is greatest. A quarter of a cycle later the charges have met in the middle and the field there is zero, while the earlier maximum has already travelled away at $\kc$. One full cycle shows where the wave's shape comes from. How far the charges separate sets its amplitude, and how long the source takes to complete a cycle sets its wavelength, so a high frequency makes a short wave.

concepts.name: Magnetic part of the wave
concepts.statement: The same charges that separate along the antenna are a current while they move, and by Ampere's law a current makes a magnetic field, whose lines circle the wire. As the current varies, that field varies with it and propagates away at the speed of light, exactly as the electric field does. The magnetic part has the same period and the same wavelength as the electric part, because the same motion of the same charges makes both.

concepts.name: Transverse electromagnetic wave
concepts.statement: The two fields of the wave lie in different planes. The electric field oscillates in one plane, the magnetic field in a plane at right angles to it, and the wave travels along the line where the two planes meet. Both fields are therefore perpendicular to the direction of propagation, which makes an electromagnetic wave transverse. The two are also exactly in phase: they reach their maxima together and pass through zero together. This arrangement decides how a wave couples to a receiving wire or loop, so learn to picture it from any angle.

concepts.name: Ratio of field strengths
concepts.statement: The stronger the electric field made by the separated charge, the greater the current that flows and so the greater the magnetic field, so the two field strengths ought to rise and fall together. They do, and the constant ratio between them is the speed of light itself, at every instant and at every point in space. Because $\kc$ is such a large number, the result also says that the magnetic part of any electromagnetic wave is very weak beside the electric part.

concepts.name: Finding one field strength from the other
concepts.statement: Rearranging the ratio gives either field from the other in one step, and this is the calculation the section's problems ask for over and over. Dividing a field of 1000 V/m by the speed of light leaves a few microtesla, less than a tenth of the Earth's own weak field, which is the concrete form of the statement that the magnetic part of a wave is small. Checking that the units of volts per metre divided by metres per second really are teslas is worth doing once.

concepts.name: Electromagnetic wave in a medium
concepts.statement: Outside a vacuum an electromagnetic wave is slower, by the factor the medium's index of refraction names. The ratio of the field strengths is reduced in exactly the same proportion, so in a medium it is the wave's own speed, not the speed of light, that the two fields stand in. The result matters wherever a wave is not travelling through empty space, which is most of the places a reader will meet one.

concepts.name: Antenna resonance
concepts.statement: An antenna is not a circuit with a complete path. It is a wire on which the driving source sets up a standing wave of charge, and its dimensions decide the frequency at which it radiates best. That is a resonance, and tuning a radio or a television means changing electrical properties until the resonant condition is met. A receiving antenna works the same way in reverse. An arriving wave accelerates the electrons in it and sets up a standing wave that the set amplifies, so it too must resonate at the frequencies it should catch.

concepts.name: Oscillation
concepts.statement: To oscillate is to fluctuate back and forth in a steady beat, as the charges in an antenna do and as the fields of the wave they send out do.

concepts.name: Wave equation for light
concepts.statement: Propagation speed, frequency and wavelength are related for any wave by $\kvw = \kf\klam$, and for an electromagnetic wave in a vacuum the propagation speed is always the speed of light. Since $\kc$ never changes, the frequency and the wavelength can only trade against each other: the greater the frequency, the smaller the wavelength. This one relation is what lets the whole spectrum be laid out on a single axis and read in either unit.

concepts.name: Finding a wavelength or frequency
concepts.statement: Rearranged, the relation gives $\klam = \kc/\kf$, and this is the arithmetic that most of the section's problems come down to. An AM carrier of 1530 kHz is nearly 200 m long, an FM carrier of 105.1 MHz is 2.85 m, and a cell phone's 1.90 GHz signal is 15.8 cm; those three numbers explain why an AM mast is enormous and a phone's antenna is hidden inside the case. Carrying the units through as cycles per second keeps the answer in metres.

concepts.name: Electromagnetic spectrum
concepts.statement: All electromagnetic waves are the same phenomenon, and only frequency, and therefore wavelength, separates a radio wave from a gamma ray. Sorting them by frequency gives the named bands, radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma ray, over a remarkable range of frequencies and wavelengths. Some of the dividing lines are sharp and others are not. Where two bands overlap, the name of a wave depends on how it was made rather than on how fast it oscillates.

concepts.name: Rules of thumb for the spectrum
concepts.statement: Three statements hold across the whole spectrum and are worth carrying: a higher-frequency wave is more energetic and penetrates better, a higher-frequency wave carries more information in a given time, and the shorter the wavelength of a wave used to probe something, the smaller the detail it can resolve. Each has exceptions — magnetic resonance imaging uses 3 m radio waves to see detail smaller than a millimetre — and knowing that the rules are rules of thumb is part of knowing them.

concepts.name: Transmission, reflection and absorption
concepts.statement: When a wave meets a material, it may pass through, turn back, or be absorbed, and usually some of each happens. How a material behaves depends on the material and the frequency together, not on the material alone. Glass passes visible light and stops ultraviolet, and skin stops visible light and passes X-rays. A substance is transparent or opaque only for a named band.

concepts.name: Radio waves and modulation
concepts.statement: Radio waves are defined by their source: any electromagnetic wave produced by currents in wires and circuits is one. To carry information, a station varies a carrier at its own frequency, either in amplitude, which is AM, or in frequency, which is FM. The receiver resonates at the carrier frequency and responds to whichever kind of variation it uses. Noise adds to amplitude, so an FM receiver can throw away what an AM receiver must treat as part of the signal, which makes FM the quieter of the two.

concepts.name: Most efficient antenna length
concepts.statement: An antenna radiates best when a standing wave fits on it, and for a linear antenna that length is $\klam/2$. With one end on the ground, a quarter wavelength does the same work, just as a tube closed at one end resonates at a quarter of its fundamental wavelength. The rule explains the sizes of antennas you see. An AM broadcast antenna must be hundreds of metres long, while an FM or mobile phone antenna is small enough to hide and goes high up for a clear line of sight.

concepts.name: Uses of microwaves
concepts.statement: Microwaves are the highest frequencies that currents in ordinary circuits can produce, from about $10^{9}$ Hz up to the highest practical $LC$ resonance near $10^{12}$ Hz, and their short wavelengths make them good for carrying information and for seeing detail. Radar finds a distance by timing an echo and a speed by the Doppler shift in it, and maps a planet through cloud that stops visible light. In a microwave oven the frequency is chosen so that polar molecules turning to follow the alternating field absorb the energy, which heats the food and not the plate, and the hot spots are an interference pattern.

concepts.name: Sources across the spectrum
concepts.statement: Each band comes from a process of a particular size. Accelerating charges in circuits give radio waves and microwaves. The thermal agitation of atoms and molecules, and their vibrations and rotations, give microwaves, infrared and some visible light. Electronic transitions within atoms and molecules give visible light and ultraviolet. Transitions of inner electrons and the braking of fast electrons in matter give X-rays, and the nucleus itself gives gamma rays. The source decides the name where two bands overlap, since an X-ray and a gamma ray of the same frequency differ only in origin.

concepts.name: Radiation and living tissue
concepts.statement: The higher the frequency, the more energy a wave delivers to whatever absorbs it, and above visible light that energy begins to break molecules apart. Ultraviolet-B excites and distorts DNA and causes skin cancer and cataracts, and the ozone layer is what keeps most of it off the surface; X-rays penetrate further and damage more, which is both their hazard and, aimed carefully, their use against cancer; gamma rays do the same at higher energies. The same properties make them useful: sterilization, vitamin D, imaging by shadow and by emission, and therapy.

concepts.name: Thermal agitation
concepts.statement: Thermal agitation is the thermal motion of the atoms and molecules of any object above absolute zero, which makes them emit and absorb radiation, mostly in the infrared.

concepts.name: Infrared radiation
concepts.statement: Infrared radiation is the band of the electromagnetic spectrum with frequencies from just below those of red light down to the microwaves.

concepts.name: Visible light
concepts.statement: Visible light is the narrow band of the electromagnetic spectrum to which the normal human eye responds, with wavelengths from about 380 nm to 760 nm.

concepts.name: Ultraviolet radiation
concepts.statement: Ultraviolet radiation is the band of the electromagnetic spectrum extending upward in frequency from violet light and overlapping the lowest x rays.

concepts.name: X rays
concepts.statement: X rays are invisible, penetrating electromagnetic radiation of very high frequency, overlapping the ultraviolet below and the gamma rays above.

concepts.name: Gamma rays
concepts.statement: Gamma rays are electromagnetic radiation of extremely high frequency, emitted by the nucleus of an atom in nuclear decay or in other nuclear and particle processes.

concepts.name: Carrier wave
concepts.statement: A carrier wave is an electromagnetic wave that carries a signal by the modulation of its amplitude or of its frequency.

concepts.name: Amplitude modulation
concepts.statement: Amplitude modulation places information on an electromagnetic wave by varying the amplitude of a carrier wave with the signal, while its frequency stays fixed.

concepts.name: Frequency modulation
concepts.statement: Frequency modulation places information on an electromagnetic wave by varying the frequency of a carrier wave with the signal, while its amplitude stays fixed.

concepts.name: Radar
concepts.statement: Radar is a common application of microwaves: it finds the distance to objects as diverse as clouds and aircraft from the time a reflected pulse takes to return.

concepts.name: Extremely low frequency
concepts.statement: Extremely low frequency radiation is electromagnetic radiation of the lowest frequencies, usually from 0 to 300 Hz but also up to about 1 kHz.

concepts.name: Television
concepts.statement: Television carries video and audio signals on electromagnetic waves, broadcast in the radio band.

concepts.name: Very high frequency
concepts.statement: Very high frequency TV channels use frequencies in the two ranges from 54 to 88 MHz and from 174 to 222 MHz.

concepts.name: Ultra-high frequency
concepts.statement: Ultra-high frequency TV channels use frequencies above those of VHF, from 470 to 1000 MHz.

concepts.name: Wave energy and field amplitude
concepts.statement: A wave brings energy into a system because its fields exert forces on charges and move them, and the larger the fields, the more work they can do. For waves of every kind the energy goes as the amplitude squared, and for an electromagnetic wave the amplitude is the maximum field strength, so the energy goes as $\kEfo^2$ and as $\kBmago^2$. Doubling the fields quadruples the energy, which is the whole content of the section's first figure and the reason a microwave oven with half the field takes four times as long.

concepts.name: Average intensity from the electric amplitude
concepts.statement: Intensity is power per unit area, and for a continuous sinusoidal electromagnetic wave you can write it from the electric amplitude alone. The factor of a half comes from averaging the square of a sine over a cycle, and the speed of light and the permittivity of free space turn a field strength into a power per square metre. Use this form when the electric field is the quantity given or wanted.

concepts.name: Average intensity from the magnetic amplitude
concepts.statement: Substituting $\kBmag = \kEf/\kc$ and $\varepsilon_0 = 1/\mu_0\kc^2$ into the first expression gives the intensity in terms of the magnetic amplitude, and substituting only part of the way gives it in terms of both amplitudes at once. The three forms are not three results but one, written in whichever quantities a problem happens to supply, and the principle behind all three is the same: energy in a wave is related to amplitude squared.

concepts.name: Peak intensity
concepts.statement: The three expressions are written for a sinusoidal wave, and averaging the square of a sine over a cycle leaves half of its maximum. So the intensity at the crest of the wave is twice the average intensity the same expressions give, and a problem that asks for a peak rather than an average needs the factor of two. The same factor is why the root mean square field is the amplitude divided by the square root of two.

concepts.name: Finding field amplitudes from intensity
concepts.statement: The common problem of the section runs in one direction: a source of known power spreads it over a known area, which gives the intensity, and the intensity gives the electric amplitude by rearranging the first expression, after which dividing by the speed of light gives the magnetic amplitude. Doing it in that order avoids the awkward constants twice over, and the answers are worth a glance for size, since a kilowatt in an oven gives a field of a few kilovolts per metre and a few microtesla.

concepts.name: Maximum field strength
concepts.statement: The maximum field strength of an electromagnetic wave is the amplitude of its electric or magnetic field, the largest value the field reaches as it oscillates.

concepts.name: Eye as a single thin lens
concepts.statement: The cornea and lens of the eye can be treated as a single thin converging lens a fixed distance from the retina, on which it forms a real, inverted image. The thin lens equations then describe the eye, and every defect and correction becomes a question about that one lens.

concepts.name: Power of the cornea
concepts.statement: The largest change in refractive index, and so the greatest bending of light, is where light passes from air into the cornea, so the cornea supplies about two-thirds of the power of the eye and the lens the rest. This is why reshaping the cornea corrects vision.

concepts.name: Accommodation
concepts.statement: Accommodation is the ability of the eye to adjust its focal length. Because the lens-to-retina distance is fixed, the eye focuses on objects at different distances by changing the power of its lens.

concepts.name: Thin lens equations for the eye
concepts.statement: Written in terms of power, the thin lens equation for the eye is $P = 1/d_{\text{o}} + 1/d_{\text{i}}$, with the image distance fixed at the lens-to-retina distance, and the magnification is $h_{\text{i}}/h_{\text{o}} = -d_{\text{i}}/d_{\text{o}}$.

concepts.name: Finding an image on the retina
concepts.statement: To find the power the eye needs or the size of an image on the retina, set the image distance to the lens-to-retina distance, put every distance in meters, and apply the thin lens equations for the eye.

concepts.name: Presbyopia
concepts.statement: Presbyopia is a condition in which the lens of the eye becomes progressively unable to focus on objects close to the viewer, as the ability to accommodate shrinks with age. It is a loss of added power for close vision, and a converging lens supplies the missing power.

concepts.name: Nearsightedness and farsightedness
concepts.statement: Nearsightedness, or myopia, is a visual defect in which distant objects appear blurred because their images are focused in front of the retina; the eye has too much power. Farsightedness, or hyperopia, is the condition in which incoming rays reach the retina before they converge into a focused image; the eye has too little power for close objects.

concepts.name: Near point and far point
concepts.statement: The far point is the object point imaged on the retina by an unaccommodated eye, normally at infinity. The near point is the point nearest the eye at which an object is accurately focused on the retina at full accommodation, normally 25 cm away.

concepts.name: Correcting nearsightedness
concepts.statement: A diverging lens corrects nearsightedness by making an image of a distant object at the person's far point. Its power follows from the thin lens equation, with the image distance negative and measured from the spectacle.

concepts.name: Correcting farsightedness
concepts.statement: A converging lens corrects farsightedness by making an image of a close object at the person's near point, farther away than the object itself. Measure both distances from the spectacle and give the image distance its negative sign.

concepts.name: Astigmatism
concepts.statement: Astigmatism is the result of an inability of the cornea to focus an image properly onto the retina, a difference in the power of the eye along different axes. It is corrected with a cylindrical lens rather than a spherical one.

concepts.name: Power of lenses in contact
concepts.statement: The power of thin lenses placed close together is approximately the sum of their powers. This lets a contact lens, a tear layer or a reshaped cornea be treated as an addition to the power of the eye.

concepts.name: Laser vision correction
concepts.statement: Laser vision correction is a medical procedure that corrects myopia, hyperopia and astigmatism by reshaping the cornea, which supplies most of the power of the eye. The laser uses ultraviolet light, which the cornea absorbs strongly.

concepts.name: Myopia
concepts.statement: Myopia, or nearsightedness, is a visual defect in which distant objects appear blurred because their images are focused in front of the retina rather than on it.

concepts.name: Hyperopia
concepts.statement: Hyperopia, or farsightedness, is the condition of an eye in which incoming rays of light reach the retina before they converge into a focused image, so that close objects appear blurred.

concepts.name: Near point
concepts.statement: The near point is the point nearest the eye at which an object is accurately focused on the retina at full accommodation, normally 25 cm away.

concepts.name: Far point
concepts.statement: The far point is the object point imaged on the retina by an unaccommodated eye, normally at infinity.

concepts.name: Rods and cones
concepts.statement: Rods and cones are the two types of photoreceptors in the human retina. Rods are sensitive and colorless and serve vision at low light levels; cones are active at higher light levels, give color and fine detail, and crowd the fovea.

concepts.name: Simplified theory of color vision
concepts.statement: The simplified theory of color vision states that there are three primary colors, which correspond to the three types of cones, each sensitive to a different range of wavelengths. It explains how three colors of light can produce thousands of hues, though some evidence shows that it is incomplete.

concepts.name: True color of an object
concepts.statement: The true color of an object is set by the wavelengths it absorbs and reflects, a property of the object rather than of the light falling on it. From it we can predict how a colored object appears under light that is not white.

concepts.name: Color of a light source
concepts.statement: The color of a light source is set by the spectrum of wavelengths it emits, from the sharp line of a laser to the broad spectrum of the Sun.

concepts.name: Color constancy
concepts.statement: Color constancy is the part of the visual perception system that lets people perceive color consistently in a variety of conditions, so that a white tablecloth looks white under sunlight and under candlelight. The eye and brain achieve it by comparing an object with its surroundings.

concepts.name: Hue
concepts.statement: The hue of a color is its identity as it relates specifically to the spectrum, such as red, orange or blue.

concepts.name: Retinex theory
concepts.statement: The retinex theory explains color and brightness perception and their constancies as the work of both the retina and the cortex, whose names combine in its own. It accounts for the ability to perceive color in an ambient-colored environment.

concepts.name: Compound microscope
concepts.statement: A compound microscope is constructed from two convex lenses, the objective and the eyepiece. The objective forms a large real image, and that image is the object for the eyepiece, which magnifies it further as a magnifier does.

concepts.name: Overall magnification
concepts.statement: The overall magnification of a system of thin lenses and mirrors is the product of the magnifications of its elements, $m = m_{\text{o}}m_{\text{e}}$, since each element multiplies the height of the image it is given.

concepts.name: Solving a two-lens system
concepts.statement: To find the image and magnification of a system of two or more lenses, locate the image formed by the first lens, use its distance from the second lens as that lens's object distance, and so find the final image and the overall magnification.

concepts.name: Numerical aperture
concepts.statement: The numerical aperture of a lens, $\text{NA} = n \sin\alpha$, expresses its ability to gather light and to resolve fine detail, where $n$ is the index of refraction of the medium between the lens and the specimen and $\alpha$ is half the angle of acceptance.

concepts.name: f-number
concepts.statement: The $f$-number of a camera lens is its focal length divided by the diameter of its aperture, $f/\# = f/D \approx 1/(2\,\text{NA})$. A smaller $f$-number means a wider aperture and more light.

concepts.name: Immersion objectives
concepts.statement: Filling the gap between the specimen and the objective with oil or water lets rays that would have been refracted away enter the lens, which makes the numerical aperture larger than one.

concepts.name: Microscopes beyond visible light
concepts.statement: A specimen must be illuminated by transmission, scattering or reflection, and microscopes that use x rays or electrons in place of light resolve far finer detail with the same focusing physics.

concepts.name: Objective lens
concepts.statement: The objective lens of an optical instrument is the lens nearest to the object being examined.

concepts.name: Eyepiece
concepts.statement: The eyepiece of an optical instrument is the lens or combination of lenses nearest to the eye of the observer.

concepts.name: Image of a distant object
concepts.statement: For an object at a very great distance, the thin lens equation puts the image one focal length behind the objective, which fixes where the eyepiece of a telescope goes.

concepts.name: Angular magnification of a telescope
concepts.statement: The angular magnification of a telescope with two convex lenses is $M = \theta'/\theta = -f_{\text{o}}/f_{\text{e}}$, so a large magnification needs an objective of long focal length and an eyepiece of short focal length.

concepts.name: Upright and inverted telescopes
concepts.statement: A telescope of two convex lenses forms an inverted image. Galileo's concave eyepiece, or a third convex lens that inverts the image again, gives an upright one.

concepts.name: Reflecting telescopes
concepts.statement: A concave mirror can serve as the objective of a telescope. Mirrors can be made far larger than lenses, gather more light, reach long focal lengths and do not suffer from chromatic aberration.

concepts.name: Telescopes across the spectrum
concepts.statement: Telescopes are not limited to visible light: radio dishes and grazing-incidence x-ray mirrors extend them across the electromagnetic spectrum.

concepts.name: Angular magnification
concepts.statement: The angular magnification of an instrument is the ratio of the angle the image subtends at the eye to the angle the object subtends when viewed by the unaided eye.

concepts.name: Adaptive optics
concepts.statement: Adaptive optics is an optical technology in which computers adjust the lenses and mirrors of a device to correct rapidly changing distortions of the image, such as those the atmosphere causes in a telescope.

concepts.name: Chromatic aberration
concepts.statement: Chromatic aberration is the dependence of the focal length of a lens on the color of the light. Because the index of refraction depends on wavelength, a single lens brings violet light to a focus closer than red. Mirrors are free of it, and a doublet of two glasses partly corrects it.

concepts.name: Coma and spherical aberration
concepts.statement: Coma is the failure of rays from an off-axis object to meet at one point. Spherical aberration is the focusing of rays through the edge of a lens closer than rays near its axis. Both occur even in light of one color.

concepts.name: Reducing aberrations
concepts.statement: Aberrations are reduced by stopping down the aperture, by shaped surfaces, by systems of several elements, by graded index lenses and by correcting the image with a computer, at a cost in brightness or complexity.

concepts.name: Aberration
concepts.statement: An aberration is a failure of rays to converge at one focus because of limitations or defects in a lens or mirror.

concepts.name: Wave optics
concepts.statement: Wave optics is the branch of optics that considers the behavior of light when it exhibits wave characteristics, particularly when it interacts with objects not much larger than its wavelength, such as a narrow slit. Only waves explain effects such as the colors of a soap bubble or an oil slick.

concepts.name: Interference as the hallmark of a wave
concepts.statement: A ray passing through slits would continue straight ahead, while a wave spreads out and forms a pattern of bright and dark regions by interference. Such a pattern is the most certain indication that something is a wave, whether water, sound, light or even matter.

concepts.name: Wavelength in a medium
concepts.statement: When light enters a medium its speed drops to $c/n$ but its frequency stays fixed, so its wavelength shrinks by the same factor: $\lambda_n = \lambda/n$.

concepts.name: Color in a medium
concepts.statement: Light in a medium behaves like a forced oscillation that keeps the frequency of its source. Its speed and wavelength change, but its color does not, because color goes with frequency. Red light does not turn blue when it enters water.

concepts.name: Huygens’s principle
concepts.statement: Huygens's principle states that every point on a wavefront is a source of wavelets that spread out in the forward direction at the same speed as the wave itself. The new wavefront is a line tangent to all of the wavelets. This one construction explains reflection, refraction and diffraction.

concepts.name: Reflection and refraction from Huygens’s principle
concepts.statement: The laws of reflection and refraction were stated for rays in the previous chapter.
