concepts.statement: An object whose escape velocity exceeds the speed of light lets nothing out. The event horizon is the distance at which the escape velocity is exactly the speed of light, and it is the edge of the black hole.

concepts.name: Schwarzschild radius
concepts.statement: The radius of the event horizon of a black hole is $R_{\text{S}} = 2GM/c^{2}$, in proportion to its mass. Since $G$ is small and $c^{2}$ is large, a black hole of a few solar masses is only a few kilometers across.

concepts.name: Finding a Schwarzschild radius
concepts.statement: The Schwarzschild radius $R_{\text{S}} = 2GM/c^{2}$ turns the mass of a black hole into the size of its event horizon, from a stellar black hole to a supermassive one at a galaxy's core.

concepts.name: Neutron star
concepts.statement: In a supernova the core's electrons and protons are forced together into neutrons, and the strong force halts the collapse at a star of nuclear density. A neutron star is slightly larger than a black hole of the same mass.

concepts.name: Gravitational waves
concepts.statement: Gravitational waves are ripples in the curvature of space itself, sent out by moving masses as a water bug's foot sends waves across a pond. They travel at the speed of light and only extreme events make them strong enough to detect.

concepts.name: Black hole radiation
concepts.statement: Where gravity is strong enough to act on the quantum scale, quantum mechanics and general relativity must be used together. A black hole can then radiate, as pairs created near its horizon split and one member escapes.

concepts.name: General relativity
concepts.statement: General relativity is Einstein's theory of gravitation, in which mass curves space and time and the curvature governs the motion of matter and light.

concepts.name: Thought experiment
concepts.statement: A thought experiment is an experiment carried out in the mind rather than with apparatus, to reason out what a theory implies.

concepts.name: Escape velocity
concepts.statement: The escape velocity of a body is the smallest speed an object must have at its surface to escape the body's gravity entirely.

concepts.name: Black hole
concepts.statement: A black hole is an object so dense that its escape velocity exceeds the speed of light, so that nothing, not even light, can escape from it.

concepts.name: Event horizon
concepts.statement: The event horizon is the distance from a black hole at which the escape velocity equals the speed of light; nothing inside it can get out.

concepts.name: Quasar
concepts.statement: A quasar is an extremely distant and luminous object, thought to be the center of a young galaxy powered by a supermassive black hole.

concepts.name: Quantum gravity
concepts.statement: Quantum gravity is the theory, not yet found, that would describe gravity where it is strong enough to act on the quantum scale, by joining quantum mechanics and general relativity.

concepts.name: Superstring theory
concepts.statement: Superstring theory is an attempt at a Theory of Everything, and so must contain quantum gravity. Its particles, the graviton among them, act like one-dimensional vibrating strings in a superspace whose extra dimensions curled up as the forces separated.

concepts.name: Smallest length and time
concepts.statement: Quantum gravity suggests that space and time are grainy, with no meaning to intervals shorter than some tiny finite size. Superstrings would sit at that limit, with no further substructure.

concepts.name: Flat rotation curve
concepts.statement: The orbital speed of the stars in a galaxy stays almost constant out to great distances from its center, instead of falling off as it would if the galaxy's mass were concentrated, like its luminous stars, near the center. This flat rotation curve is the first evidence for dark matter.

concepts.name: Dark matter
concepts.statement: Dark matter is matter that cannot be seen but whose gravity shows it is there; there is about ten times as much of it in the universe as there is luminous matter, and what it is remains unknown.

concepts.name: Critical density
concepts.statement: The critical density $\rho_{\text{c}} \approx 10^{-26}\;\text{kg/m}^{3}$ is the average density of the universe that would just halt its expansion in a universe with no cosmological constant, a few nucleons per cubic meter.

concepts.name: Open, closed and flat universes
concepts.statement: An open universe is negatively curved and expands forever, a closed one is positively curved and returns a traveler to the start, and a flat one lies between. Measurements show the universe is very close to flat.

concepts.name: MACHOs and microlensing
concepts.statement: MACHOs, small dark bodies in a galaxy's halo, would not block a star's light but would focus it as they pass in front of it, and the star would brighten in a characteristic manner. Searches for such microlensing test whether dark matter is ordinary matter.

concepts.name: Neutrino oscillations
concepts.statement: A neutrino can change from one flavor to another only if it has mass, since a massless neutrino travels at the speed of light and no time passes for it. Oscillations explain the missing solar neutrinos and could supply some of the dark matter.

concepts.name: WIMPs
concepts.statement: WIMPs are proposed weakly interacting massive particles, chargeless and of a completely new kind, that could make up dark matter. They would gather in halos rather than coalesce into spirals.

concepts.name: Cosmological constant
concepts.statement: The cosmological constant is a term in Einstein's equations of general relativity that acts as a repulsion causing the expansion of the universe to accelerate.

concepts.name: Negatively curved universe
concepts.statement: A negatively curved universe is an open one, curved like a saddle, in which the angles of a large triangle add to less than $180^{\circ}$ and the expansion continues forever.

concepts.name: Positively curved universe
concepts.statement: A positively curved universe is a closed one, curved like a sphere, in which the angles of a large triangle add to more than $180^{\circ}$ and a traveler going straight returns to the start.

concepts.name: Flat universe
concepts.statement: A flat universe has zero curvature, so that the angles of a triangle add to exactly $180^{\circ}$; it lies between an open and a closed universe.

concepts.name: MACHO
concepts.statement: MACHOs, massive compact halo objects, are dark bodies of ordinary matter, such as faint stars and planets, in a galaxy's halo, proposed as part of the dark matter.

concepts.name: Microlensing
concepts.statement: Microlensing is the brightening of a distant star when a small dark body passes in front of it and focuses its light by gravitational lensing.

concepts.name: Axion
concepts.statement: Axions are a proposed kind of light, weakly interacting particle that could make up some of the dark matter.

concepts.name: Neutralino
concepts.statement: Neutralinos are proposed neutral, weakly interacting massive particles predicted by some theories, candidates for the dark matter.

concepts.name: Complexity
concepts.statement: Complexity is the study of complex adaptive systems, those that obey the simple laws of physics yet can adapt, organize themselves and evolve.

concepts.name: Chaos
concepts.statement: Chaos is a system's extreme sensitivity to its initial conditions, so that a small change in where it starts changes its outcome tremendously and its long-term behavior cannot be predicted with precision.

concepts.name: Order in chaos
concepts.statement: There can be organization in chaos, and it can be quantified. Some chaotic systems settle into a stable self-organized form.

concepts.name: High-temperature superconductors
concepts.statement: High-temperature superconductors are ceramics, found since 1986, that superconduct above 77 K, the boiling point of cheap liquid nitrogen, which makes them economically interesting.

concepts.name: Flux exclusion by superconductors
concepts.statement: A superconductor keeps magnetic flux out and so repels a magnet. A magnet floating above a cooled sample is the evidence that it is superconducting.

concepts.name: Comparing superconductor cooling cost
concepts.statement: A superconducting wire pays only when cooling it costs less than the energy a normal wire loses to heat, a comparison made with the power dissipated in a resistance and the price of electric energy.

concepts.name: Reproducibility at the frontier
concepts.statement: A result at the frontier is accepted only when it can be reproduced or is of such quality that a single observation is meaningful. Reports of superconductors above 200 K have not passed that test.

concepts.name: Superconducting critical temperature
concepts.statement: The critical temperature $T_{\text{c}}$ of a superconductor is the temperature at and below which it has zero resistivity.

concepts.name: Open questions at every scale
concepts.statement: The open questions of physics lie on three scales, the largest, the intermediate and the smallest, and each rests on physics already known.

concepts.name: Connection of small and large scales
concepts.statement: Many of the open questions of cosmology have answers in particle physics, and the reverse. The closure of the universe, for example, depends on the type and number of particles that may contribute to it.

concepts.name: Energy quantization
concepts.statement: A quantized system can have only certain energies and not a continuum of them, which would be like a car that could travel only at certain speeds. This was the first break with classical physics.

concepts.name: Blackbody radiation
concepts.statement: An ideal radiator, a blackbody, emits a spectrum whose shape depends only on its temperature, and that shape could not be explained by classical physics. It was the curve of intensity against wavelength that gave the first clue that the energies of atoms are quantized.

concepts.name: Planck’s quantized oscillator energy
concepts.statement: Planck found that the atoms and molecules of a blackbody, treated as oscillators, could have only the energies $E = (n + \frac{1}{2})hf$. With this one assumption he described the measured blackbody spectrum correctly, and Planck’s constant $h$ entered physics.

concepts.name: Quantum energy step
concepts.statement: An oscillator of frequency $f$ can gain or lose energy only in discrete steps of size $hf$, much as a person on a staircase can stand only on the steps. Because $h$ is so small, these steps are far too small to notice in a macroscopic system.

concepts.name: Correspondence principle
concepts.statement: In the classical limit of large, slow-moving objects, quantum mechanics gives the same results as classical physics. This is why quantization goes unnoticed in everyday life.

concepts.name: Quantized energies from atomic spectra
concepts.statement: A hot gas emits only certain wavelengths, a line spectrum, and if each emission carries an energy $\Delta E = hf$, the energies of the electrons in the emitting atoms must be quantized.

concepts.name: Quantized
concepts.statement: A physical quantity is quantized when it exists only with particular discrete values and not with every value in a continuum.

concepts.name: Blackbody
concepts.statement: A blackbody is an ideal radiator, one that can radiate equally well at all wavelengths.

concepts.name: Planck’s constant
concepts.statement: Planck’s constant $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}$ J·s is the constant that sets the size of the quantum steps of energy; Planck found its value by fitting his theory to the measured blackbody spectrum.

concepts.name: Atomic spectra
concepts.statement: Atomic spectra are the electromagnetic emission from atoms and molecules, which for a hot gas consists of only certain wavelengths.

concepts.name: Photoelectric effect
concepts.statement: When light strikes a material it can eject electrons, and the energy of those electrons can be measured with a retarding voltage. The details of this simple experiment are what forced Einstein to treat light itself as quantized.

concepts.name: Photon energy
concepts.statement: Einstein proposed that EM radiation is itself made of quanta, photons, each with an energy $E = hf$ proportional to its frequency. This is a quantization of the radiation, not only of the oscillators that emit it.

concepts.name: Properties of the photoelectric effect
concepts.statement: A threshold frequency below which no electrons leave however intense the light, ejection without delay, a number of electrons that grows with intensity and a maximum kinetic energy that does not: each of these follows from one photon meeting one electron, and several contradict a simple wave.

concepts.name: Einstein’s photoelectric equation
concepts.statement: The photon gives all its energy to one electron; part of it breaks the electron away from the material and the rest becomes the electron’s kinetic energy. This one line explains the photoelectric effect quantitatively, and its graph against frequency has Planck’s constant as its slope.

concepts.name: Photoelectric threshold
concepts.statement: A photon whose energy is less than the binding energy cannot free an electron at all, so each material has a threshold frequency $f_0 = \text{BE}/h$, and a longest wavelength, below which no electrons are ejected.

concepts.name: Finding a photon’s energy from its wavelength
concepts.statement: We usually describe light by its wavelength, so you most often find the photon energy by combining $E = hf$ with $c = f\lambda$. With it you can compare any photon with the energies of atoms and molecules.

concepts.name: Photon
concepts.statement: A photon is a quantum, or particle, of electromagnetic radiation.

concepts.name: Work function
concepts.statement: The binding energy, also called the work function, is the energy needed to eject an electron from a material.

concepts.name: Photon energies in electron volts
concepts.statement: On the scale of atoms the electron volt is the natural unit, and with $h = 4.14 \times 10^{-15}$ eV·s and $hc = 1240$ eV·nm a photon energy is found in one division.

concepts.name: Photon energy and radiation effects
concepts.statement: Because photons interact one at a time with individual atoms and molecules, what a kind of radiation can do depends on how the energy of one photon compares with molecular and atomic energies. This explains why UV sunburns and visible light does not, and why dyes fade in a particular order.

concepts.name: Ionizing photons
concepts.statement: A photon with more energy than the 10 to 1000 eV needed to ionize an atom can damage tissue on its own, so the high-frequency end of the spectrum is hazardous in a way the low-frequency end is not. The same energy makes these photons useful in medical imaging and cancer treatment.

concepts.name: Maximum x-ray photon energy
concepts.statement: An electron accelerated through a voltage $V$ gains an energy $qV$, and when it strikes the anode it can give all of it to a single photon. So an x-ray tube’s voltage in kilovolts is its highest photon energy in keV, which is how its penetrating power is adjusted.

concepts.name: X-ray tube spectrum
concepts.statement: The x-ray spectrum of a tube has two parts: a smooth distribution from electrons braking in the anode, and sharp peaks that belong to the anode material. The peaks, like the lines of atomic spectra, are one more sign that the energy levels of atoms are quantized.

concepts.name: Counting photons per second
concepts.statement: Power is energy per unit time, so dividing a source’s power by the energy of one photon gives the number of photons it emits each second. The enormous numbers that result show why individual photons go unnoticed in ordinary life.

concepts.name: Microwaves
concepts.statement: Microwaves are the band of electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths from about a millimeter to about a meter, below the infrared in photon energy.

concepts.name: Bremsstrahlung
concepts.statement: Bremsstrahlung, German for braking radiation, is the radiation produced when electrons are decelerated, as in the anode of an x-ray tube.

concepts.name: Characteristic x rays
concepts.statement: Characteristic x rays are x rays whose energies depend on the material they were produced in, appearing as sharp peaks in the spectrum of an x-ray tube.

concepts.name: Photon momentum
concepts.statement: Photons have no mass, yet they carry momentum, and a photon of wavelength $\lambda$ carries $p = h/\lambda$. This is why comet tails point away from the Sun and why a space sail could be pushed by sunlight.

concepts.name: Compton effect
concepts.statement: When an x-ray photon scatters from an electron, the two collide like particles, energy and momentum are both conserved, and the scattered photon leaves with less energy and a longer wavelength. This was among the earliest direct evidence that momentum is conserved in quantum mechanics.

concepts.name: Photon momentum and energy
concepts.statement: Setting the mass to zero in the relativistic relation between energy and momentum gives $E = pc$ for a photon, and with $E = hc/\lambda$ this is Compton’s $p = h/\lambda$ again. The two routes to the same momentum tie the chapter to special relativity.

concepts.name: Size of photon momentum
concepts.statement: Because $h$ is so small, the momentum of visible light is tiny, which is why mirrors do not recoil. It becomes important only for short-wavelength photons meeting light particles, as in Compton’s experiment, or for enormous numbers of photons with nothing to stop the recoil.

concepts.name: Applying momentum conservation to photons
concepts.statement: A photon absorbed gives its momentum to the absorber, and a photon reflected straight back gives twice its momentum. With these two facts you can find the recoil of a dust grain, a sail or a mirror.

concepts.name: Particle-wave duality of EM radiation
concepts.statement: Light shows interference, which is a property of waves, and it interacts as discrete photons, which is a property of particles. The duality is the name for having both, and the next question it raises is whether matter has it too.

concepts.name: Particle or wave in one observation
concepts.statement: The duality seems strange because the words wave and particle come from large objects, which never act like both. On the quantum level our observations reveal one set of properties or the other, but not both simultaneously.

concepts.name: De Broglie wavelength
concepts.statement: De Broglie proposed that every particle, with mass or without, has a wavelength $h/p$. It is the same relation as the photon’s, now applied to matter, and it opened the era in which quantum mechanics was founded.

concepts.name: Wave effects and obstacle size
concepts.statement: A wave must meet an object about as large as its wavelength to show interference, and a macroscopic body has a wavelength far smaller than anything known. This is why a bowling ball never diffracts and why the wave nature of matter was first seen with electrons.

concepts.name: Electron diffraction
concepts.statement: Davisson and Germer, and independently G. P. Thomson, scattered electrons from crystals and found diffraction patterns exactly consistent with the de Broglie wavelength. Interference is the hallmark of a wave, so these patterns showed that electrons are waves as well as particles.

concepts.name: Finding an electron’s speed and energy from its wavelength
concepts.statement: With $p = mv$ for a nonrelativistic particle, the de Broglie wavelength gives the speed, $v = h/m\lambda$, and from it the kinetic energy. Check that the speed really is well below the speed of light.

concepts.name: Electron microscope
concepts.statement: Resolution is limited to about one wavelength, and electrons from a modest voltage have wavelengths far smaller than those of visible light. The transmission and scanning electron microscopes use this to see details as small as individual atoms.

concepts.name: Bragg equation
concepts.statement: Planes of atoms in a crystal act like the slits of a diffraction grating: electrons scattered from successive planes interfere constructively when the extra path is a whole number of wavelengths. The same relation applies to x rays.

concepts.name: Probability distribution
concepts.statement: Each electron arrives at a definite place that cannot be predicted, yet many of them together build up a wave’s diffraction pattern. What quantum mechanics predicts is the probability of finding the particle at each location.

concepts.name: Measurement affecting the system
concepts.statement: A single electron at a time still builds up a double-slit pattern, so each electron interferes with itself. But if the slit it passes through is determined, the pattern becomes a single-slit one: measurement affects the system being observed.

concepts.name: Position-momentum uncertainty principle
concepts.statement: A probe short enough in wavelength to locate a particle well carries a large momentum and disturbs the particle’s momentum, so the two cannot both be known exactly. The product of their uncertainties can never be smaller than $h/4\pi$.

concepts.name: Energy-time uncertainty principle
concepts.statement: Energy cannot be measured precisely in a short time, so a short-lived state has an uncertain energy. The spread in the decay energies of short-lived particles is used to find their lifetimes.

concepts.name: Finding a minimum uncertainty
concepts.statement: Using the equals sign in either form of the principle gives the smallest possible uncertainty, and $\Delta p = m\Delta v$ turns a momentum uncertainty into a velocity uncertainty. Compare the result with atomic energies to judge whether it matters.

concepts.name: Uncertainty for large objects
concepts.statement: Planck’s constant is so small that the limits the principle sets are far below anything that matters for a planet or a ball. This is the correspondence principle again, and it is why we never notice the uncertainty principle in everyday life.

concepts.name: Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle
concepts.statement: Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle sets a fundamental limit to the precision with which pairs of quantities, such as position and momentum or energy and time, can be measured together.

concepts.name: Uncertainty in position
concepts.statement: The uncertainty in position is the lack of precision, or lack of knowledge, in the results of measurements of a particle’s position.

concepts.name: Uncertainty in momentum
concepts.statement: The uncertainty in momentum is the lack of precision, or lack of knowledge, in the results of measurements of a particle’s momentum.

concepts.name: Uncertainty in energy
concepts.statement: The uncertainty in energy is the lack of precision, or lack of knowledge, in the results of measurements of energy.

concepts.name: Uncertainty in time
concepts.statement: The uncertainty in time is the lack of precision, or lack of knowledge, in the results of measurements of time, such as the lifetime of a state.

concepts.name: Particle-wave duality of all particles
concepts.statement: Every particle, massless like the photon or with mass like the electron, has a wavelength and behaves as a particle, and so do combinations of them such as nuclei, atoms and molecules. The duality is a universal attribute of nature, one more connection between matter and energy.

concepts.name: Classical limit of particle-wave duality
concepts.statement: A large combination of massive particles has a wave nature too small to observe, and a large combination of photons shows mostly wave behavior. This is why classical physics saw matter only as particles and light only as waves.

concepts.name: Solving an integrated photon problem
concepts.statement: A problem that joins photon energy and momentum to momentum conservation, heat transfer, circuits, wave optics or relativity is solved by identifying the physical principles involved and solving each part with the strategy of its own chapter.

concepts.name: Temperature
concepts.statement: Temperature is operationally defined to be what we measure with a thermometer. Your senses of hot and cold are relative: tepid water feels cool to a hand that was in hot water and warm to a hand that was in cold water. Two accurate thermometers placed in the same water give the same reading. Many physical quantities are defined solely by how we measure them, and later in the chapter temperature gains a more physical meaning, tied to the kinetic energies of atoms and molecules.

concepts.name: Thermometer
concepts.statement: Any physical property that depends on temperature, and whose response to temperature is reproducible, can serve as the basis of a thermometer. Volume increases with temperature for most substances, which is the basis for the alcohol thermometer, the mercury thermometer and the bimetallic strip. Electrical resistance, color and the emission of infrared radiation serve as well. Because so many properties depend on temperature, the variety of thermometers is remarkable.

concepts.name: Temperature scales
concepts.statement: A temperature scale starts from two easily reproducible temperatures, commonly the freezing and boiling points of water at standard atmospheric pressure. The Celsius scale puts them at 0 °C and 100 °C and the Fahrenheit scale at 32 °F and 212 °F, so one Celsius degree is 1.8 times the size of one Fahrenheit degree. The Kelvin scale is the absolute scale of science. Its zero is absolute zero, its unit is the kelvin with no degree sign, and a kelvin equals a degree Celsius in size, so water freezes at 273.15 K and boils at 373.15 K.

concepts.name: Converting a temperature between scales
concepts.statement: Temperatures on the three common scales are converted with the equations of Table 13.1. Celsius to Fahrenheit multiplies by nine fifths and adds 32, Celsius to Kelvin adds 273.15, and the conversions between Fahrenheit and Kelvin, which look complicated, are simple combinations of those two. A temperature difference converts differently from a temperature: a change of one degree Celsius is a change of one kelvin and of nine fifths of a Fahrenheit degree, with no offset.

concepts.name: Absolute zero
concepts.statement: The concept of absolute zero arises from the behavior of gases. The pressure of a gas kept at constant volume falls in a straight line as its temperature falls, and the lines for different gases all extrapolate to zero pressure at the same temperature, −273.15 °C. This suggests that there is a lowest temperature, and other thermodynamic relationships lead to the same conclusion. At absolute zero, 0 K, molecular motion is at the minimum energy possible; most gases liquefy and then freeze before it is reached, and it is not actually possible to reach it.

concepts.name: Thermal equilibrium
concepts.statement: Two systems in thermal contact are in thermal equilibrium when they have the same temperature, so that no heat flows between them and neither temperature changes. Any two systems placed in thermal contact but isolated from the rest of the environment reach this state: heat flows from the hotter object to the cooler one until their temperatures are equal. That is why a thermometer, which actually takes its own temperature, reads the temperature of the object it touches once enough time has passed. A single object is in internal thermal equilibrium when no heat flows within it and its temperature is uniform.

concepts.name: Zeroth law of thermodynamics
concepts.statement: If two systems, A and B, are in thermal equilibrium with each other, and B is in thermal equilibrium with a third system, C, then A is also in thermal equilibrium with C. The conclusion may seem obvious, because all three have the same temperature, but it is basic to thermodynamics. It bears the name zeroth law because it comes logically before the first and second laws, although physicists stated it after them. It lets you trust two thermometers, each touching a different block on the same plate, to read the same number, and so it makes temperature a meaningful concept.

concepts.name: Celsius scale
concepts.statement: The Celsius scale is the temperature scale on which the freezing point of water is 0 °C and its boiling point is 100 °C, both at standard atmospheric pressure.

concepts.name: Degree Celsius
concepts.statement: The degree Celsius is the unit of the Celsius scale, one hundredth of the interval between the freezing and boiling points of water. It is the same size as the kelvin.

concepts.name: Fahrenheit scale
concepts.statement: The Fahrenheit scale is the temperature scale on which the freezing point of water is 32 °F and its boiling point is 212 °F, both at standard atmospheric pressure.

concepts.name: Degree Fahrenheit
concepts.statement: The degree Fahrenheit is the unit of the Fahrenheit scale, one hundred eightieth of the interval between the freezing and boiling points of water, so a degree Celsius is 1.8 times as large.

concepts.name: Kelvin scale
concepts.statement: The Kelvin scale is the absolute temperature scale of science. Its zero is absolute zero, and its unit, the kelvin, is written K with no degree sign and equals a degree Celsius in size, so water freezes at 273.15 K and boils at 373.15 K.

concepts.name: Thermal expansion
concepts.statement: Thermal expansion is the change in size or volume of a given mass with temperature. It is why hot air rises, since air that expands has a smaller density than the air around it and a larger buoyant force on a given mass, and it is why railroad tracks and bridges need expansion joints. Its cause is that an increase in temperature increases the kinetic energy of the atoms, whose small, rapid vibrations push their neighbors slightly farther apart on average, and that slightly greater spacing adds up to a larger body. For most substances there is no preferred direction, and the body grows by the same fraction in every dimension.

concepts.name: Linear thermal expansion
concepts.statement: The change in length of a body is proportional to its length and to the change in temperature, with a coefficient of linear expansion that depends on the material and varies slightly with temperature. Because a kelvin and a degree Celsius are the same size, the coefficient and the temperature change may use either. The equation is accurate for small changes in temperature and serves for large ones with an average value of the coefficient.

forms.condition: small changes in temperature

concepts.name: Thermal expansion in two dimensions
concepts.statement: Objects expand in all dimensions, so an area grows because both its length and its width grow. For small temperature changes the change in area is twice the coefficient of linear expansion times the area times the change in temperature, since each of two dimensions contributes the linear fraction.

forms.condition: small changes in temperature

concepts.name: Expansion of a hole
concepts.statement: If you cut a hole in a metal plate, the remaining material expands exactly as it would if the plug were still in place. The plug would get bigger, and so the hole must get bigger too: the ring of neighboring atoms on the wall of the hole push each other farther apart as the temperature rises, and the ring gets slightly larger. Holes do not close up when a body is heated.

concepts.name: Thermal expansion in three dimensions
concepts.statement: The change in volume is very nearly three times the linear coefficient times the volume times the temperature change. The equation usually uses a coefficient of volume expansion about three times the coefficient of linear expansion, as the values in Table 13.2 show almost exactly. Liquids and gases have only a volume coefficient, and the coefficient for gases is the largest of all and nearly the same for every gas.

concepts.name: Finding what spills from an expanding liquid
concepts.statement: When a full container and the liquid in it warm together, both expand, but the liquid expands more, and the amount that spills is the difference of their volume changes. Because the original volumes are equal, the three equations combine into one: the spill is the difference of the two volume coefficients times the volume times the temperature change. The same difference is why a gasoline gauge reads empty with less mass in the tank in summer than in winter, and why a beaker filled to the brim overflows as it warms.

concepts.name: Anomalous expansion of water
concepts.statement: Water is the most important exception to the rule that objects expand with increasing temperature. Above 4 °C it expands as its temperature rises, but between 4 °C and 0 °C it expands as its temperature falls, so that it is densest at 4 °C. The most striking effect is the freezing of a pond: water at the surface cools to 4 °C, sinks, and turns the pond over until the whole of it is at 4 °C; a surface layer that cools further is less dense than the water below and stays on top, so the surface freezes over and the ice insulates the water beneath, where fish survive the winter.

concepts.name: Thermal stress
concepts.statement: Thermal stress arises when something constrains thermal expansion or contraction. To find the pressure a heated body would exert if it could not expand, take the volume change it would make at fixed pressure and use the bulk modulus to find the pressure that squeezes that volume back out. Such pressures are typically enormous: gasoline held at fixed volume through a 20 °C rise would reach 1.83 × 10⁷ Pa, about 2500 lb/in², far more than a tank can hold. Thermal stress buckles rails, snaps power lines, cracks unevenly cooled glass, weathers rock and pavement, and bursts biological cells when food freezes.

concepts.name: Coefficient of linear expansion
concepts.statement: The coefficient of linear expansion is the change in length per unit length per degree of temperature change. It depends on the material and varies slightly with temperature, and its unit is the inverse degree Celsius, 1/°C.

concepts.name: Coefficient of volume expansion
concepts.statement: The coefficient of volume expansion is the change in volume per unit volume per degree of temperature change. For a solid it is very nearly three times the coefficient of linear expansion, and liquids have much larger values than solids.

concepts.name: An ideal gas
concepts.statement: Atoms and molecules in a gas are widely separated compared with their sizes, so the forces between them can be ignored except when they collide, and the gas expands to fill whatever volume it can reach. That is why gases have the largest coefficients of volume expansion and why they all have nearly the same one, when liquids and solids differ widely: the properties of a gas depend on how many molecules there are per unit volume and on temperature, not on what kind of molecule it is. A gas whose particles have negligible volume and interact only through perfectly elastic collisions is called an ideal gas, and room temperature air is one in most circumstances.

concepts.name: Ideal gas law
concepts.statement: The ideal gas law relates the absolute pressure of a gas, its volume, the number of atoms and molecules in it and its absolute temperature through the Boltzmann constant. It is an equation of state, a relation among the thermodynamic properties of a system. It first came from experiment: Charles' law says volume is proportional to temperature at fixed pressure, and Boyle's law says pressure times volume is constant at fixed temperature. It describes real gases under most conditions, and it holds for any gas or mixture of gases, since only the total number of molecules enters. Always use absolute pressure and absolute temperature.

concepts.name: Boltzmann constant
concepts.statement: The constant that turns the count of molecules and the absolute temperature into the product of pressure and volume is the Boltzmann constant, named for Ludwig Boltzmann, with the value 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K. Its unit says what it does: it relates an energy to a temperature, so that kT is an energy per molecule.

concepts.name: Using the ideal gas law as a ratio
concepts.statement: When a gas changes state with some of its properties fixed, write the law once for the initial state and once for the final state and divide one by the other. Whatever stays constant cancels, and so does the Boltzmann constant, leaving a relation among the quantities that changed. For a tire whose volume and contents do not change, the ratio of final to initial pressure equals the ratio of final to initial absolute temperature, which is why the temperatures must be in kelvins.

forms.condition: constant volume and number of molecules

concepts.name: Mole
concepts.statement: The mole is the SI unit for the amount of a substance, and it is convenient because the number of molecules in any ordinary object is enormous. One mole contains Avogadro's number of particles, whatever the substance, and a mole of any substance has a mass in grams equal to its molecular mass, which is read off the periodic table. The number of moles is the number of molecules divided by Avogadro's number.

concepts.name: Avogadro’s number
concepts.statement: Avogadro's number is the number of particles in one mole, 6.02 × 10²³ per mole to three significant figures. It honors Amedeo Avogadro, who proposed, correctly, that equal volumes of gas at the same pressure and temperature contain equal numbers of molecules. Since 2019 one mole is exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ elementary entities. The number is so large that a mole of table tennis balls would cover the Earth to a depth of about 40 km.

concepts.name: Ideal gas law in moles
concepts.statement: Multiplying and dividing the ideal gas law by Avogadro's number turns the count of molecules into a number of moles and the Boltzmann constant into the universal gas constant. That constant is Avogadro's number times the Boltzmann constant: 8.31 J/(mol·K) in SI units, 1.99 cal/(mol·K) or 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K) in others. Use the form of the law that matches what you know, the number of molecules or the number of moles, and the value of the gas constant that matches the units of the problem.

concepts.name: Molar volume at STP
concepts.statement: Standard temperature and pressure are 0 °C and atmospheric pressure. At STP the ideal gas law gives 2.68 × 10²⁵ molecules in every cubic meter of any gas, 44.5 mol per cubic meter, and 22.5 L per mole to the precision of three-figure inputs (the accepted value is 22.4 L/mol). Because the count is the same for every gas, the mass of a cubic meter follows from the molar mass alone. Dry air at 28.8 g/mol weighs 1.28 kg per cubic meter, so a living room holds about 90 kg of air, the mass of a person.

forms.condition: at standard temperature and pressure, 0 °C and 1 atm

concepts.name: Ideal gas law as energy
concepts.statement: Both sides of the ideal gas law have the dimensions of energy, joules in SI units. Pressure is force per unit area, so pressure times volume is force times displacement, which is work. The right-hand side is proportional to the translational kinetic energy of the molecules at that temperature, as the next section shows. A gas holds energy related to both its pressure and its volume, and the ideal gas law is another expression of the conservation of energy: the work of pumping up a tire goes into the pressure of the air and into warming the pump and the air.

concepts.name: Universal gas constant
concepts.statement: The universal gas constant is the product of Avogadro's number and the Boltzmann constant, R = 8.31 J/(mol·K). It plays the part for a mole of gas that the Boltzmann constant plays for a single molecule.

concepts.name: Kinetic theory
concepts.statement: Kinetic theory assumes that atoms and molecules are in continuous random motion, and it explains pressure and temperature from that assumption. When a molecule collides elastically with a rigid wall, the component of its momentum perpendicular to the wall is reversed, so the wall exerts a force on it and, by Newton's third law, it exerts a force on the wall. A huge number of molecules strike the wall in a short time, and we observe the average force per unit area. More molecules mean more collisions and more pressure; faster molecules mean harder collisions and more pressure.

concepts.name: Ideal gas law from molecules
concepts.statement: Following one molecule in a box gives the pressure of the gas. Its momentum changes by twice its perpendicular momentum at each collision, the average time between collisions with one wall is the time to cross the box and back, so the average force from one molecule is its mass times the square of its perpendicular speed over the length of the box. Multiplying by the number of molecules, replacing the perpendicular component by a third of the mean square speed because the motion is random and the three directions are alike, and dividing by the area of the wall gives the pressure. The result, PV = ⅓Nm v̄², is another expression of the ideal gas law, now in terms of the mass and speed of the molecules.

concepts.name: Thermal energy of a molecule
concepts.statement: Setting the molecular form of the ideal gas law equal to PV = NkT and rearranging shows that the average translational kinetic energy of a molecule is three halves of the Boltzmann constant times the absolute temperature. This average kinetic energy is the thermal energy. The equation gives a molecular interpretation of temperature, valid for gases and reasonably accurate in liquids and solids. It defines temperature in terms of the energy of molecular motion, and at a given temperature it is the same for every kind of molecule.

forms.condition: monatomic ideal gas

concepts.name: rms speed
concepts.statement: Solving the thermal energy equation for speed gives the root-mean-square speed of the molecules, the square root of the average of the speed squared, which grows with the square root of the absolute temperature and falls with the square root of the mass of the molecule. It is surprisingly large, 511 m/s for nitrogen at room temperature, yet it produces no wind, because the molecules move in every direction alike and travel only a tiny mean free path between collisions. The speed of sound, about 340 m/s at room temperature, reflects it, which is why sound is faster in hot air and in light gases such as helium.

concepts.name: Finding the mass of a molecule
concepts.statement: The mass of a single atom or molecule is the molar mass, read from the periodic table in grams per mole and converted to kilograms, divided by the number of particles in a mole. A nitrogen molecule is two atoms of 14.0067 g/mol, so it has a mass of 4.65 × 10⁻²⁶ kg; a helium atom has 6.65 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. Every calculation of an rms speed or of a temperature from a speed passes through this step.

forms.latex: m = \frac{\text{molar mass}}{\text{number of atoms per mole}}

concepts.name: Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution
concepts.statement: The motion of any one molecule is random in magnitude and direction, but a gas of many molecules has a predictable distribution of speeds, the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, calculated from kinetic theory and confirmed by experiment. The distribution has a long tail, since a few molecules move at several times the rms speed, and its peak, the most probable speed, lies below the rms speed. As the temperature rises the whole distribution shifts to higher speeds and broadens, which is why a person with a fever loses more water from the linings of the mouth and lungs.

concepts.name: Escape of light gases from an atmosphere
concepts.statement: To escape Earth's gravity from the top of the atmosphere an object must travel at 11.1 km/s, and helium would need a temperature near 2 × 10⁴ K for its rms speed to reach that. Yet the air holds very little helium. The speed of an atom changes from instant to instant, and at any instant a small fraction in the tail of the distribution exceeds the escape velocity; over billions of years that fraction leaks away. Heavier molecules, oxygen, nitrogen and water, have smaller rms speeds, and so few of them ever reach escape speed that Earth keeps its atmosphere. The Moon's gravity is so much weaker that it has lost almost all of its atmosphere, and its daytime sky is black.

concepts.name: Condensation of a real gas
concepts.statement: Real gases behave like ideal gases at high temperatures, but at lower temperatures the interactions between molecules and the volumes of the molecules begin to matter. The molecules come very close, the gas condenses, and the volume drops precipitously as the substance becomes a liquid. Cooled further it becomes a solid, and the volume shrinks a little more but never reaches zero, because the molecules themselves have volume. High pressure can also liquefy a gas, which is how industry makes liquid carbon dioxide and liquid nitrogen.

concepts.name: PV diagram
concepts.statement: A graph of pressure against volume is a PV diagram. For an ideal gas at fixed temperature and number of molecules the product PV is constant, so each isotherm, a curve at one temperature, is a hyperbola, and the upper curves are the hotter ones. At lower temperatures the curves stop looking like hyperbolas, since the gas no longer behaves ideally and may contain liquid; along the flat part of a low isotherm the pressure stays constant while the volume changes, because the substance is changing phase.

forms.condition: ideal gas, constant temperature and number of molecules

concepts.name: Critical point
concepts.statement: Above a substance's critical temperature the liquid phase cannot exist at any pressure. The isotherm at that temperature is the highest one with a flat, two-phase part, and above it a gas compressed hard enough may reach the density of a liquid without condensing. The critical pressure is the minimum pressure needed for the liquid to exist at the critical temperature. Carbon dioxide cannot become a liquid above 31 °C, nor oxygen above −118 °C, so no amount of squeezing liquefies oxygen at room temperature.

concepts.name: Phase diagram
concepts.statement: A graph of pressure against temperature is a phase diagram: there are well-defined regions in which the substance is solid, liquid or gas, and the solid lines between them are the temperatures and pressures at which two phases coexist. For water the liquid-vapor curve gives the boiling point at each pressure, 100 °C at 1.00 atm rising to 374 °C at 218 atm, which is why a pressure cooker cooks faster; the solid-liquid curve gives the melting point, and for water it leans so that the melting temperature falls with increasing pressure, which is why a snowball packs and why tires melt snow into an ice layer. Knowing the pressure and temperature, you can read the phase off the diagram.

concepts.name: Sublimation
concepts.statement: At sufficiently low pressures there is no liquid phase, and the substance goes directly between solid and gas. The phase change from solid to gas is sublimation; it accounts for snow pack that is lost without ever running into a river, for the automatic defrosting of a freezer and for freeze-drying. For water there is no liquid below 0.00600 atm, while carbon dioxide sublimates at ordinary atmospheric pressure, which is why solid carbon dioxide is dry ice: it does not melt.

concepts.name: Triple point
concepts.statement: The three curves of a phase diagram meet at a single point, the triple point, where solid, liquid and gas all exist in equilibrium. For water it is at 273.16 K and 0.00600 atm, and because it is a single well-defined temperature and pressure it is a more accurate calibration temperature than the melting point at 1.00 atm, which is 273.15 K. Every substance has one, and Table 13.4 lists several.

concepts.name: Phase equilibrium
concepts.statement: Liquid and gas are in equilibrium at the boiling temperature. In a closed container the liquid boils and the gas condenses at the same rate, with no net change in their amounts, because molecules leave the liquid as gas as fast as gas molecules stick to the liquid. At a higher temperature the liquid boils faster, more molecules are in the gas, the gas pressure is higher and condensation speeds up to match, so the pair reaches equilibrium again at the new pressure. An open pot of water at 100 °C boils away, and an open glass at 20 °C evaporates, because the gas above them is air rather than pure water vapor. A gas below its boiling temperature is a vapor.

concepts.name: Vapor pressure
concepts.statement: Vapor pressure is the pressure at which a gas coexists with its solid or liquid phase. It is created by the faster molecules that break away from the liquid or solid and enter the gas, so it depends on the substance and on its temperature, and an increase in temperature increases it. Water evaporates and ice sublimates when their vapor pressure exceeds the partial pressure of water vapor in the surrounding gas, and droplets or frost form when it is less.

concepts.name: Dalton’s law of partial pressures
concepts.statement: The partial pressure of a gas is the pressure it would create if it alone occupied the total volume available, and in a mixture of gases the total pressure is the sum of the partial pressures of the components, assuming ideal gas behavior and no chemical reactions. This is Dalton's law, and it follows from kinetic theory: each gas creates its pressure by its own molecular collisions, independent of the other gases present, and pressures add as Pascal's principle says they do.

concepts.name: Vapor
concepts.statement: A vapor is a gas at a temperature below the boiling temperature of its substance, so that it can coexist with the liquid.

concepts.name: Partial pressure
concepts.statement: The partial pressure of a gas in a mixture is the pressure it would create if it alone occupied the total volume available.

concepts.name: Critical temperature
concepts.statement: The critical temperature of a substance is the temperature above which its liquid phase cannot exist, however great the pressure.

concepts.name: Critical pressure
concepts.statement: The critical pressure of a substance is the minimum pressure needed for its liquid phase to exist at the critical temperature.

concepts.name: Relative humidity and saturation
concepts.statement: Relative humidity tells how much water vapor is in the air compared with the maximum possible. At the maximum, saturation, the relative humidity is 100%, evaporation is inhibited and we feel hotter, because sweat no longer cools us. The amount of water vapor the air can carry depends on temperature through the vapor pressure of water: at 100% humidity the partial pressure of water vapor equals the vapor pressure, below it evaporation goes on, above it condensation. The water is not held by the air; the amount of water in air is set by the vapor pressure of water alone and has nothing to do with the properties of air.

concepts.name: Finding the saturation vapor density
concepts.statement: Water vapor behaves like an ideal gas. The density of vapor that creates a given partial pressure follows from PV = nRT, solved for the moles per cubic meter and converted to grams with the molar mass of water, 18.0 g/mol. At 20.0 °C the vapor pressure of 2.33 × 10³ Pa gives 17.2 g/m³, exactly the saturation vapor density in Table 13.5. The table's densities are the maximum amounts of water vapor a cubic meter can carry at each temperature.

concepts.name: Percent relative humidity
concepts.statement: Percent relative humidity is the ratio of the vapor density actually in the air to the saturation vapor density at that temperature, times 100. With Table 13.5 it answers many questions about a day's weather: air at 25.0 °C holding 9.40 g/m³ has a relative humidity of 40.9%, and the same air with a dew point of −10.0 °C has only 10.3%.

concepts.name: Dew point
concepts.statement: The dew point is the temperature at which the air's water vapor would be the saturation density, so that the relative humidity would be 100%. At that temperature water starts to condense out of the air as dew, fog or frost. The air temperature cannot fall below the dew point without water condensing, and condensation releases considerable heat, which holds the temperature up. That is why farmers watch the dew point, why desert nights are so cold and why fog forms as the evening cools.

concepts.name: Reading humidity from the saturation table
concepts.statement: Every humidity problem runs through Table 13.5. The vapor density in the air, the saturation density at the air temperature and the saturation density at the dew point are three entries of the same column. Any one of humidity, vapor density, dew point and temperature follows from the others. The humidity is the ratio of two densities, the dew point is the temperature whose saturation density equals the vapor density in the air, and the water that condenses when air cools is the difference of two saturation densities. Where a temperature falls between rows, interpolate.

concepts.name: Boiling point and pressure
concepts.statement: Water boils at 100 °C because that is where its vapor pressure reaches 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa, one atmosphere, so that it can evaporate without limit. Bubbles form because water holds dissolved air: a bubble at the bottom of a pot contains air and water vapor at a total pressure of 1.00 atm, and as the temperature rises the water vapor in it increases and the bubble expands to keep its pressure; at 100 °C vapor enters continuously, the bubble grows, its buoyant force grows, and it breaks away and rises. Where the pressure on the water is different the boiling temperature is different: higher in a pressure cooker or at depth, lower at altitude and in a vacuum chamber.

concepts.name: Evaporation cools what it leaves
concepts.statement: We keep cool in hot weather by evaporating sweat from our skin and water from our breathing passages, and high humidity inhibits that evaporation, which is why humid heat is worse. The molecules most likely to escape a liquid are those with the greatest speeds, so the molecules that remain have a lower average speed and a lower temperature; lowering the surrounding pressure lowers the partial pressure of water, speeds evaporation, and can cool food until it freezes, which is what a freeze-dryer does. Blowing hot air dries hair faster because the higher temperature raises the rate of evaporation.

concepts.name: Saturation
concepts.statement: Air is saturated when its relative humidity is 100%, so that it holds the most water vapor it can at its temperature and the partial pressure equals the vapor pressure of water.

concepts.name: Radioactivity
concepts.statement: Radioactivity is the spontaneous decay of some nuclei, which destroys a small part of their mass and emits energetic rays from the nucleus.

concepts.name: Nuclear origin of radiation
concepts.statement: The rays of radioactivity come from the nucleus, not the electrons: they do not vary with chemical state, temperature, pressure or ionization, all of which affect electrons, and each event carries energies of the order of a million electron volts, far beyond atomic energies of a few eV.

concepts.name: Alpha, beta and gamma rays
concepts.statement: Physicists named the three kinds of nuclear radiation before anyone knew what they were. A magnetic field bends alphas and betas in opposite directions and leaves gammas alone, which shows their charges. Later work showed that an alpha is a helium nucleus, a beta is an electron created at the instant of decay, and a gamma is a high-energy photon from a nucleus.

concepts.name: Ionizing radiation
concepts.statement: Ionizing radiation is radiation, whether nuclear in origin or not, that ionizes the material that absorbs it. Nuclear decays emit from a few keV to more than 10 MeV per event, while it takes only a few eV to ionize an atom, so the radiation damages tissue and electronics and can be detected.

concepts.name: Range of radiation
concepts.statement: The range of radiation is the distance it travels through a material. Higher energy gives a greater range, a material dense in electrons gives a smaller one, and at the same energy alphas stop first, betas go farther and gammas farthest, because a greater charge and a lower speed make a particle ionize more readily.

concepts.name: Nuclear radiation
concepts.statement: Nuclear radiation is the rays that originate in the nuclei of atoms, the first examples of which were discovered by Becquerel.

concepts.name: Radioactive
concepts.statement: A substance or object is radioactive when it emits nuclear radiation.

concepts.name: Alpha rays
concepts.statement: Alpha rays are the kind of nuclear radiation bent by a magnetic field as positive charges, later found to be helium nuclei.

concepts.name: Beta rays
concepts.statement: Beta rays are the kind of nuclear radiation bent by a magnetic field opposite to alpha rays, later found to be electrons created at the instant of decay.

concepts.name: Counting ion pairs
concepts.statement: The number of ion pairs a particle can create is the energy it deposits divided by the energy needed to create each pair, which connects the MeV energies of nuclear radiation to the tens of eV of an ionization.

concepts.name: Detection by ionization
concepts.statement: Ionizing radiation cannot be sensed directly, and every radiation detector, from photographic film to a semiconductor, turns the ionization or excitation that radiation produces into something that can be seen or measured.

concepts.name: Geiger tube
concepts.statement: In a Geiger tube a voltage between a cylinder and a wire along its axis sweeps up the ion pairs that radiation creates in the gas, and the counter records the brief current as a count. A count does not give the energy, charge or type of the radiation.

concepts.name: Scintillators and photomultipliers
concepts.statement: A second family of detectors records light instead of charge. A scintillator converts the energy of radiation into brief flashes of light, and a photomultiplier multiplies the photoelectrons from each flash at a series of dynodes into a measurable current proportional to the energy deposited. Because the output is proportional, these detectors can tell energy, charge and type as a Geiger tube cannot.

concepts.name: Solid-state detector
concepts.statement: A semiconductor built to conduct only when ionization frees charge in it acts like a solid Geiger tube, and because it is solid it stops radiation in a short distance and misses few particles. The current is closely related to the energy deposited, so these detectors give sophisticated information as scintillators do.

concepts.name: Radiation detector
concepts.statement: A radiation detector is a device that detects and tracks the radiation from radioactive decay, directly or indirectly through the ionization it creates.

concepts.name: Scintillator
concepts.statement: A scintillator is a radiation detector that records the light produced when radiation interacts with its material.

concepts.name: Photomultiplier
concepts.statement: A photomultiplier is a device that converts light into an electrical signal by multiplying the photoelectrons a flash produces.

concepts.name: Nucleons
concepts.statement: Nucleons are the particles found inside nuclei, the positive proton and the neutral neutron, with nearly the same mass and both far heavier than an electron.

concepts.name: Unified atomic mass unit
concepts.statement: The unified atomic mass unit is defined so that a neutral $^{12}$C atom has a mass of exactly 12 u, and $1\;\text{u} = 1.6605 \times 10^{-27}$ kg $= 931.5$ MeV/$c^{2}$. A mass in MeV/$c^{2}$ becomes an energy in MeV when multiplied by $c^{2}$.

concepts.name: Writing a nuclide
concepts.statement: A nuclide is written ${}^{A}_{Z}\text{X}_{N}$, with the mass number $A$ above, the atomic number $Z$ below, the element symbol, and the neutron number $N$ after it, and with $A = N + Z$ any one of these can be found from the others.

concepts.name: Isotopes
concepts.statement: Isotopes are nuclei with the same $Z$ and different $N$, such as hydrogen, deuterium and tritium. Their chemistry follows $Z$, while their mass and stability follow the whole nucleus.

concepts.name: Nuclear radius
concepts.statement: The radius of a nucleus is $r = r_0 A^{1/3}$ with $r_0 = 1.2$ fm, so its volume is proportional to the number of nucleons $A$. This is what happens if nucleons are packed so closely that there is no empty space between them.

concepts.name: Finding nuclear density
concepts.statement: The density of nuclear matter is found from $r = r_0 A^{1/3}$ and a mass of $A$ u; every nucleus has about the same density, about $2 \times 10^{14}$ times that of water.

concepts.name: Strong and weak nuclear forces
concepts.statement: Two forces act in the nucleus beside the Coulomb force: the strong nuclear force, about 100 times more attractive than the electromagnetic repulsion between protons but falling to zero within a few fm, and the weak nuclear force. Their strength is why nuclear decay energies are so large.

concepts.name: Chart of the nuclides
concepts.statement: The chart of the nuclides plots every known nuclide by $N$ against $Z$. Stable nuclei lie near $N = Z$ for light nuclei and with progressively more neutrons than protons for heavier ones, and nuclei off this band decay toward it.

concepts.name: Magic numbers
concepts.statement: Nuclei with certain numbers of protons or neutrons, the magic numbers, are unusually stable, which means the nucleus has shells as the atom does and closed shells are more stable.

concepts.name: Nucleus
concepts.statement: The nucleus is the region at the center of an atom, consisting of protons and neutrons.

concepts.name: Neutron
concepts.statement: A neutron is a neutral particle found in the nucleus, with nearly the same mass as a proton.

concepts.name: Nuclide
concepts.statement: A nuclide is a type of atom whose nucleus has specific numbers of protons and neutrons.

concepts.name: Mass number
concepts.statement: The mass number $A$ is the number of nucleons in a nucleus, the sum of its neutron number $N$ and its atomic number $Z$.

concepts.name: Neutron number
concepts.statement: The neutron number $N$ is the number of neutrons in a nucleus.

concepts.name: Atomic mass
concepts.statement: The atomic mass is the total mass of the protons, neutrons and electrons in a single atom.

concepts.name: Parent and daughter nuclides
concepts.statement: A decay turns a parent nuclide into a daughter, and a daughter may itself be unstable, so some parents start a whole series of decays that ends only at a stable nuclide, as the $^{238}$U series ends at $^{206}$Pb.

concepts.name: Writing an alpha decay equation
concepts.statement: An $\alpha$ decay equation is written by removing a $^{4}$He nucleus from the parent, ${}^{A}_{Z}\text{X}_{N} \to {}^{A-4}_{Z-2}\text{Y}_{N-2} + {}^{4}_{2}\text{He}_{2}$: the daughter is the element two places lower in the periodic table, with a mass number four smaller.

concepts.name: Energy of a nuclear reaction
concepts.statement: The energy released in a nuclear reaction comes from the mass destroyed in it, $E = (\Delta m)c^{2}$. When the products have less total mass than the parent, the reaction releases energy and can happen spontaneously; when they have more, it needs an input of energy.

concepts.name: Finding a decay energy
concepts.statement: A decay energy is found from the atomic masses in the tables, which are those of neutral atoms, so the electrons must be counted. In $\alpha$ and $\beta^{-}$ decay they balance and the atomic masses can be subtracted directly; in $\beta^{+}$ decay two electron masses must also be subtracted.

concepts.name: Beta minus decay and the neutrino
concepts.statement: In $\beta^{-}$ decay a neutron in the nucleus becomes a proton, and the nucleus creates and emits an electron and an electron’s antineutrino, ${}^{A}_{Z}\text{X}_{N} \to {}^{A}_{Z+1}\text{Y}_{N-1} + \beta^{-} + \bar{\nu}_{e}$. Without the antineutrino, energy, linear momentum and angular momentum would not be conserved.

concepts.name: Beta plus decay and electron capture
concepts.statement: Nuclei with too many protons for stability lower $Z$ by one, either by emitting a positron and an electron’s neutrino, ${}^{A}_{Z}\text{X}_{N} \to {}^{A}_{Z-1}\text{Y}_{N+1} + \beta^{+} + \nu_{e}$, or by capturing one of their own inner electrons. The two have the same effect on the nucleus.

concepts.name: Conservation of electron family number
terms: conservation of total electron family number
concepts.statement: The total number of members of the electron family is constant: electrons and electron’s neutrinos count $+1$ and their antimatter partners count $-1$, so an electron can never be created without an antimatter family member.

concepts.name: Conservation of nucleon number
concepts.statement: In every decay the total number of nucleons $A$ is the same before and after, even when protons turn into neutrons or the reverse, and the total charge is conserved as always.

concepts.name: Gamma decay
concepts.statement: In $\gamma$ decay a nucleus left in an excited state falls to lower levels by emitting photons, as an excited atom does, but with MeV energies. $\gamma$ decay does not change the nuclide.

concepts.name: Parent
concepts.statement: The parent is the original nucleus before a decay.

concepts.name: Daughter
concepts.statement: The daughter is the nucleus produced when a parent nucleus decays.

concepts.name: Decay
concepts.statement: Decay is the process by which the nucleus of an unstable atom loses mass and energy by emitting radiation.

concepts.name: Alpha decay
concepts.statement: Alpha decay is the type of radioactive decay in which a nucleus emits an alpha particle, a $^{4}$He nucleus.

concepts.name: Beta decay
concepts.statement: Beta decay is the type of radioactive decay in which a nucleus emits a beta particle, an electron or a positron.

concepts.name: Positron
concepts.statement: The positron, or antielectron, is the antiparticle of the electron, with the electron’s mass and a positive charge; it is emitted in positive beta decay.

concepts.name: Positron decay
concepts.statement: Positron decay is the type of beta decay in which a proton in the nucleus is converted to a neutron, releasing a positron and an electron’s neutrino.

concepts.name: Neutrino
concepts.statement: A neutrino is an electrically neutral, weakly interacting elementary particle.

concepts.name: Electron neutrino
concepts.statement: The electron’s neutrino is the neutrino of the electron family, an elementary particle with no net electric charge.

concepts.name: Electron antineutrino
concepts.statement: The electron’s antineutrino is the antiparticle of the electron’s neutrino.

concepts.name: Antimatter
concepts.statement: Antimatter is matter composed of antiparticles, each with the same mass as its partner and the opposite charge.

concepts.name: Decay series
concepts.statement: A decay series is a chain of decays in which each daughter is itself unstable and decays in turn, until a stable nuclide is produced.

concepts.name: Electron capture
concepts.statement: Electron capture is the process in which a proton-rich nuclide absorbs one of its own inner atomic electrons and emits an electron’s neutrino, ${}^{A}_{Z}\text{X}_{N} + e^{-} \to {}^{A}_{Z-1}\text{Y}_{N+1} + \nu_{e}$.

concepts.name: Half-life
concepts.statement: The half-life $t_{1/2}$ is the time in which each nucleus has a 50% chance of decaying, whatever its history. A large sample falls to half in one half-life, to a quarter in the next, and so on.

concepts.name: Radioactive decay law
concepts.statement: The number of radioactive nuclei left at any time is $N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$, an exponential decay that halves in each half-life.

concepts.name: Decay constant
concepts.statement: The decay constant $\lambda$ sets how fast the exponential decay falls, and it is related to the half-life by $\lambda = 0.693/t_{1/2}$: the shorter the half-life, the larger $\lambda$.

concepts.name: Dating an object
concepts.statement: An age is found from the fraction $N/N_0$ of a radioactive nuclide left in an object and its half-life, given the starting abundance. Carbon-14 dating reaches back 50 or 60 thousand years, and $^{238}$U dating billions of years.

concepts.name: Activity
concepts.statement: The activity $R = \Delta N/\Delta t$ of a source is its rate of decay, the number of decays per unit time, measured in becquerels or curies.

concepts.name: Activity of a source
concepts.statement: The activity of a source grows with the number of radioactive nuclei and falls with their half-life, $R = 0.693N/t_{1/2}$.

concepts.name: Exponential decay of activity
concepts.statement: Since activity is proportional to the number of radioactive nuclei, it falls exponentially along with them, $R = R_0 e^{-\lambda t}$, by half in each half-life.

concepts.name: Becquerel
concepts.statement: The becquerel is the SI unit of activity, one decay per second.

concepts.name: Curie
concepts.statement: The curie is a unit of activity equal to the activity of 1 g of $^{226}$Ra, $3.70 \times 10^{10}$ Bq.

concepts.name: Radioactive dating
concepts.statement: Radioactive dating is the use of radioactive decay to determine the age of a material from the amount of a radioactive nuclide left in it.

concepts.name: Carbon-14 dating
concepts.statement: Carbon-14 dating is a radioactive dating technique based on the decay of carbon-14, whose abundance in living tissue is fixed until the organism dies.

concepts.name: Binding energy
concepts.statement: The binding energy of a nucleus is the energy required to completely disassemble it into separate protons and neutrons. The more tightly a nucleus is bound, the larger its binding energy.

concepts.name: Mass defect
concepts.statement: Pulling a nucleus apart puts energy in, and that energy appears as extra rest mass of the separated pieces. So a nucleus has less mass than its protons and neutrons would have apart, by $\text{BE}/c^{2}$. This is why the products of a spontaneous decay have less mass than the parent.

concepts.name: Calculating binding energy
concepts.statement: The binding energy of a nucleus is found from atomic masses as $\text{BE} = \{[Zm({}^{1}\text{H}) + Nm_{\text{n}}] - m({}^{A}\text{X})\}c^{2}$, and dividing by $A$ gives the binding energy per nucleon.

concepts.name: Binding energy per nucleon curve
concepts.statement: The binding energy per nucleon averages about 8 MeV, rises steeply for light nuclei, peaks near $A = 60$ and falls slowly for heavy ones, with spikes at especially tightly bound nuclei such as $^{4}$He. The larger BE/$A$, the more stable the nucleus.

concepts.name: Binding energy per nucleon of heavy nuclei
concepts.statement: The nuclear force is strong but short ranged, so beyond about $A = 60$ a new nucleon feels only its neighbors, while the Coulomb repulsion reaches every proton. Repulsion grows as nuclei get heavier and nuclear attraction does not, so BE/$A$ falls, and heavy stable nuclei carry extra neutrons.

concepts.name: Binding energy per nucleon
concepts.statement: The binding energy per nucleon is the binding energy of a nucleus divided by its number of nucleons; it reveals the details of the nuclear force, and the larger it is, the more stable the nucleus.

concepts.name: Particle bound in a potential well
concepts.statement: Nucleons are bound in the nucleus as a marble sits in a bowl: they move about but lack the energy to get over the rim, and outside the rim the Coulomb repulsion would push an $\alpha$ away. Classically such a particle stays trapped forever.

concepts.name: Tunneling
concepts.statement: A quantum particle's wave function does not stop at a barrier but decreases exponentially inside it, so a small part of it reaches the other side, and the particle has a small probability of being found there. It goes from one side to the other without ever being in between. The thinner the barrier, the greater the chance, which is why tunneling is negligible for anything classical.

concepts.name: Alpha decay by tunneling
concepts.statement: An $\alpha$ particle escapes the nucleus by tunneling through the barrier. A more energetic $\alpha$ meets a thinner barrier and escapes more readily, so its half-life is shorter, across 17 orders of magnitude.

concepts.name: Scanning tunneling microscope
concepts.statement: Electrons can tunnel across a thin gap between two objects, and because the probability is extremely sensitive to the thickness, the current between a probe and a surface in a scanning tunneling microscope reveals surface features as small as single atoms.

concepts.name: Atom
concepts.statement: An atom is the smallest unit of an element, a positively charged nucleus surrounded by negatively charged electrons. Atoms can be subdivided, but they lose their identity in the process, and they combine to form molecules, the smallest units of compounds.

concepts.name: Brownian motion
concepts.statement: Brownian motion is the continuous random movement of a visible particle suspended in a fluid, struck unevenly by the invisible molecules around it. It was the first direct evidence that atoms and molecules exist.

concepts.name: Size of atoms
concepts.statement: Einstein’s theory of Brownian motion, with Perrin’s measurements, gives atoms a size of about $10^{-10}$ m. Knowing the size of an atom gives Avogadro’s number, since it tells how many atoms fit into a certain volume.

concepts.name: Cathode rays
concepts.statement: In a gas discharge tube, electrons freed from the gas accelerate from the cathode to the anode, and a magnet bends their path in the direction expected for a negative charge, so cathode rays are streams of electrons.

concepts.name: Electron charge-to-mass ratio
concepts.statement: Thomson measured the ratio of the electron’s charge to its mass, $\kqe/m_{\text{e}} = \ka/\kEf = -1.76 \times 10^{11}$ C/kg, using crossed electric and magnetic fields. The ratio is about a thousand times the charge per kilogram needed to plate a material, so the electron has a very small mass.

concepts.name: Millikan oil drop experiment
concepts.statement: Millikan measured the charge of the electron directly by holding a charged drop of oil still between two plates, where the electric force balances its weight. Every charge he found was a multiple of one basic charge.

concepts.name: Electron mass
concepts.statement: The charge from Millikan and the ratio from Thomson give the mass of the electron, $m_{\text{e}} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}$ kg, the smallest of any particle that has mass. The proton is about 1836 times heavier and carries nearly all the mass of a hydrogen atom.

concepts.name: Identical electrons
concepts.statement: Every electron has exactly the same charge and mass; the values are not averages over many electrons. This kind of fact has no counterpart among the grains of sand or the planets of everyday physics.

concepts.name: Rutherford scattering
concepts.statement: In Rutherford’s gold foil experiment most alpha particles went straight through the foil, but a few came almost straight back, which only a very small, very massive, positively charged center could do. The nucleus is about $10^{-15}$ m across, 100,000 times smaller than the atom.

concepts.name: Planetary model of the atom
concepts.statement: In the planetary model of the atom, low-mass electrons orbit a small, massive nucleus at distances large compared with its size, held by the Coulomb force as the planets are held by gravity.

concepts.name: Cathode-ray tube
concepts.statement: A cathode-ray tube is a vacuum tube containing a source of electrons and a screen on which their beam makes a visible spot.

concepts.name: Discrete atomic spectra
concepts.statement: An atom emits and absorbs only certain wavelengths, and each element has its own set. The lines are the atom’s fingerprint, and their discreteness means that the atom’s energies are quantized.

concepts.name: Hydrogen spectrum wavelengths
concepts.statement: Every line of hydrogen’s spectrum is given by $1/\lambda = R(1/n_{\text{f}}^2 - 1/n_{\text{i}}^2)$. Each series ends on one level: $n_{\text{f}} = 1$ for the Lyman series in the ultraviolet, 2 for the Balmer series that reaches into the visible, and 3 for the Paschen series in the infrared. The formula was found to fit the data before Bohr’s theory derived it.

concepts.name: Bohr transition energy
concepts.statement: Bohr proposed that the orbits of an atom are quantized and that an electron moves between them by absorbing or emitting a photon whose energy is exactly the difference between the two orbital energies, $\Delta E = hf = E_{\text{i}} - E_{\text{f}}$. A quantized set of orbits gives a quantized set of photons, which is a discrete spectrum.

concepts.name: Reading an energy-level diagram
concepts.statement: An energy-level diagram is read and drawn by plotting the allowed energies of a system vertically, the ground state at the bottom, and drawing each transition as an arrow between two levels.

concepts.name: Bohr’s quantized angular momentum
concepts.statement: Bohr assumed that the angular momentum of an electron in its orbit can take only whole multiples of $h/2\pi$, $L = m_{\text{e}}vr_n = nh/2\pi$. With this rule and the physics of circular motion he calculated the spectrum of hydrogen.

concepts.name: Bohr orbit radii
concepts.statement: Setting the Coulomb force equal to the centripetal force, with the speed from the quantized angular momentum, gives the radius of every allowed orbit of a hydrogen-like atom, $r_n = (n^2/Z)a_{\text{B}}$. The radii grow as $n^2$, and the smallest, the Bohr radius, agrees with the measured size of hydrogen.

concepts.name: Energies of hydrogen-like atoms
concepts.statement: The orbital energy is the sum of the electron's kinetic energy and its negative electric potential energy, and with Bohr's radii it comes out as $-13.6$ eV divided by $n^2$ for hydrogen. The energies are negative because the electron is bound, they crowd together toward zero as $n$ grows, and their differences reproduce every line of the spectrum. The same formula, with $Z^2$, serves any atom stripped to one electron.

concepts.name: Finding an ionization energy
concepts.statement: The energy needed to ionize an atom from level $n$ is the size of $E_n$, since an electron at zero energy is free: 13.6 eV from the ground state of hydrogen, less from an excited state. Any energy beyond that goes into the freed electron’s kinetic energy.

concepts.name: Limits of Bohr’s theory
concepts.statement: Bohr’s theory explains the spectrum and the size of hydrogen and shows that orbital energies and angular momentum are quantized. But its orbits are semiclassical, quantized yet imagined as circles, and it cannot treat an atom with two electrons or explain doublets.

concepts.name: Rydberg constant
concepts.statement: The Rydberg constant, $R = 1.097 \times 10^{7}$ m⁻¹, is the measured constant that sets the scale of the wavelengths of hydrogen’s spectrum.

concepts.name: Energy-level diagram
concepts.statement: An energy-level diagram is a diagram of the allowed energies of the electrons of an atom, or of any system, drawn as horizontal lines one above another.

concepts.name: Bohr radius
